It is also made clear that Isaac was sixty years old when they were born.

Here the narrator of Genesis is speaking, recounting the birth of Isaac and Rebekah's children. Earlier, God had told Rebekah that two nations were in her womb. The name Jacob foreshadows the struggle between the brothers, which will mark their whole story.

For today: God can work through imperfect people from the very beginning of their story. If you struggle with your own flaws, do not lose heart; trust that God is shaping you with patience and grace.
exp.25:0:
It says there was hunger in the region where Isaac lived, and that this was a different famine from the one his father Abraham had gone through years before. That is why Isaac went to Gerar, where Abimelech, king of the Philistines, ruled. "Went" is the plain word here, and "Abimelech" is the same name spelled in the usual modern way.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks. He presents Isaac's situation right after God confirmed his family as the heir of the promise. The next verse shows that God appears to him and tells him not to go down to Egypt, but to stay in the land. So Isaac is in a crisis and about to decide where to go. The text does not say whether he was planning to go to Egypt, only that God spoke to him.

For today: when times of scarcity come, before you decide out of fear, stop and seek God's guidance. He can give you direction and remind you that he still keeps his promises.
exp.25:8:
Abimelech calls Isaac in and confronts him: when he saw how they were treating each other, he realized that Rebekah was his wife and not his sister. He asks him why he said otherwise. Isaac answers honestly: he did it out of fear that he would die because of her.

The speaker is Abimelech, king of the Philistines in Gerar. Isaac had settled there during a time of famine. Out of fear, and because Rebekah was beautiful, he said she was his sister. It was a half-truth, since it hid the fact that she was his wife. His father Abraham had done something similar before. Abimelech is concerned because someone might have sinned without knowing it.

Today, fear can lead us to hide the truth and to trust our own plans more than God. When we feel afraid, let us ask him for courage to be honest and to rest in his care.
exp.25:17:
Isaac dug again the wells that his father Abraham had dug. The Philistines had stopped them up with earth after Abraham died. To "stop" a well means to block it or fill it in. Isaac also gave them the same names that Abraham had given them.

Here the narrator of Genesis is speaking. Isaac had just been sent away by Abimelech, because he had become very prosperous. In that dry land, water meant life for people and livestock. By reopening the wells, Isaac was also affirming the inheritance and the promises that God had given to his father.

For today: value the good that others planted in your life, such as faith, prayer, or good habits. If they have been stopped up over time or by difficulties, you can open them again with patience and trust in God.
exp.25:26:
Isaac asks Abimelech and his companions why they have come to him, since they earlier treated him with hostility. "Hate" means that they rejected him or held ill will toward him, and "sent me away" means that they expelled him from their land.

Isaac speaks in Beersheba, after having left Gerar. Earlier, Abimelech had asked him to leave because Isaac had become very powerful (Genesis 26:16), and the herdsmen of Gerar had quarreled with his servants over the wells. Now the king arrives with his friend and his army commander. Isaac speaks frankly and lets it be seen that the wound is still there.

We can be honest about the pain others have caused us, without repaying evil with evil. Isaac asks plainly, and then listens and accepts peace. With humility, God can open doors to reconcile us.
exp.25:29:
He prepared a special meal for his visitors, and they all ate and drank together. The word "feast" here means a festive meal, made to honor the guests and mark an important moment.

The ones who spoke before are Abimelech and his companions, who had come to Isaac. Years earlier they had driven him out of their land, but now they recognized that God was with him. That is why they asked for a covenant of peace. Isaac did not respond with resentment but with hospitality. The next day they swore the agreement and departed in peace. The Bible does not say what Isaac felt, but his actions show a generous heart.

When someone who harmed us seeks peace, we can respond with kindness instead of revenge. Sharing a meal, offering a kind word, or opening the door can be a first step toward healing a relationship, trusting that God cares for us.
exp.25:31:
This verse tells us that on the very day Isaac made a peace agreement with Abimelech, his servants arrived with good news. They had been digging a well and had found water. The word "servants" here means the workers or attendants who served him, and the phrase "We have found water" is the servants' report to their master.

Here Isaac's servants speak, and they inform their master. In that dry land, water meant life for the family and the animals. There had been earlier conflicts over other wells (Genesis 26:15-22). Isaac chose peace, and now this provision arrives. The text does not say that the well is a reward for making peace, but it does show a contrast.

For today: when we seek peace and do not let ourselves be dragged into quarrels, God can give us rest and provision in his time. Keep doing good, even when you do not yet see the water.
exp.26:12:
Rebekah tells Jacob that if his plan goes wrong, the curse may fall on her. She only asks him to obey her voice, go, and bring her the young goats.

Rebekah had heard that Isaac wanted to bless Esau, and she wanted the blessing to go to Jacob. Jacob fears being discovered and receiving a curse instead of a blessing. She reassures him, but the Bible does not present this deception as an example to imitate. Later on, the family suffers the consequences.

Today we can learn not to use shortcuts or lies to reach what we believe God has promised. No one can bear the consequences of our decisions for us. Let us rather trust that God fulfills his plans by honest paths, and ask him for wisdom before we act.
exp.26:15:
Rebekah covers Jacob's hands and the smooth part of his neck with the skins of the young goats. "Neck" is the nape or back of the neck, and "smooth" refers to the hairless skin there, in contrast to the hairy skin of Esau. In this way, Jacob would feel hairy like his brother Esau.

Rebekah had heard that Isaac wanted to bless Esau. She planned for Jacob to receive that blessing and prepared a deception, because Isaac was already old and could not see well. Although God had said earlier that the older would serve the younger (Genesis 25:23), the account does not approve of the deception. It shows how a divided family falls into trickery and pain.

For today: when we believe God has promised something, we do not need to hurry it along with lies or manipulation. Trusting God includes waiting and acting with honesty, even when the path seems slow or difficult.
exp.26:18:
Jacob speaks to his father Isaac, who is now old and blind. He pretends to be Esau, saying that he is the firstborn and that he has done what his father asked. He invites him to sit up and eat the game so that he may bless him.

Rebekah, the mother, planned this deception so that Jacob would receive the blessing that belonged to Esau. Here Jacob tells a direct lie. The Bible records the event without approving it, and then shows the painful consequences for the family. God had said earlier that the younger would serve the older, but that does not make the lie right.

For today: there is no need to deceive in order to obtain what God promises. Trusting Him means waiting and acting with honesty, even when it seems that the opposite would be to our advantage.
exp.26:19:
Isaac is surprised that his son has found the game so quickly. Jacob answers that the Lord God brought it to him.

Isaac, now old and almost blind, wants to bless Esau, his firstborn. Rebekah and Jacob have planned to deceive him so that Jacob will receive the blessing. Here Jacob lies and, even worse, uses God's name to lend strength to his lie. The Bible tells this without approving it; it shows the facts in all their harshness.

Today it reminds us that we must not use God's name to cover our lies or our own interests. God wants us to seek his promises with honesty and trust, not with deceit that harms others.
exp.26:24:
Isaac asks the person he believes is Esau to bring him the game he has hunted. He wants to eat so that his soul, meaning his whole being, may bless his son. Jacob serves him the food and also wine, and Isaac eats and drinks.

Isaac, now old and nearly blind, is getting ready to give the family blessing to his firstborn son. But the one standing before him is Jacob, who is pretending to be Esau, encouraged by his mother Rebekah. The Bible tells the story of this deception without praising it, and later shows its painful consequences.

For today: God can carry out his plans even in the middle of our failures, but that does not make lying right. If you want something good, seek it honestly, and trust that God knows how to work without tricks.
exp.26:25:
Isaac, now an old man, asks his son to come near and kiss him. A kiss was a normal gesture of affection in the family.

Isaac is the one speaking. He is blind and wants to bless Esau, his older son. But the one standing in front of him is Jacob, disguised on the advice of his mother Rebekah. Isaac is suspicious and uses touch, taste, and smell to check who it is. Here a gesture of affection becomes part of the deception.

For today: lies can hide behind gestures that seem loving. This scene invites us to be honest with those we love and to seek God's blessings without shortcuts or deceit.
exp.26:39:
He says that Esau will live by the sword, that is, by war or violence, and that he will serve his brother Jacob. But a time will come when Esau will rebel and shake off Jacob's rule. "Neck" refers to the back of the neck or the throat, and "yoke" is the heavy wooden frame placed on working animals. In this way the verse speaks of a heavy submission that will eventually be broken.

It is Isaac, the father, now old, who speaks. Jacob had received the principal blessing, though by deception, and Esau weeps, asking for something. This answer is more a harsh prediction than a full blessing. Many relate it to Esau's descendants, the Edomites, and their relationship with Israel, although the historical details are interpreted in various ways.

For today: resentment can come to dominate the heart, as happened with Esau. When something hurts us, let us ask God for help to forgive and not to seek revenge.
exp.27:1:
Isaac tells Jacob to get up and go to Padan-aram, to the house of Bethuel, the father of his mother Rebekah. There he is to look for a wife among the daughters of Laban, Rebekah's brother. Padan-aram was a region of Mesopotamia, where the part of Abraham's family that had stayed behind lived.

Isaac speaks as an old man, just after blessing Jacob. He forbids him to marry Canaanite women, just as Abraham had made sure Isaac would not do. It is likely that he wanted to preserve the family faith and the promise of God, which Isaac mentions next. In addition, Jacob had to flee from Esau's anger, although the text here emphasizes the reason for the marriage.

For today: important decisions, such as choosing a spouse, are best made with God's guidance and the counsel of wise people, thinking about faith and the future of the family.
exp.27:2:
Isaac asks that God Almighty bless Jacob. He asks that God make him fruitful and multiply his family, until he becomes a multitude of peoples, that is, a gathering of many nations or tribes.

Isaac speaks to his son Jacob before sending him to Padan-aram. He wants Jacob to find a wife among his relatives and not among the Canaanite women. This blessing recalls the promise God made to Abraham about a numerous descendance. Readers often see here the continuation of that promise in Jacob.

For today: we can bless and pray for those we love, trusting that God keeps his promises in his own time. A father or a mother can pray for their children before they set out on a journey or enter a new stage of life.
exp.27:5:
What it says: Esau realizes what his father Isaac had done. Isaac had blessed Jacob and sent him to Padan-aram to find a wife among his own kin. Moreover, in blessing him, Isaac had charged him not to marry a woman of the daughters of Canaan.

Context: Here the narrator of the book speaks, not a character. He tells how Esau reacts. Isaac wanted Jacob to keep the faith and the promise of Abraham, and that is why he was sending him away from the customs of Canaan. Shortly afterward Esau tries to please his father by marrying another wife (Genesis 28:8-9). The Bible does not explain all of his motives.

For today: Decisions about a spouse and about friendships shape the faith of an entire family. Before deciding, ask God for direction and listen to the wise counsel of those who love you and walk with Him.
exp.27:9:
This verse tells that Jacob left Beersheba, in the south of Canaan, and set out on the road toward Haran, a distant city in the north. The comment about the old spelling does not apply to the wording you see, so it has been omitted. It is a transitional verse: Jacob begins a long journey.

The narrator is Moses, according to tradition. Jacob leaves because his brother Esau was very angry with him, and also because Isaac sent him to find a wife among the family of his mother Rebekah, and not among the Canaanite women. Soon after, on this same road, Jacob will have the dream of the ladder.

For today: sometimes we are called to leave what is familiar, because of conflict or difficult decisions, without having everything clear. Jacob did not know everything that lay ahead, but God met him on the way. Take the next step in faith, and remember that God accompanies you also on uncertain journeys.
exp.27:13:
God promises Jacob a descendance too numerous to count, as the dust of the earth. He tells him that he will spread out in every direction: west, east, north and south. He adds that through Jacob and his seed, that is, his descendants, all the families of the earth would be blessed.

Jacob was fleeing from his brother Esau and was sleeping on the road, alone and afraid. In a dream, the LORD himself speaks to him and renews the promise he had earlier given to Abraham and Isaac. God does not wait for Jacob to earn it; he gives it out of pure grace. Many Christians see in the blessing for "all the families" a foreshadowing of Christ, a descendant of Jacob.

God can work in your moments of loneliness and uncertainty. Your plans may be broken, but his promises still stand. Trust that he is present, even if you do not yet notice it.
exp.27:15:
Jacob wakes from his sleep and realizes something he did not expect: God was present in that place. The verse uses "the Lord" for God here. Jacob admits that he had not realized God was there.

Jacob was running from his brother Esau and sleeping out in the open, with a stone for a pillow. In the dream, God repeated to him the promises made to Abraham: land, descendants, and blessing for all peoples. He promised to be with him and watch over him. When he wakes, Jacob speaks with awe and reverence.

For today: God can be near even in moments of fear, loneliness, or uncertainty, even when we do not notice. Today you can pause for a moment and pray: "Lord, help me see your presence here, in my everyday life."
exp.28:2:
This verse describes the custom of that place. All the flocks would gather there beside the well. The shepherds would roll the large stone off the mouth of the well, water the sheep (to "water" means giving them water to drink), and then put the stone back in its place.

The one speaking is the narrator, who explains how that well worked. Jacob is fleeing from his brother Esau and seeks his mother's family in Haran. This detail sets up the next scene: Jacob will speak with the shepherds, and Rachel will soon arrive. The text does not say why the flocks were expected to gather together; some think it was to look after the water or to move the heavy stone together.

For today: there are blessings that are received best in community and with order. Let us learn to wait and to cooperate, trusting that God is also at work in everyday life.
exp.28:7:
The shepherds tell Jacob that they cannot water the sheep yet. First all the flocks must be gathered together, and only then do they roll the stone away from the mouth of the well. "Water" here means giving the animals something to drink.

Jacob has just arrived in Haran, looking for his family. He asks some shepherds about Laban, and suggests that they water the sheep and keep grazing them, since it is still daytime. They answer with the custom of the place: wait for everyone before moving the stone. The text does not explain why, but it seems to be a rule for sharing the water in an orderly way. Right after this, Rachel arrives.

For today: before you skip over the agreements of a group, try to understand why they exist. And when you have the strength and an opportunity to serve, as Jacob did, do it with generosity.
exp.28:12:
When Laban heard the news about Jacob, his sister's son, he ran out to meet him. He embraced him, kissed him, and brought him into his house. Then Jacob told Laban everything that had happened to him.

The narrator tells this meeting after Rachel ran to tell her father. Jacob was fleeing from his brother Esau and was seeking his mother's family. Laban welcomes him warmly, although later we will see that he also had interests of his own. The Bible here shows only the welcome, without explaining his motives.

A sincere welcome can bring great relief to someone who arrives tired or afraid. Today we can open the door, listen with patience, and give a place to someone who needs it. And if someone receives us this way, we can thank them with humility.
exp.28:15:
This verse introduces the two daughters of Laban: Leah, the older, and Rachel, the younger. It is a simple detail, but it prepares what comes after. The word "older" means the one who is of greater age, and "younger" the one who is newer in age.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Jacob has already arrived at the house of his uncle Laban, fleeing from his brother Esau, and he has been living there for a month. Laban asks him how much he wants to earn for his work. Before the account of Jacob's answer, the story introduces the two daughters, because what follows will depend on them. The Bible does not explain here all the reasons behind each person's actions.

For today: God works within complicated family stories and with imperfect people. If your family or your situation is not ideal, trust that God can work in the midst of them.
exp.28:19:
This verse says that Jacob worked seven years in order to marry Rachel. Those years seemed to him "a few days" because he loved her. The word "served" means that he worked for Laban, and the original's "seemed" simply means that they seemed to him to be a few days.

The account is told by the narrator of Genesis. Jacob had arrived at the home of his uncle Laban and fell in love with Rachel, the younger daughter. Since he had no bride-price to offer, he proposed to work seven years in exchange for her, and Laban agreed. In that time, serving in this way was a known way of paying for a marriage.

For today: true love makes sacrifice lighter. When we serve God and people with love, the effort and the waiting weigh less. Ask God to renew your love for what He has entrusted to you.
exp.29:13:
Genesis 30:14 tells how Reuben, Leah's eldest son, went out into the field at the time of the wheat harvest and found mandrakes. In that period these plants were associated with fertility. He brought them to his mother.

Rachel, Jacob's beloved wife, could not have children and lived in pain. Leah already had several children, but she suffered from feeling less loved. The two women were competing for Jacob's affection. That is why Rachel asks for the mandrakes, hoping for a solution. The text does not say that the plants worked.

Today, when something hurts us, it is easy to look for quick fixes or to compete with others. The story invites us to bring our longings to God, who is the giver of life, and not to depend on human remedies.
exp.29:14:
Leah says to her sister Rachel with sorrow: "Is it a small matter that you have taken my husband, and now you want my son's mandrakes too?" Rachel proposes a deal: Jacob will sleep with Leah that night in exchange for the mandrakes. Mandrakes were a plant that in that time was associated with fertility, though it is not known for certain whether they actually worked.

Leah and Rachel were sisters, both wives of Jacob, and they lived in a painful rivalry. Rachel was loved but had no children; Leah had children but felt less loved. That is why the two of them argue and bargain, trying to resolve their pain by their own means.

For today: when we compare ourselves with others, envy leads us to haggle and to wound those closest to us. Better to bring our lacks to God, who, as we see later, listened to Leah.
exp.29:15:
Leah goes out to meet Jacob as he comes in from the field in the evening. She tells him that he must come in to her, because she has hired him, that is, engaged or paid for his company, with her son's mandrakes. Mandrakes were plants that at that time were believed to have power to promote fertility. Jacob agrees, and he spends the night with her.

The speaker is Leah, the less loved wife. Rachel, her sister, longed for children and asked for the mandrakes in exchange for a night with Jacob. It was a family marked by rivalry and by human attempts to win affection or solve problems. Afterward, the text says that God heard Leah.

For today: when you feel competition, lack, or pain, avoid manipulating others or bargaining for affection. Bring your need to God, who sees and hears, even when our decisions are clumsy.
exp.29:30:
Laban asks Jacob what he should pay him, and Jacob replies that he does not want to receive anything up front. He only asks that Laban accept a proposal, and in return he will go on tending Laban's flocks.

Jacob has worked for his father-in-law Laban for years, and Laban has grown very prosperous. Now Jacob wants to build his own property for his family. The proposal that follows is that he ask, as his wages, the spotted and dark-colored animals, which were the minority, so that everything would be clear and fair.

For today: when you negotiate something, be clear and honest from the very start. A transparent agreement prevents misunderstandings and protects relationships. And trust that God can bless you as you work with integrity.
exp.29:37:
Jacob set peeled rods, with their white stripes, in the gutters and watering troughs. That was where the flocks came to drink, and it was there that the animals would conceive, that is, become sexually excited while drinking.

The text is a narrative; Moses tells the story, and there is no speech. Jacob has worked for years for his father-in-law Laban and seeks to prosper, since Laban had cheated him before. Many think the method of the rods was a belief of the time and not a science. Later, Jacob will say that God saw Laban's mistreatment and blessed him (Genesis 31:9-12).

For today: do your part with diligence and wisdom, but do not put your trust in your tricks. Recognize that true provision comes from God, who cares for you even in the midst of injustice.
exp.30:3:
Jacob sends for his two wives, Rachel and Leah, asking them to meet him in the field where he is tending his flock. The words "sent" and "called" show that he wants to speak with them privately. "To the field" means the meeting takes place far from Laban's house.

The narrator tells us what Jacob is doing. He notices that Laban, his father-in-law, no longer treats him as he did before, and God has told him to return to the land of his fathers. Before deciding something so important, Jacob wants to talk it over with his family. He chooses a secluded place, probably so that Laban will not overhear, although the text does not state this clearly.

When we face an important change, it is wise to speak with the people closest to us, in a quiet place and with honesty. Seeking God's direction does not remove the need to listen to and respect our family, because great decisions affect all of us.
exp.30:13:
Rachel and Leah answer Jacob with a question: do we still have any portion or inheritance in our father's house? "Portion" is a share of the goods, and "inheritance" is what is received as heritage. They imply that the answer is no.

Jacob had told them that God commanded him to leave Laban's land and return to Canaan. Laban's daughters speak here and side with Jacob. Later they say that their father treated them as strangers and spent what had been paid for them. For this reason they support the departure and ask Jacob to obey God. Some scholars see in this a complaint about unfair treatment; the text gives no further detail.

For today: when God guides us into a difficult change, it helps to listen to family with honesty and to seek agreement. Obeying God can cost something, but he cares for those who obey him.
exp.30:17:
This verse tells us that Jacob set out with all his livestock and all his possessions, everything he had acquired during his years in Padan-aram, to return with his father Isaac to the land of Canaan.

The explanation is given by the narrator. Before this, Jacob had listened to Rachel and Leah, who told him to do what God had commanded him. After twenty years with Laban, God directed him to go back to his own land. Jacob left without telling Laban, and the text says that he kept his plans hidden from him. Some readers see prudence in this, others fear.

For today: when God calls us to change, obeying requires decision and order. We can take concrete steps, trusting that God cares for what he has placed in our hands, even when the road is hard.
exp.30:29:
Laban tells Jacob that if he left because he greatly longed for his father's house, that can be understood. But what he does not understand is why Jacob stole his gods. The word "stolen" means taken without right. The "gods" were figures or household idols, called teraphim in other passages.

Laban catches up with Jacob after he left without warning, taking his wives, children and livestock. Laban complains that he was not able to say goodbye, but he acknowledges that God warned him in a dream not to harm Jacob. Now he accuses Jacob of stealing the idols, not knowing that Rachel had taken them. Scholars discuss why she did it.

For today: before accusing someone, it is wise to speak with calm and with truth. And if we doubt our own conduct, we can ask God to show us what is in our hearts.
exp.30:31:
Jacob tells Laban that if anyone is found holding his gods, that person must not live. He also invites Laban to search in front of all their relatives and to take back whatever belongs to him. The text makes clear that Jacob did not know Rachel had stolen them. "Gods" here refers to small images or household idols.

Jacob speaks with Laban, his father-in-law, who has caught up with him to complain about his leaving in secret and about the disappearance of his idols. Jacob, certain of his own innocence, makes a very strong statement without knowing that his wife Rachel had them. Why Rachel took them, the Bible does not explain, and several ideas have been proposed.

For today: before speaking firmly or making drastic promises, it is wise to make sure we know the facts well, because our words can affect those we love.
exp.30:33:
Here Rachel takes the household idols of her father Laban and hides them in the camel's saddle, which is the pack or basket in which a load is carried on the animal. Then she sits on top of them. Laban searches the whole tent and does not find them. "Searched" here means he felt around by touch with his hands.

Laban caught up with Jacob because he accused him of stealing his gods. Jacob, not knowing that Rachel had taken them, said that whoever had them would not live. Rachel, without saying anything, hid the idols and deceived her father. The Bible recounts the event without approving or explaining it; we do not know with certainty why she took them.

For today: a secret or a small deception can put at risk those we love. It is better to live with sincerity, and to ask God to free us from clinging to any hidden "idol" in the heart.
exp.30:34:
Rachel tells her father Laban not to be angry that she cannot stand up before him, since she has her period. Laban searches for the household gods but does not find them.

Laban caught up with Jacob, who was leaving with his family without telling him, and accused him of stealing his gods. Jacob did not know that Rachel had taken them. She hid them and deceived her father. The Bible only records the event; it does not say why she took them, and interpreters give different reasons.

For today: lies and hidden things may seem to save the moment, but they put others at risk. Let us seek to live honestly before God and our family.
exp.30:52:
Laban asks that the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor be the judge between him and Jacob. Jacob promises to keep the covenant, and he swears by the one his father Isaac feared, a way of naming the God whom Isaac respected and worshiped.

Laban and Jacob had quarreled for years over distrust and deception. Now they make a covenant of peace, with a heap of stones as the witness. Laban calls on God as judge. Some believe Laban mixed his faith with other beliefs, but the text does not make this clear. Jacob, on the other hand, swears by the God of his father.

For today: when there are conflicts, let us seek peace with sincerity, knowing that God sees what no one else sees. Keeping our word is a way of honoring him.
exp.31:5:
This verse tells how the messengers Jacob had sent came back with news. They tell him that they went to Esau, and that he is already on his way to meet him, accompanied by four hundred men.

Jacob was returning to his land after many years with Laban. Long before, he had deceived Esau and fled from his anger. For that reason he sent a kind message, seeking peace. The Bible does not say what Esau's intentions were. The four hundred men could be understood as a threat or as an escort, but Jacob saw them with fear.

When we face a situation that frightens us, such as an unresolved conflict, we can do what Jacob did: take steps of humility and seek reconciliation, and then bring our fear to God in prayer, as Jacob will do in the following verses.
exp.31:8:
Jacob begins to pray. He addresses God as the God of Abraham and of Isaac, that is, the God of the family promise. Then he reminds God of what God himself had told him: that he should return to his land and to his family, and that God would deal well with him. "Kindred" means relatives, and "the Lord" is the name of God.

Jacob is speaking as he returns to Canaan after years with Laban. He learns that his brother Esau is coming to meet him, and he is afraid, because years earlier he had deceived him. That is why he prays: he does not begin by asking, but by resting on God's promise.

For today: when you are afraid, pray by remembering what God has already said in his Word. You can be honest about your fears and, at the same time, rest in the fact that God is faithful to what he has promised.
exp.31:13:
This verse lists part of the gift Jacob prepared for his brother Esau: two hundred female goats, twenty male goats, two hundred ewes, and twenty rams. A male goat is the male of the goats, and a ram is the male of the sheep. These are valuable animals, chosen with care.

Jacob is returning to his homeland and fears the meeting with Esau, whom he deceived years earlier. He has just prayed, remembering God's promise to bless him. Then, from what he owned, he sets aside a present for his brother. The text does not tell us everything that was in his heart, but it shows that he wanted to seek peace and soften the encounter.

For today: trusting God does not remove the responsibility to act. If there is a broken relationship, we can pray and also take concrete steps of humility, such as asking for forgiveness or making a generous gesture.
exp.31:15:
Jacob hands the animals over to his servants, one herd for each group. He orders them to go on ahead of him and to leave a space between one herd and the next. A herd is a group of animals.

Jacob is returning to his homeland and fears meeting his brother Esau, whom he had earlier deceived. He knows Esau is coming with four hundred men. So he prepares a large gift. By separating the herds, the gift arrives in waves and, according to many interpreters, seeks to gradually soften Esau's anger. The Bible does not state exactly what Jacob was thinking, but the context points to that purpose.

For today: when you have to repair a broken relationship, you do not need to wait until you feel ready. You can take concrete, humble, and patient steps, and at the same time place everything in God's hands in prayer, as Jacob did before this.
exp.31:18:
Jacob gives the same instruction to the second servant, the third, and all who followed the droves. Each of them was to say the same thing to Esau when they came upon him.

Jacob returns to Canaan after many years away. Years earlier he had deceived Esau and fled out of fear of his anger. Now he learns that Esau is coming with four hundred men, and he is afraid. Before meeting him, he prays to God, and then he sends gifts in waves to soften his brother's heart. The text does not say here how Esau will react; we see that later.

For today: when a broken relationship needs repair, it is wise to combine prayer with concrete and humble actions. Asking forgiveness or making a kind gesture does not guarantee the outcome, but it shows a sincere heart, and we can leave the result in God's hands.
exp.31:25:
Here the "man" asks Jacob to let him go because dawn is already coming. Jacob answers firmly that he will not let go unless he first receives a blessing.

Jacob is alone at night, about to meet his brother Esau, whom he had deceived years earlier. He wrestles with a mysterious man. The text later calls him God, and some believe he was an angel or a manifestation of God himself. Although he is wounded in the thigh, Jacob does not give up and asks for a blessing.

When you are in a difficult situation, do not run from God. Come to Him with sincerity and perseverance, asking for His help, even if the process hurts or leaves you marked.
exp.32:0:
Jacob lifts up his eyes and sees Esau coming toward him with four hundred men. Then he divides his children into groups: some with Leah, some with Rachel, and some with the two maidservants. The word "divided" means that he separated them and arranged them in order. The "maidservants" were women who served in the household and who were also mothers of some of his children.

This is a narrative, not a speech. Jacob is returning to Canaan after many years away. Long before, he had fled from Esau, who wanted to kill him because Jacob had taken his blessing. Now Jacob does not know whether his brother comes in peace or in anger, and for that reason he arranges his family with care. The Bible does not state here what Esau's intention was; the account will show it as it goes on.

For today: when you face a difficult reconciliation, pray and prepare wisely, but do not let fear paralyze you. Take prudent steps and trust that God can work in the heart of the other person.
exp.32:4:
It says Esau lifted up his eyes and saw the women and the children who were coming with Jacob. He asked, "Who are these with you?" Jacob answered that they were the children God had graciously given him, his servant.

Esau speaks, and then Jacob replies. The brothers had been separated for years, and Jacob feared that Esau might want revenge. After a reunion full of tears, Esau asks about the family. Jacob calls himself "your servant" out of humility and respect. He does not boast about his family, but presents it as a gift from God.

For today: when we talk about what we have, whether family, work, or achievements, we can do so with humility and gratitude, recognizing that every good gift comes from God and not from our own merit.
exp.32:6:
This verse tells how Leah came near with her children, and they all bowed down before Esau. After that, Joseph and Rachel came near, and they bowed down too.

Jacob is returning to his land after years away, and he fears meeting his brother Esau, whom he had deceived long before. So he presents his family in order: first the servants, then Leah, and last Rachel and Joseph, whom he loved most. Bowing was a sign of respect. Esau, instead of attacking, responds with kindness. Some think the order shows Jacob's favoritism; the text does not explain it.

For today: when a relationship is broken, seeking reconciliation with humility and respect is a good step. We do not know how the other person will respond, but God can soften hearts.
exp.32:12:
Jacob answers Esau, who has just proposed that they continue the journey together. Jacob says that the children are tender and that his sheep and cattle have young ones with them. If they are pushed too hard, even for a single day, the whole flock could die.

It is Jacob speaking, as he meets his brother Esau again after many years apart and after fearing the old offense. Esau received him with warmth. Jacob kindly declines to travel at Esau's pace and asks to move slowly. Some think it is a sincere and prudent excuse. Others believe he also wanted to keep a cautious distance. The text does not make this clear.

For today: caring for those who are most fragile means respecting their pace, even when others want to go faster. Speaking with honesty and kindness helps sustain peace.
exp.33:9:
Hamor offers Jacob's sons the chance to live alongside his people. He tells them the land is open to them: they may stay, live there, trade, and take possession of property.

Hamor, the father of Shechem and the leader of the city, speaks after Shechem dishonored Dinah, Jacob's daughter (Gen 34:2). Now he seeks to settle the matter through alliances and marriages. His offer seems generous, but it also protects the interests of his son and his city. The Bible does not present this proposal as full justice, since there is no real acknowledgment of the harm done to Dinah.

For today: Be wary of kind offers that try to cover over an injustice. Before accepting any settlement, ask yourself whether the harm is acknowledged and whether the person who was hurt is being protected.
exp.33:12:
The sons of Jacob answered Shechem and his father Hamor with deceit, and they spoke in this way because Shechem had defiled Dinah, that is, he had dishonored her and abused her. The word "deceitfully" means that they answered with lies and trickery.

Shechem had asked to marry Dinah and offered to pay whatever bride price they demanded. Dinah's brothers, especially Simeon and Levi, were filled with anger over what had happened. They hid their true intention behind words of negotiation. The text clearly states that there was deceit, and what follows shows a plan of revenge, which the Bible does not present as an example to imitate.

For today: pain and injustice are real, but answering with lies and revenge only adds more harm. When someone wounds you, seek justice honestly, ask for counsel, and surrender your anger to God before you act.
exp.33:15:
Here the sons of Jacob propose a deal to Hamor and Shechem: if all the males of the city are circumcised, they may intermarry, live together, and become one people.

The brothers of Dinah, the sons of Jacob, are speaking. Shechem had dishonored their sister, and now he asked to marry her. The brothers answer with deceit: they use circumcision, the sign of the covenant with God, as a pretext. The text shows that they did not speak sincerely. Later their true intention becomes clear, which was revenge.

For today: let us take care that our words are sincere. Using sacred things to cover an evil purpose harms others and dishonors God. Let us seek justice without deceit or violence.
exp.33:19:
This verse tells us that Hamor and his son Shechem went to the gate of the city, which was the place where the leaders gathered to deal with public matters. There they spoke with the men of the city.

After Shechem dishonored Dinah, he and his father propose an agreement to Jacob and his sons. Now they must win over their own people. What they say next emphasizes the economic advantages and does not mention what Shechem did. For this reason, some see here a self-interested persuasion.

Today we can learn to be wary of speeches that sound reasonable but hide self-interest. Before deciding, it is good to ask: is the whole truth being told? Is justice being sought, or only convenience? Let us ask God for wisdom and honesty.
exp.34:4:
The explanation says that Jacob and his family left Shechem on their way to Bethel. Along the way, God caused a great fear to fall on the neighboring cities, so no one pursued them. The word "terror" here refers to a fear sent by God, not one caused by Jacob's strength.

Here the narrator of Genesis is speaking. Shortly before, Jacob and his sons had acted violently in Shechem (chapter 34), and Jacob feared revenge from the nearby peoples. Then God told him to go up to Bethel. Jacob asked his household to put away the foreign gods and the earrings, and he buried them under an oak. After that cleansing, protection came.

For today: when God calls us to obey him, we can trust that he watches over our path. First remove whatever gets in the way of your faith, and take the next step with confidence in his protection.
exp.34:8:
This verse says that God appeared to Jacob once more, after he came back from Padan-aram, and blessed him. Padan-aram is the region of Mesopotamia where Jacob lived with the family of his uncle Laban.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Jacob was already in Bethel, the place where God had shown himself to him when he was fleeing from his brother Esau. Now that he was returning, God appeared to him again and then confirmed his new name, Israel, and repeated his promises. In this way he reminded Jacob that he was still at his side.

For today: God does not forget us on the long and difficult roads of life. If you are coming back today from a hard season, draw near to him in prayer and give him thanks, because he keeps seeking you out and blessing you.
exp.34:22:
This verse is part of a list of the twelve sons of Jacob, whom God also called Israel. Here the six sons he had with Leah are named: Reuben, the firstborn, and then Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun. "Firstborn" means the oldest son. The names are spelled in the older style, such as "Issachar," which is the same name rendered in modern spelling today.

The narrator is Moses, according to tradition, and the passage presents the family from which the people of Israel would come. The list comes right after Reuben's sin with Bilhah, a serious matter that Jacob learned of. Even so, Reuben remains in the list as a son and as the firstborn. Later, the Bible shows that he lost privileges because of that wrongdoing, and from Judah would come the royal line.

For today: God works through imperfect families and through real mistakes. Acknowledge your own failures with humility, but trust that God can fulfill his purposes even in the middle of a difficult story.
exp.34:23:
This verse is part of the list of the twelve sons of Jacob, who is also called Israel. Here the sons of Rachel, his beloved wife, are named: Joseph and Benjamin. They are the last two sons of Rachel, and the only ones she had.

The narrator is Moses, according to tradition, and no character speaks here. The text pauses to set in order the family that will give rise to the twelve tribes of Israel. It comes right after Rachel's death in giving birth to Benjamin, and after a painful scene of sin within the family.

For today: God notices every name. Even in a family that is wounded and flawed, he keeps his promises and works with patience. If your family is not perfect, do not lose heart; God can work with real people.
exp.34:25:
The verse mentions the last two sons of Jacob on this list: Gad and Asher, sons of Zilpah, Leah's maidservant. It then summarizes that these were the sons born to Jacob in Padan-aram, the region of Mesopotamia where he lived with his uncle Laban. A maidservant was a woman who served in the household and who, in that culture, could bear children for her mistress.

The narrator is speaking. Moses, according to tradition, closes a list of Jacob's twelve sons, who would become the tribes of Israel. It is worth noting that Benjamin was born near Bethlehem, not in Padan-aram; the summary is general, and it is understood that way.

Today we can see that God works faithfully even in complicated and unequal families. If your family story is not perfect, God can keep his promises through it. Trust that he is still working in what seems disordered to you.
exp.35:11:
Timna is said to have been a concubine of Eliphaz, son of Esau, and she bore him a son named Amalek. "Concubine" meant a secondary wife, with fewer legal rights than the principal wife. The text concludes by clarifying that all these descendants belong to the household of Adah, Esau's wife.

Here the speaker is not a character but the narrator of Genesis, who records the genealogy of Esau, also called Edom. The author wants to show that God fulfilled his promise to make Esau into a nation. Amalek is the ancestor of the Amalekites, who would later become enemies of Israel. Some scholars debate exactly how they relate to other peoples of the region.

For today: God pays attention to families and to their stories, even imperfect ones. Our decisions leave marks on the generations that follow, so it is wise to live with wisdom and faith.
exp.35:21:
This verse is part of a list of families. It says that Lotan had two sons, Hori and Hemam, and that Timna was his sister.

The writer of Genesis records here the family line of the Horites, the people who lived in the region of Edom before the descendants of Esau settled there. The Bible includes these records to show that God knows all peoples and to explain how they were related to one another. Nothing more is said here about Timna; some think she is the same woman who appears in other passages connected with Esau, but this is not certain.

For today: God takes notice of every person, even those whose names almost no one remembers. If you ever feel forgotten, remember that your life matters to God.
exp.35:24:
This verse says that Anah had two children: Dishon and a daughter named Aholibamah. It is part of a list of families. The word "children" here includes a son and a daughter, which is why the daughter is named as well.

Genesis 36 is a genealogy of Esau, also called Edom. No character speaks here; it is the narrator, traditionally identified with Moses, who records the lineages of the peoples neighboring Israel. Anah belonged to the people of Seir, with whom Esau's family became connected. Some scholars debate exactly how these families fit together, so it is best not to claim more than the text says.

For today: God notices every person and every name, even those that seem unimportant. Remember that you too are precious to Him, and treat others with that same respect.
exp.35:25:
This verse is part of a list of families. It says that Dishon had four sons: Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran. Dishon was a grandson of Seir, a man from the region of Edom. Do not confuse Dishon with Dishan, who appears later and is a different person with a similar name.

The text is a record of families, written in the third person. Tradition attributes it to Moses, although some scholars think others added details later. Chapter 36 details the peoples who lived in the land of Edom, where Esau, the brother of Jacob, settled. In this way, the account shows how those neighboring nations of Israel grew.

For today: God does not overlook anyone, not even people we know only by name. If He records them in His Word, He also knows you and values you. You can trust that your life matters to Him.
exp.35:26:
This verse is part of a list of families. It says that Ezer had three sons: Bilhan, Zaavan, and Akan. There are no hard words here; they are just ancient names. Ezer was a descendant of Seir, the ancestor of the Horites, a people who lived in the region of Edom.

The narrator, whom tradition identifies with Moses, records the family lines of Esau and of the peoples who lived in his territory. In this way he shows how Edom, a neighbor of Israel, came to be. Some names in other biblical lists are spelled a little differently, and it is not always known why.

For today: God pays attention to each person, even to names that almost no one remembers. If He preserves them in His Word, you matter to Him too. Today you can treat with respect those who go unnoticed.
exp.35:35:
This verse says that Hadad, king of Edom, died, and that Samlah, a man from Masrekah, began to reign in his place. Masrekah was probably a place or region in Edom, although it is not known with certainty where it was. The word "reigned" means that he took over the government.

Genesis 36 is a list of the descendants of Esau, also called Edom, and of the kings who ruled that land. The text tells it as a narrator, without any speech. Note that these kings were not passed down from father to son: each one comes from a different place. The list shows that God kept his promise that Esau would also form a nation.

For today: all human power passes away, and every leader dies and is replaced. We can serve with humility in whatever task falls to us, and trust in God, whose kingdom never ends.
exp.36:4:
This verse says that Joseph dreamed a dream and told it to his brothers. They already hated him, and they hated him even more.

Here the narrator of Genesis is speaking. Joseph was about seventeen years old, and his father Jacob (also called Israel) treated him with favoritism, even making him a special coat. His brothers already felt envy and resentment. When he told them the dream, which suggested that they would bow down to him, the tension grew. The Bible does not say what Joseph intended in telling it; some see it as naivety and others as a lack of good sense.

For today: when God gives us something, whether a gift or a hope, it is wise to share it with humility and wisdom, thinking about how it will affect those who hear us. And if there is envy in the heart, we need to bring it to God before it grows.
exp.36:6:
Here Joseph tells his brothers a dream. They were tying bundles of grain in the field, and suddenly his bundle rose up and stood upright, while their bundles gathered around it and bowed down before his.

Joseph, a young man of about seventeen, speaks with his older brothers, who already hated him because their father Jacob favored him. They understood the dream as a claim to rule over them. We do not know for certain whether Joseph told it innocently or with pride; the text does not make this clear. Later, in Egypt, the dream comes true.

For today: when God shows you something good for your life, be humble in sharing it. Let your words serve others and not wound them, and trust that God fulfills his plans in his own time.
exp.36:13:
Here Jacob (also called Israel) asks his son Joseph to go and see how his brothers and the flocks are doing, and to come back with word. He sends him out from the vale of Hebron, and Joseph comes to Shechem.

Jacob speaks as an anxious father. His sons were far away, tending the flocks, and he wanted to know whether all was well. Joseph obeys willingly, answering his father readily. This journey will be the beginning of his separation from the family, though no one knew it yet. The story shows how God can work through events that seem ordinary.

For today: when a simple task comes to you, do it faithfully. We do not know where it may lead us, but God does, and He can use our obedience on paths we cannot yet see.
exp.36:16:
A man whom Joseph met in the field tells him that his brothers have already left that place. He heard them say they were going to Dothan, so Joseph followed after them and found them there.

The speaker is an unknown man; the text does not say who he was. Jacob had sent Joseph to see how his brothers and the flocks were doing. Joseph looked for them in Shechem, but they were no longer there. This man, without knowing it, guides him toward them. What follows shows that the brothers, filled with envy, were planning to harm him.

For today: Joseph obeyed his father and kept searching even though the path changed. Many times God guides us through ordinary people and small details. We can remain faithful in what is ours to do, trusting that God works even when we cannot see the whole picture.
exp.36:24:
They sat down to eat after throwing Joseph into the empty pit, and the narrator says that when they looked up they saw a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead. Their camels were loaded with spices, balm, and myrrh, valuable goods they were taking down to Egypt. "Spices" here refers to fragrant spices or resins.

The narrator tells what happened after his brothers, full of envy, stripped Joseph and threw him into an empty pit. What is shocking is that they eat calmly while their brother suffers. The arrival of the caravan opens the way to Judah's idea of selling Joseph instead of killing him. In the Bible, the Ishmaelites are sometimes also called Midianites, and scholars explain this in several ways.

For today: do not get used to eating in peace while someone close to you suffers because of your fault or your indifference. God can work even through evil, but that does not excuse our wrongdoing.
exp.36:27:
It says that some merchants passed by the place, and Joseph was pulled out of the dry pit where his brothers had thrown him. They sold him for twenty pieces of silver, which were coins or weights of silver, and the merchants took him to Egypt. A cistern is a pit dug to store water. The Midianites and the Ishmaelites appear here almost as interchangeable names, and scholars explain this in several ways.

Joseph's brothers envied and hated him, and at first they thought about killing him. Judah proposed selling him, arguing that they would gain nothing from his death and that, after all, he was their own brother. The others agreed. Reuben was not present at that moment.

Today, the envy we keep in our hearts can grow until it leads us to hurt the very people we love. If you feel jealousy or resentment toward someone close to you, do not feed it in silence: bring it to God in prayer and seek reconciliation before it becomes a decision you regret for the rest of your life.
exp.36:28:
Reuben returned to the pit where they had thrown Joseph, but he no longer found him there. Then he tore his clothes. A "pit" was a hole used to store water, and tearing one's clothes was a way of showing very deep grief.

The speaker is the narrator of the account. Earlier, Reuben had suggested throwing Joseph into the pit, and the text implies that he meant to rescue him afterward. The Bible does not say where he was when they sold him. That is why he reacts with anguish: his plans fell apart and his brother had disappeared.

For today: good intentions are not enough. Reuben wanted to help, but he did not clearly stand against his brothers. When you must defend what is right, do it with courage and in time, without leaving it for later.
exp.36:35:
The verse says that Midianite traders sold Joseph in Egypt to a man named Potiphar. He was an official of Pharaoh, and the word used for him here can also mean a court officer or official. He was also the captain of the guard, that is, the chief of the king's guards. In the account, these traders are also called Ishmaelites, and it is not known for certain how the two names are related.

The one speaking is the narrator of Genesis. He closes the chapter with a contrast: Jacob weeps for Joseph, believing him dead, but Joseph is alive, though as a slave in a foreign country. In this way the reader sees what Jacob cannot see.

For today: when a situation seems lost, remember that we do not see everything. God may be at work in what is hidden. Trust him and keep waiting with patience.
exp.37:4:
The explanation says that Judah's wife became pregnant again and had a third son, whom she named Shelah. It also notes that Judah was in Chezib when the child was born.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks. He tells how Judah's family grew after he separated from his brothers and went to live near Canaanite people. His wife was the daughter of Shua. Chezib is mentioned as the place of birth, but it is not known for certain where it was; it could be the same as Achzib in the region of Judah. This detail prepares the story that follows, in which Shelah will be important for Tamar.

For today: God watches the small details of our families. Even when a story has dark moments, He keeps working in it. Entrust your home to Him, including what you do not understand.
exp.37:6:
This verse says that Er, Judah's oldest son, did evil things that God saw and rejected, and for that reason God took his life. "Firstborn" means the eldest son. "Was wicked in the sight of the Lord" means that his conduct was displeasing to God. The Bible does not say what his sin was, so it is better not to invent one.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks. He tells the story of Judah's family, who had married and had three sons. Er had married Tamar. His death left her a widow without children, and this leads to what follows: Judah asks Onan to fulfill the duty of raising up offspring for his brother.

For today: God sees beyond appearances, even what others do not know about us. Today you can ask him to show you something in your life that needs to change, and to respond to him with humility and without delay.
exp.37:10:
Judah tells Tamar, his daughter-in-law, to remain a widow in her father's house until his son Shelah grows up. But in truth he fears that Shelah will also die, as his brothers did. Tamar obeys and goes to live with her father.

Judah speaks as the father of Er and Onan, Tamar's two earlier husbands, who both died. According to the custom of the time, Shelah was to give Tamar a son to carry on the name of the dead man. Judah makes a promise, but he does not intend to keep it. He blames Tamar, although the text has already pointed to the wickedness of Er and Onan.

For today: when we make a promise, we should keep it or be honest about why we cannot. Avoiding the truth out of fear or convenience can hurt others, especially those who are most vulnerable.
exp.37:13:
She took off her widow's clothes, covered herself with a veil, and wrapped herself up well. Then she sat down in an open place, by the road to Timnath. The word "veil" here means covering her face with cloth. She did this because she saw that Shelah, Judah's youngest son, was now grown up, and she had not been given to him as a wife.

Here the narrator is speaking. Tamar had been widowed by two of Judah's sons, and Judah had promised her Shelah, but he did not keep his word. She was left without a son or protection. Her plan was deceptive and risky. The Bible tells the story without approving of everything she did, and Judah later admits his own wrongdoing (v. 26).

For today: when someone has failed us, let us not justify wrong with another wrong. It is better to keep our promises and seek justice with honesty and prayer.
exp.37:16:
Judah promises Tamar that he will send her a young goat from his flock as payment. She asks him for a pledge, that is, a guarantee or something of value that he leaves in her hands until he keeps his promise. The word "pledge" is the one the verse uses, so it stays as is.

Judah speaks without knowing she is his daughter-in-law, since she had covered her face. Tamar had been left a widow, and Judah had not given her his youngest son as a husband, as was expected. She acts with deception, and the Bible neither approves nor condemns every step she takes here. Her pledge would later serve as proof of the truth.

Today we can learn that promises made lightly, and decisions taken on impulse, leave traces that later come to light. Let us live with integrity, keeping what we have promised and not expecting that anyone will see us.
exp.37:22:
Judah tells his friend to let the woman keep the items he gave her as a pledge. He says this way they will avoid being put to shame. He recalls that he did his part by sending the young goat, but the friend did not find her.

Judah speaks after his friend searched, without success, for the woman he believed to be a prostitute. In reality she was Tamar, his daughter-in-law, in disguise. She had in her possession Judah's seal, cord, and staff. He wants to close the matter quietly, worried about his reputation more than about the truth. Soon those items will expose him.

Today we can notice that we sometimes care more about our image than about our integrity. What is hidden sooner or later comes to light. God invites us to live with honesty and to acknowledge our mistakes in time.
exp.37:29:
After Pharez, his twin brother was born, the one who had a scarlet thread tied on his hand. They named him Zarah. The word "scarlet" here refers to a bright red dye, and "came out" means that he was born.

This is the end of the story of Judah and Tamar. Tamar had been widowed and left without children, and Judah had not fulfilled his duty toward her. In the end she becomes pregnant by Judah. The narrator (Moses, according to tradition) recounts the birth of the twins. The thread marked the first to come out, but Pharez got ahead. Pharez later appears in the line of David and of Jesus (Matthew 1:3).

For today: God does not always follow the order we expect. Our first human plans sometimes fall apart, but God can work even in messy stories and carry forward his purposes with grace.
exp.39:0:
It says that, after the events before, two important officials of the king of Egypt, the cupbearer (who served the king's wine) and the baker (who prepared his bread and food), "offended", that is, committed a fault against their lord, the Pharaoh. The Bible does not say what that offense exactly was.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks. He introduces these two men because they will end up in the same prison where Joseph was, unjustly held. Their dreams, which Joseph will interpret, will be an important step for Joseph to later come before Pharaoh.

For today: God can use even difficult and unexpected moments, including the mistakes of others, to carry out his plans. If today you are waiting in an unjust situation, remain faithful and serve with love. Your waiting does not go unnoticed by God.
exp.39:21:
It says that Pharaoh had the chief baker hanged, just as Joseph had explained to him. The word "hanged" here can mean hanging the body after the execution, or putting someone to death by hanging; scholars understand it in several ways. What matters is that the dream was fulfilled exactly.

The narrator tells what happened on Pharaoh's birthday. Joseph was unjustly imprisoned and had interpreted the dreams of two officials: the chief cupbearer was restored and the chief baker was condemned. Both outcomes matched Joseph's words, which shows that God was giving him understanding. But the cupbearer forgot about him.

For today: when God gives you a word or a promise, do not depend on people remembering what you did for them. Even if they forget you, God does not forget. Remain faithful and trust in his timing.
exp.40:6:
It says that the seven thin ears swallowed up the seven full and plump ears. Then Pharaoh woke and realized that all of it had been a dream.

Here the narrator of Genesis speaks. Pharaoh has just had his second dream, similar to the first, which was about the cows. No one in his court is able to explain it, and that is why Joseph appears, who will say that God is showing him what is coming: seven years of plenty and seven years of famine.

For today: God can speak in ways we do not understand right away. If He warns us or shows us something, the wise thing is to prepare ourselves with humility and seek trustworthy counsel, as Pharaoh eventually did, neither ignoring it nor falling into panic.
exp.40:7:
In the morning, the text says, Pharaoh was troubled and anxious because of his dreams. He then sent for all the magicians of Egypt and all its wise men. He told them what he had dreamed, but none of them could explain it to him.

The account follows the dream of seven fat ears of grain being devoured by seven thin ones. The narrator tells us the king sought help from his most respected advisers, but they had no answer. This prepares the next scene, where the cupbearer remembers Joseph, who was in prison and who, according to the text, could interpret dreams with God's help.

There are moments when human wisdom reaches its limit and leaves us unsettled. Such moments can teach us humility and lead us to seek God in prayer, asking for his guidance, and also to listen with respect to those whom he places in our path.
exp.40:9:
Here the chief cupbearer reminds Pharaoh of what happened before. He says that Pharaoh was angry with his servants and put him in prison, in the house of the captain of the guard, together with the chief baker.

The one speaking is the chief cupbearer, the man who served the king his cup. Pharaoh is troubled by his dreams, and no one in Egypt is able to explain them. Then the cupbearer remembers his own failure and tells how he came to know Joseph in prison, years earlier, when he himself was locked up.

For today: sometimes God prepares answers in places and moments that seem dark or lost. We can trust that nothing we go through is wasted, and also be grateful and remember those who helped us, just as the cupbearer was slow to remember Joseph.
exp.40:19:
This verse describes part of Pharaoh's dream: the seven lean, ugly cows devoured the seven fat cows that had come up first. The word "devoured" means they swallowed them up greedily.

The one speaking is Pharaoh, who tells his dream to Joseph. No one in Egypt had been able to explain it. According to the account, God was showing him what would come: seven years of plenty followed by seven years of famine. The dream seemed strange, but it carried a serious and urgent message.

For today: good seasons do not last forever, and God invites us to be wise. When things are going well, we can save, help others, and trust in Him, without living as if hard times will never come.
exp.40:20:
It says that the lean cows ate up the fat ones, yet nothing could be noticed: they remained just as lean and ugly as before. Here the Pharaoh of Egypt is speaking. He is telling Joseph his dream, because no one in his court could explain it. He repeats it almost exactly as he dreamed it, and adds that the lean cows did not improve even though they devoured the fat ones. Joseph will later explain that these are seven years of plenty followed by seven years of famine, and that God had warned Pharaoh of what He was going to do.

For today: abundance without planning runs out quickly and leaves no trace. We can ask ourselves how we manage what God gives us in good times: saving wisely, sharing generously, and trusting that He sustains us in difficult times too.
exp.40:22:
This verse describes the second part of Pharaoh's dream about the ears of grain. After the seven full and beautiful ears, seven others appear that were thin, dried up, and scorched by the scorching east wind, a hot, dry wind from the east that damaged the crops.

Here Pharaoh is speaking. He tells Joseph his dream, because none of the magicians of Egypt could explain it to him. He was troubled and looking for an answer. Shortly afterward, Joseph makes clear that God himself was giving warning of what was going to happen: years of plenty followed by years of famine.

For today: God can speak and give warning ahead of time, and he invites us to be wise. When we live in good times, we can learn to save, to share, and to trust in him, so that we are not caught off guard when difficulties come.
exp.40:26:
Here José continues explaining Pharaoh's dream. The seven thin and ill-favoured cows that came up after the fat ones represent seven years. The seven empty ears blasted with the east wind are also seven years, and they will be years of famine.

José speaks before Pharaoh, who had had two dreams that no one in Egypt could interpret. José, who was in prison, is summoned and makes clear that the interpretation does not come from him but from God. He tells Pharaoh that the two dreams are really one: a warning of what God is about to do in Egypt.

For today: God sometimes warns us of difficult times so that we may prepare with wisdom, not with fear. We can learn to save, to plan, and not to waste what we have in good times, trusting that God cares for us always.
exp.40:37:
Pharaoh asks his servants whether they could find another man like Joseph, a man in whom is the Spirit of God. It is a question that already carries its answer: there is no one else like him.

Joseph had just interpreted Pharaoh's dreams and proposed a plan to store up food during the seven years of plenty. Pharaoh was an Egyptian king who worshiped many gods. Even so, he recognizes that there is something special in Joseph, something that comes from God. Some understand that Pharaoh was speaking according to his own idea of the divine, and not as someone who already knew the God of Israel.

Today, the wisdom and character of a person who trusts in God can speak for themselves, even before those who do not believe. Work with honesty and humility, and let God be the one who opens doors for you.
exp.40:41:
Here, Pharaoh takes the ring off his hand and puts it on Joseph's hand. Then he dresses Joseph in garments of fine linen, a very fine and costly cloth, and places a gold chain around his neck. These are three visible signs of honor and authority.

Joseph had been a slave and then a prisoner. Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, has just heard his interpretation of the dreams and his counsel for facing the years of famine. Convinced that God was with him, Pharaoh raises him to the highest authority after himself. The ring was used to seal documents, so it gave him power to act in the king's name.

God can lift a person up at the moment He chooses, even after years of injustice and waiting. In the meantime, we can remain faithful and do well with what is at hand.
exp.40:47:
This verse says that Joseph gathered all the food of the seven good years that there were in Egypt. He stored it in the cities, and in each city he put the grain that was harvested in the fields around it. Here "food" means provision or supplies, above all grain.

This is the account of the narrator of Genesis. Pharaoh had dreamed of seven years of plenty and seven of famine, and Joseph, already in charge of the plan, put it into action. Keeping the food close to where it was produced was an orderly way of preparing. The text gives no further details of how it was stored.

For today: times of plenty are a good time to be wise, not careless. We can keep some of what God gives us, with order and steadiness, for hard times, and share it generously when the need arises.
exp.40:55:
This verse says that the famine spread across the whole land of Egypt and grew more severe. Then Joseph opened all the storehouses, that is, the places where grain was kept, and began to sell it to the Egyptians. The word "sold" shows that he was not giving it away freely, but offering it in exchange for payment.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is speaking. During seven years of plenty, Joseph had stored up grain, just as God had shown him through Pharaoh's dreams. Now the seven years of scarcity had arrived, the people asked Pharaoh for bread, and Pharaoh told them to go to Joseph. Thus what Joseph had announced came to pass.

For today: preparing wisely and in an orderly way helps us serve better when difficult times come. Saving, planning, and being responsible with what God gives us can become a blessing for our family and for other people.
exp.40:56:
The explanation says that people from all the neighboring countries traveled to Egypt to buy grain from Joseph. The reason was that the hunger had become very severe everywhere. The phrase "all the earth" here refers to the region known at that time, not necessarily the whole planet.

The one who tells this is the narrator of Genesis. Joseph had interpreted Pharaoh's dreams and, after seven years of abundance, was managing the stored grain. Now the time of scarcity he had foretold had arrived, and Egypt had food when others did not.

For today: preparation and wisdom can become a blessing for many. God used Joseph's faithfulness to sustain lives. We can ask ourselves what resources, time, or skills we have and how we might use them responsibly to help those who are in need.
exp.41:6:
This verse tells us that Joseph recognized his brothers right away when he saw them. But he pretended to be a stranger and spoke to them harshly. He asked them where they came from, and they answered that they came from Canaan, to buy food.

The narrator describes the scene. There is famine throughout the region, and Joseph, already a ruler in Egypt, is selling grain. His brothers, who years earlier had sold him as a slave, arrive and bow down before him without recognizing him. The Bible does not fully explain his reasons, but the passage that follows shows that Joseph remembers his dreams and seems to be testing his brothers. Some think he wanted to see whether they had changed.

For today: when someone has hurt us, we do not need to respond in haste or in anger. We can ask God for wisdom to seek the truth, repentance, and reconciliation with patience and care.
exp.41:22:
The verse says that Joseph's brothers did not know that he understood what they were saying. Because Joseph used an interpreter, they assumed he did not understand their language. The word "interpreter" refers to someone who translates from one language into another.

The brothers were talking among themselves, believing they spoke in private. They acknowledged their guilt for having mistreated Joseph years earlier, and Reuben reminded them that he had warned them. Joseph heard them, stepped away, and wept. Here the account shows that his heart was still tender, even though he was testing them.

For today: what we say when we think no one is listening reveals what is in our heart. God does know everything. We can ask him to lead us to sincere repentance and to repair the harm we have done, without waiting to be found out.
exp.41:23:
He turned away from them and wept by himself. Then he came back, spoke to them, and chose Simeon. He ordered that he be tied up and held right there, while they watched. "Bound" means he was tied up and kept prisoner; "before their eyes" means in front of them.

Joseph, already governor of Egypt, treats his brothers harshly, and they do not recognize him. They have just been talking among themselves about what they did to him years earlier, believing he could not understand their language. Hearing them, Joseph was moved. The Bible does not explain why he chose Simeon; some think it was because Simeon had been especially cruel to him, but the text does not say so. It also does not make clear everything Joseph was thinking.

For today: truth and reconciliation can sometimes hurt. We can feel tenderness toward someone who wronged us and still seek for them to acknowledge their wrong. Let us ask God for wisdom to act with both justice and mercy.
exp.41:24:
This verse tells how Joseph ordered his servants to fill his brothers' sacks with corn. He also commanded that each man's money be put back into his sack, and that they be given provisions for the journey. It was done just as he said.

Joseph is the ruler of Egypt, and his brothers have come to buy grain because of the famine. They do not recognize him. He has tested them, wept in private, and kept Simeon in prison. The verse does not say why he returns the money; many think it shows his generosity and also sets up another test for them.

For today: even when someone has hurt us, we can choose kindness instead of revenge. God can use quiet, generous acts to touch the conscience and open the way to reconciliation.
exp.41:26:
This verse tells how, during the journey back to Canaan, one of Joseph's brothers opened his sack at the inn to give his donkey some feed. There he found his money, right in the mouth of the sack. An inn is a place where travelers spent the night, and the donkey is the animal he was feeding.

The narrator of Genesis then recounts what happened after Joseph, now ruler in Egypt, sold grain to his brothers without them recognizing him. Joseph ordered their money returned to them in secret. The Bible does not say here why he did it; some think it was an act of kindness, others that he wanted to test them. The brothers, seeing the money, became frightened and thought that God was intervening because of their past guilt.

For today: when something unexpected happens to you, do not jump to conclusions. Stop, pray, and examine your heart calmly, trusting that God works even in what you do not understand.
exp.41:29:
Here the brothers of Joseph tell their father Jacob what happened in Egypt. They say that the man who ruled that land spoke roughly to them and took them for spies, that is, people who had come to scout the country in order to attack it.

The ones speaking are Jacob's sons, now back in Canaan. Without knowing it, they had dealt with their brother Joseph, whom they had sold years before. In their account they no longer mention that Joseph locked them up for three days or that he asked them to bring the youngest brother. They tell the story carefully, and also with fear and anguish about what is still to come.

For today: when life treats us harshly, let us remember that God may be working something greater than we understand. Instead of hiding the truth, we can speak with sincerity and trust that He guides even what frightens us.
exp.42:15:
Here Joseph sees that his brothers have returned and that they have brought Benjamin, his youngest brother, with them. So he orders the steward of his house to bring the men inside, to slaughter an animal and prepare it, because they will dine with him at noon.

Joseph is the one speaking, and he speaks as governor of Egypt. His brothers had come earlier for food, and he had asked them to bring Benjamin. Now they are doing as he asked. They do not know that he is their brother, and for that reason they are frightened by the invitation. The Bible does not fully explain Joseph's motives at this moment, but his gesture shows kindness and joy at seeing Benjamin.

For today: sometimes God works in kindness, and we, out of guilt or fear, see only a threat. Let us learn to trust and to receive his grace with calm.
exp.42:18:
The explanation says that Joseph's brothers approached the manager of his house and spoke with him at the door, before going in. "Steward" is the person in charge of managing the affairs of the house.
