He accused them of being spies in order to test them. Now they explain to Jacob why Simeon is missing. They recount the facts, though not everything that had passed between them.

For today: when we have to explain something difficult to our family, let us speak with clarity and without dressing up the truth. Complete honesty, even when it hurts, helps trust to hold and heals what is broken.
exp.30:36:
Jacob tells Laban that he has already searched all of his goods and found nothing that belongs to Laban. The words "stuff" and "goods" here refer to Jacob's household belongings, not jewels. Jacob challenges Laban to bring forward whatever he has found, in front of their relatives, so that they may judge between the two of them.

Jacob speaks in anger. Laban pursued him because his household gods had been taken, and Rachel had taken them in secret, although Jacob did not know it. After a search that turned up nothing, Jacob defends his honesty. He will later recall twenty years of faithful work.

For today: when you are accused, defend yourself calmly and with facts, not rumors. Living with integrity day by day gives you the freedom to say, "Let everything be examined." And if there is something hidden in your life, now is a good time to put it right.
exp.16:18:
God answers Abraham's laughter and doubt with a clear promise: Sarah, his wife, will have a son. Abraham is to name him Isaac. God says he will keep his covenant with that son as an everlasting covenant, meaning one that never ends, and that it will extend to his descendants after him.

God is the one speaking. Abraham is ninety-nine years old and Sarah is ninety, and to him it seems impossible. For that reason he asks that Ishmael, his son already born, may live before God. God does not reject Ishmael, since he later promises to bless him, but he makes clear that the covenant will be fulfilled through Isaac. The name Isaac is usually connected with laughter.

Today we too can bring our doubts honestly to God. He is not angry with someone who speaks to him from the heart, and he can fulfill what he has said even when it seems impossible to us. Trusting means waiting for his timing and not relying only on our own plans.
exp.43:10:
They say that Joseph's brothers acted quickly. Each one set his sack (his bag of grain) down on the ground and opened it. "Lowered" here means setting the sack down on the ground in a hurry.

We are in the test that Joseph is setting up for them. His steward caught up with them and accused them of stealing the silver cup, which Joseph had ordered hidden in Benjamin's sack. The brothers, sure of their innocence, offered that whoever had the cup should die and the rest would become slaves. Their haste shows that they had nothing to hide. They did not know what was coming.

For today: when you are accused, acting with openness and without fear helps a great deal. But let us also watch our words, because the brothers promised too much without knowing what would happen. Let us think before we speak.
exp.28:31:
Leah became pregnant and had a son. She named him Reuben, which sounds like "look, a son" in Hebrew. She says that the LORD has seen her affliction, that is, her pain and her sorrow. She also hopes that now her husband Jacob will love her.

It is Leah speaking, the wife whom Jacob did not prefer. Jacob loved his sister Rachel more, and the text says Leah was "unloved," a way of saying she was less loved. The LORD saw her pain and gave her children. Leah acknowledges God, though she still longs for her husband's love.

God sees those who feel rejected or undervalued. We can bring our pain to him with confidence. We can also learn that God's love sustains the heart, even when some people do not value us as they should.
exp.4:2:
This verse says that Adam was 130 years old when he had a son in his own likeness, after his own image, and he named him Seth. The phrase "in his own likeness" means the son was like him.

The narrator of Genesis presents the record of Adam's family line. He recalls that God created human beings in his own likeness, and now shows that this likeness passes on to the next generation. It is not fully explained how this is transmitted; some think it includes the image of God, others that it also includes the fallen condition. Then we learn that Adam died, as God had warned.

For today: each generation receives and passes on something. As parents, teachers, or friends, we influence others by our example. Let us ask God that what we leave in others will reflect his character, his love, and his truth.
exp.28:21:
This verse tells us that Laban invited all the men of that place and prepared a feast. A feast was a large festive meal, and such meals were normal at weddings in that time.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Jacob had worked seven years for Rachel and now asked to marry her. Laban prepares the celebration, but the following text shows that this celebration became the occasion for giving Leah in place of Rachel. The text does not state clearly when Laban decided on the deception, so it is best not to assume more than what is written.

For today: a celebration or a good appearance does not guarantee sincerity. Let us strive to act with truth and keep what we have promised, and ask God for wisdom to see beyond what appears on the surface.
exp.0:18:
This verse closes the fourth day of creation. The phrase "there was evening, and there was morning" is the way Genesis marks each day: evening comes first and then morning, and so a day is completed.

In this chapter, the narrator tells how God orders the world step by step. On the fourth day he set the sun, the moon, and the stars to give light, to mark day and night, and to signal the seasons. People have understood the "days" in various ways: as days of twenty-four hours or as longer stages. The text itself does not settle that discussion, and believers have approached it in different ways.

For today: God works with order and patience. If you feel rushed today, remember that each day has its evening and its morning, and you can rest in the confidence that God is still sustaining all things.
exp.38:4:
This verse tells us that from the time Potiphar put Joseph in charge of his whole household and everything he owned, the Lord blessed the Egyptian's household because of Joseph. The blessing reached everything he had, both in the house and out in the field.

The wording here is simple: "put Joseph in charge" means Potiphar placed him over everything, as a manager who looked after all his property.

This is not a character speaking, but the narrator of the book of Genesis. Joseph had been sold as a slave by his brothers and taken to Egypt. His master, Potiphar, saw that the Lord was with Joseph and that everything went well under his care, so he entrusted his household to him. The text wants to show that God cared for Joseph even in an unjust and difficult situation. A new trial will come later.

For today: do your work well where God has placed you, even if it is not the place you dreamed of. Your faithfulness and your trust in God can be a blessing to others.
exp.24:5:
Explanation:
The explanation says that Abraham, while he was still alive, gave gifts to the sons he had with his concubines (Hagar and Keturah). Then he sent them away from his son Isaac to the land of the east. "Gifts" are presents, and a "concubine" was a secondary wife. "While he was still alive" means that Abraham did this during his own lifetime.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. He has just said that Abraham left everything to Isaac, the son of the promise. With this act, Abraham arranges his inheritance: he protects Isaac's line without leaving the other sons without provision. The verse does not say exactly where the land of the east was; it gives only the direction.

For today: if you have family responsibilities, arrange things in good time and with fairness. You can care for the priority God has given you without neglecting others, so as to avoid future conflicts.
exp.48:2:
Jacob speaks to Reuben, his firstborn son, and reminds him of what he represented. "Firstborn" means the first son. "The beginning of my strength" means the first fruit of his strength as a father. "Excelling in honor" means standing high in respect, and "excelling in power" means standing high in authority. By birth, Reuben held first place in the family.

Jacob, now old and near his death, gathers his twelve sons to tell them what will come upon them. He begins with Reuben with words of acknowledgment, but soon, in the verses that follow, he rebukes him for his serious offense against his father. For this reason, Reuben would lose the privileged place that belonged to him.

For today: having a good start, talent, or a position does not guarantee a good ending. Character and daily decisions matter more. Let us ask God for self-control to care for what has been entrusted to us.
exp.45:19:
Genesis 46:20 says that while Joseph was living in Egypt, two sons were born to him: Manasseh and Ephraim. Their mother was Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, a priest of On. On was an Egyptian city, later known as Heliopolis.

This verse is part of the list of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt. The narrator of Genesis, traditionally thought to be Moses, arranges the names by mothers and children. Manasseh and Ephraim are mentioned because they were born in Egypt, yet they are counted within Jacob's family. The verse does not describe Asenath's faith, and nothing more is told to us about it.

For today: God can bless and make a family grow even in a foreign land. If you find yourself living far from home or in an unfamiliar setting, do not think that God has forgotten you. Raise your children with faith, gratitude, and confidence that He continues to keep His promises.
exp.43:11:
The explanation says that Joseph's steward searched the brothers' sacks one by one, starting with the oldest and ending with the youngest. In the end, the silver cup appeared in Benjamin's sack. A "sack" in this verse is a large bag for carrying grain.

The one speaking here is the narrator. Joseph had secretly ordered that his cup be placed in Benjamin's sack. He wanted to test whether his brothers were still the same men who years before had sold him, or whether they had changed and would protect Benjamin. They knew nothing of this trap.

For today: sometimes trials come when we are innocent and do not understand what is happening. God may be working something greater than we can see. We can respond with humility, honesty, and faithfulness to others, trusting that he still guides the story.
exp.25:10:
Abimelech gives an order to all his people: whoever harms this man or his wife will surely be put to death. "Harms" here means to do injury or abuse. "Surely" means without doubt. "Warned" means that he gave a clear command.

Abimelech, the Philistine king of Gerar, had just discovered that Rebekah was Isaac's wife, not his sister, as Isaac had said out of fear. Although Isaac had lied, the king recognized the danger of sinning without knowing it and decided to protect the family. After this, God blessed Isaac with an abundant harvest.

For today: sometimes our mistakes and fears can cause problems, but God continues to watch over those who belong to him. Let us trust in his protection instead of resorting to half-truths, and act with honesty.
exp.21:15:
God says that he has sworn by himself. "You have done this" refers to Abraham's willingness to offer Isaac. "You have not held back" means "you did not refuse me." "Your son, your only son" points to Isaac as the son of the promise. The sentence is left open and is completed in the following verse with the blessing.

The one speaking is the angel of the LORD, who calls to Abraham from heaven a second time, just after stopping his hand on the mountain. Since no one can be a greater guarantor than God, he swears by himself (Hebrews 6:13 reminds us of this). He thereby confirms the promise he had already made, because Abraham showed complete trust in God.

For today: God sees the faithfulness that is lived out in secret and at cost. We can give him what we value most, trusting that he is good and keeps what he promises. His faithfulness is greater than ours.
exp.31:16:
Jacob gives instructions to the first servant who leads a herd. If his brother Esau meets him, he expects Esau to ask three questions: To whom do you belong? Where are you going? And whose animals are these in front of you?

Jacob is returning to his land after many years, and he knows that Esau is coming to meet him with four hundred men. He remembers that years earlier Esau wanted to kill him. So he prepares a large gift, sent in separate groups, to soften his brother's heart. Some see prudence here; others, fear. There is probably both.

Jacob prays to God and also acts wisely. If you have a broken relationship, ask God for help, and then take concrete and humble steps toward reconciliation, without waiting for the other person to take the first step.
exp.14:1:
Abram answers God honestly. He says, more or less: "Lord God, what can you give me, since I remain childless, and the heir of my house is Eliezer of Damascus?" In other words, what good is any gift if he has no children to receive it? He names Eliezer of Damascus as the one who would inherit his household. "Remaining childless" means living without descendants.

God had just told him: "Fear not, I am your shield and your exceedingly great reward." Abram speaks, then, with honesty and some sadness. He had received promises of a great descendance, but the years were passing and he had no son. In that era, if someone had no children, his inheritance could pass to a trusted servant. Scholars debate some details about Eliezer's exact position, but the general idea is clear.

We can speak with God frankly, even when we have doubts or pain. Abram did not pretend; he expressed his concern, and God listened and answered him with patience.
exp.26:6:
Rebekah tells Jacob what Isaac said to Esau: that he should bring him some game and prepare a tasty dish to eat, so that Isaac may bless him in the presence of the LORD before he dies. This is meant as a solemn blessing, given before God.

Here Rebekah repeats Isaac's words, since she had been listening. Isaac, now old, wanted to give the family blessing to Esau, his firstborn son. Rebekah, for her part, will use these words to push Jacob into acting. The Bible recounts what happens without approving the deception that follows. Some see here a lack of trust in the promise God had already given about Jacob (Genesis 25:23).

For today: when we believe God has promised something, we do not need to manipulate or lie to bring it about. Trusting Him means waiting and acting with honesty.
exp.21:22:
And Bethuel became the father of Rebekah. Milcah bore these eight sons to Abraham's brother Nahor.

This verse tells us that Bethuel was the father of Rebekah. It also sums up that Milcah had eight sons with Nahor, Abraham's brother.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Genesis. Right after Abraham shows his faith by offering Isaac, the text gives us news about the family of his brother Nahor. It is not a speech but a family record. It seems to serve as a bridge to what comes next: Rebekah will appear later as Isaac's wife (Genesis 24). Some see here the hand of God preparing the way, although the text does not say it in those words.

For today: God cares for the details of our lives, even those we do not yet understand. Even when it seems nothing important is happening, God may be preparing people and moments for the future. We can trust and keep obeying with patience.
exp.17:5:
Abraham went quickly into the tent and told Sarah to prepare bread right away. The words "hurried" and "Quick!" show his urgency. Three seahs of fine flour was a generous amount, and it was the good quality flour. The bread was to be baked on the hearth, which means among the hot embers and ashes.

Abraham speaks with Sarah. Three visitors had arrived at his tent, and he offered them rest and food. They accepted, and he hurried to prepare everything. The text later reveals that one of them is the Lord. Abraham did not know this at first, since he treated them as travelers. Some interpreters see in this a foreshadowing of the Trinity, and others do not; the question is debated.

Today we can practice hospitality with generosity and a good spirit. Abraham did not give what was left over, but the best. Perhaps today you can invite someone to your table, without overcomplicating things, and do it with joy.
exp.17:19:
Then the LORD said that the outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah is great, and that their sin is very grievous. The outcry is a cry of protest over the wrongs committed there, and it keeps growing. Their sin is described as very serious and heavy.

Here the LORD himself speaks. He has just decided to share with Abraham what he plans to do, because Abraham is his friend and will teach his household to walk in righteousness. Right away the LORD says that he will go down to see whether the matter is truly as grave as the outcry that has reached him. This shows that God acts with justice and not lightly.

For today: God hears the cry of those who suffer injustice. We can be people who are sensitive to their pain, pray for them, and, as far as we are able, help them and act justly in the matters that concern us.
exp.26:2:
Isaac asks his son Esau to take his weapons, his quiver and his bow, and go out into the field to hunt game for him. The quiver is the case that holds the arrows. The request is for meat from the hunt, which Isaac wants to eat.

Isaac speaks as an old man, nearly blind. He feels his life is nearing its end and wants to give his blessing to Esau, the firstborn, after eating the meal he loves. Rebekah listens, and this leads to what happens next. The text does not explain all of Isaac's reasons, but it shows that he wants to carry out this important step before he dies.

For today: let us not put off saying important words to our family. Blessing, advising and praying for our children must be done openly, honestly and with faith, not in secret or out of favoritism.
exp.30:41:
Jacob tells Laban that if the God of his father, the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac, had not been with him, Laban would have sent him away empty-handed. "The Fear of Isaac" is another way of naming God, whom Isaac honored and revered. "Empty-handed" means with nothing. "Last night He rendered judgment" refers to the dream in which God warned Laban not to harm Jacob.

Jacob speaks in anger, but with firmness, after Laban caught up with him as he was fleeing with his family. For twenty years he worked hard for Laban, who changed his wages many times. Jacob acknowledges that God saw his affliction and the toil of his hands and protected him. Laban answers by saying that everything belongs to him, but in the end he proposes a covenant.

For today: when you feel that your work is not valued or that someone is taking advantage of you, remember that God sees what others overlook. Trust in Him, and act with honesty and peace.
exp.5:5:
God was saddened that he had made human beings on the earth. The word "regretted" does not mean that God made a mistake, but that he felt deep sorrow over what he saw and his attitude toward it changed. "He was grieved in His heart" means that it hurt him deeply, like a sorrow in the innermost place.

The narrator of Genesis tells this after describing that human wickedness was constant and that every thought leaned toward evil. God responds with pain, not with indifference. Scholars explain the language of God's regret in several ways, but almost all agree that it shows how much he cares for his creation. And right after this, Noah appears, who found favor in the Lord's eyes.

Today we can remember that God is not cold toward evil or toward our sin. This invites us to draw near to him with sincerity, to ask for his grace, and to live in a way that does not grieve him.
exp.8:7:
This verse says that God spoke to Noah and to his sons who were with him. It is a short sentence that serves as a bridge: it introduces what God is about to say next. The word "said" simply marks that an important message is coming.

God is the one who speaks. He has just given Noah instructions after the flood: to value human life, because man was made in the image of God, and to fill the earth again. Now God addresses the whole family to make a covenant, that is, a solemn promise, which also includes the animals.

For today: God takes the initiative to speak to us and to promise good things. We can approach the Bible expecting to hear a God who cares for his people and his creation, and respond with trust and respect for life.
exp.40:21:
Pharaoh tells Joseph that in his dream he saw seven heads of grain, plump and ripe, growing on a single stalk. The original wording for "dreaming" means "while he was dreaming." Heads of grain are the parts of the plant where the grain forms, in this case of wheat or barley.

Here Pharaoh, king of Egypt, is telling Joseph his two dreams, because no one in his court, not even the magicians, could explain them. He was troubled, and Joseph had been brought out of prison to interpret them. Afterward, Joseph says that God was showing Pharaoh what he was about to do.

For today: when something troubles you or you do not understand what lies ahead, do not rely only on your own judgment. Pray, seek wise counsel, and ask God for direction. He can give clarity and help you prepare with responsibility.
exp.3:16:
Cain had relations with his wife, and she became pregnant and gave birth to a son named Enoch. Then Cain built a city and named it after his son Enoch.

The narrator of the book is the one speaking here, not a character. Cain had already killed his brother Abel and had moved away from the presence of God, although God protected him with a sign. The text does not explain where his wife came from, and it gives no further details. What it does show is how a family and a society begin to take shape far from God.

For today: God continues to care for people even after their mistakes, but we should ask ourselves what we are building and on what foundation. We can build our lives and families in communion with God, not only to leave behind a name.
exp.10:18:
The explanation says that Peleg, after becoming the father of Reu, lived another 209 years and had other sons and daughters. The phrase "had as a son" is the sense of "father of" in this verse, and the wording "had other sons and daughters" is the way your verse describes his later children. According to this text, Peleg was 30 years old when Reu was born, so he lived 239 years in total.

Here no one is speaking; it is the author's own account, presenting the list of descendants of Shem, son of Noah. This genealogy connects the flood with Abram, showing how God preserved the line of the promise. Some scholars think these figures are literal; others believe they have a symbolic meaning or that the list contains gaps. There is no complete agreement.

For today: God pays attention to every life, even to those that seem like "just a name" in a list. Your daily life, your family, and your simple faithfulness matter in his greater plan.
exp.23:61:
The explanation says that this verse tells how Isaac had just returned from Beer-lahai-roi, a well whose name means "the well of the Living One who sees me." That place was in the Negev, the dry southern country of the land of Canaan, where Isaac was living at that time. The phrase "was living" simply means he was staying there.

Here the book's narrator speaks. After Abraham's servant found Rebekah and her family welcomed her, the caravan arrives in the south. That well already had a history: there God had seen and comforted Hagar (Genesis 16:14). That is why the name recalls that God sees the one who suffers. We do not know for certain why Isaac had gone there, but the text places him in a place tied to God's presence.

For today: God sees us, even in places and seasons of waiting. Look for a quiet moment to speak with Him, trusting that He watches over you with care.
exp.6:20:
This verse says that the flood destroyed every living thing that moved on the dry land: birds, livestock, animals, creatures that swarm along the ground, and all mankind. "Every living thing" refers to all creatures. "Livestock" are the domesticated animals, "animals" covers the wild creatures, and "every creature that swarms upon the earth" refers to any creature that crawls or moves in groups along the ground.

The account is told by the narrator of Genesis. God had seen that human wickedness was very great and the earth was filled with violence (Genesis 6). For this reason he sent the flood, but he cared for Noah, a righteous man, and his family in the ark. Scholars debate whether the flood was worldwide or regional, but the text stresses that the destruction was total for everything living on that land.

For today: this passage reminds us that God takes evil seriously, but he also saves those who trust in him. Today we can respond to his mercy with an obedient faith, like Noah's.
exp.43:30:
Judah says to Joseph, whom he does not yet recognize, that if Jacob sees that the boy is not returning, he will die. A "boy" here means a young man, and "gray hair" refers to the white hair of an old man. "Sheol" is the place of the dead. In this way, the brothers would bring their aged father down to the grave in sorrow.

Judah speaks, defending Benjamin before the ruler of Egypt. Joseph had put his cup in Benjamin's sack and wanted to keep him as a servant. Jacob had already lost Joseph, as he believed, and his life was closely bound up with Benjamin's. Judah offers to stay himself as a slave in Benjamin's place.

For today: our decisions affect those who love us. Judah went from being the brother who sold Joseph to being the one who offers to suffer on behalf of another. God can transform the heart, and we can ask him for the courage to care for our family with love and responsibility.
exp.9:9:
This verse says that Nimrod's kingdom started with four cities: Babylon, Erech, Accad, and Calneh, all in the land of Shinar. "Began" means the start or the main center. "Shinar" is the region later linked with Babylon, that is, the area between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers.

The author, following the traditional view that Moses wrote the book, is presenting the list of nations after the flood. Here he tells how Nimrod, a descendant of Cush, went from being a mighty man to ruling cities. Some see in him an admirable leader; others, a figure of pride, because Babylon appears later in the story of the tower. The text does not fully clarify this.

For today: power and achievements can impress, but it is wise to ask ourselves for whom we are building. Let us ask God that our work and our goals honor Him and serve others.
exp.20:13:
Abraham got up early and gave Hagar bread and a skin of water. A skin was a leather bag for carrying water. He placed them on her shoulders, handed her the boy, Ishmael, and sent her away. She left and wandered through the Wilderness of Beersheba.

This is a narrative, not a speech. Sarah had asked that Hagar and Ishmael be sent away, and Abraham was distressed by it. God told him to obey and promised that He would also make a nation of Ishmael. Abraham acts early in the morning, trusting that promise, even though the parting was painful.

For today: sometimes we have to make difficult decisions that hurt. We can take the step in obedience and entrust to God the people we love, because He cares for them even when we are unable to do so ourselves.
exp.33:6:
When Jacob's sons heard what had happened, they came back from the field. They were filled with grief and fury. The verse says Shechem had committed an outrage in Israel by lying with Jacob's daughter, and it states plainly that such a thing should not be done.

This is part of the story of Dinah, Jacob's daughter, and Shechem. Jacob heard about it and kept silent until his sons came home. The narrator describes their outrage, while Hamor, Shechem's father, is already on his way to speak and propose a marriage. Later, the sons will respond with deceit and violence, and the Bible does not present that as an example to follow.

For today: it is right to feel indignation at injustice and abuse, and to protect the one who was harmed. But we must carry that anger with self-control, seeking justice without revenge, so that we do not cause even more harm.
exp.29:20:
This verse tells us that Leah gave birth to a daughter and named her Dinah. It is the first time the Bible mentions a daughter of Jacob. Unlike the names of the earlier children, the verse gives no explanation of why she was named Dinah.

The one speaking in the story is the narrator. Leah had already had six sons and hoped in this way to win Jacob's love, since he preferred Rachel. This time no words of Leah are recorded, and the Bible does not say why. Some think it is only a brief note about the family, but that is not certain. Right after, it mentions that God remembered Rachel.

For today: God sees and remembers each person, even when the Bible gives only a few words to their story. If you feel little noticed, remember that your life matters to God. And look at those who go unnoticed around you, so that you can value them.
exp.3:15:
Here Cain is said to have gone out from the LORD's presence. In other words, he moved away from the place where God dealt with his family, and he settled in a land called Nod, east of Eden. "Nod" sounds like the Hebrew word for "wandering," and many understand it as a symbolic place. It is not known for certain where it was.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Cain had just killed his brother Abel. God punished him, but also protected him with a sign. Now Cain goes out to live far away, bearing the consequences of his sin, and later he will start a family and build a city.

For today: when we fail, the temptation is to pull away from God. But He invites us to return with sincerity, to acknowledge the wrong, and to receive His forgiveness and His help.
exp.46:22:
Here Joseph speaks to the Egyptian people after the famine. He tells them that he has now acquired them and their land for Pharaoh, but he gives them seed to plant. The seed is grain they can sow in the land, and it is given to them so they can work the land again.

Joseph is the administrator of Egypt under Pharaoh. During the years of famine, the people had already spent their money and their livestock to buy food. Now they also hand over their land. Joseph gives them seed and sets one condition: a fifth of the harvest will go to Pharaoh. The priests were left out because they already received their allowance. The text describes what happened and does not say whether everything was fair or ideal.

For today: when someone goes through hardship, helping them is not only giving temporary relief but also giving them a way to work and support themselves again, with clear and fair arrangements.
exp.45:7:
This verse opens a list of the names of the sons of Israel, that is, of Jacob and his descendants, who went to Egypt. It begins with Reuben, Jacob's firstborn son. "Firstborn" means the eldest son, the one who was born first. "Went to" refers to their traveling there to live.

The narrator is the author of the book, traditionally identified as Moses. Jacob was already old, and he moved to Egypt because of the famine, since his son Joseph lived there. The narrator lists the family to record who they were and how many went in. In this way the beginning of the people of Israel is shown, a people who would later grow greatly in Egypt.

For today: God knows each person by name, and He also values families. We can remember and give thanks for those who went before us in the faith, and pray for our family by name, trusting that God cares for each one.
exp.6:13:
This verse continues the list of those who entered the ark. First Noah and his family are named, and then the animals: the wild animals, the livestock, the creeping things that crawl, and the birds and winged creatures. Each group is named in its own category, and the list covers the many kinds of living things that were brought on board.

Here the speaker is the narrator of the book, who tells how what God had commanded Noah was carried out. The text dwells on the details to show that everything was done in an orderly way, just as God had directed. After this, the account says that God shut the door.

For today: God cares for even the smallest details and takes an interest in every creature. We can trust that he also cares for our lives. And like Noah, we can obey him step by step, even when we do not understand everything that lies ahead.
exp.25:2:
God tells Isaac to stay and live in the land of Canaan, and promises to be with him and to bless him. He also promises to give all these lands to Isaac and to his offspring. "Offspring" means descendants, and "oath" is a solemn promise that God had already made to Abraham, Isaac's father.

It is the LORD who speaks, appearing to Isaac in the middle of a famine. Isaac had gone to Gerar, and it was natural to think of going down to Egypt for food. But God tells him not to go and to remain where he is. In this way he confirms that the promise given to Abraham now continues with Isaac.

For today: when difficult times come, the most logical way out is not always the one God wants. Before deciding out of fear, seek God in prayer and in his Word. If he asks you to wait, trust that his presence and his faithfulness will sustain you.
exp.31:27:
The explanation says that the man who wrestled with Jacob changes his name. He will no longer be called Jacob but Israel, because he has struggled with God and with men, and has prevailed. "Prevailed" means that he kept wrestling and came out the winner, and "struggled" describes that long, determined contest. Many explain that "Israel" sounds like "struggles with God" or "God struggles," although its exact meaning is debated.

Jacob is alone, at night, and fears meeting his brother Esau, whom he had deceived. A mysterious man wrestles with him until dawn. Jacob holds on and asks for a blessing. Later, he himself says that he saw God face to face. The new name marks a change in his life.

For today: when you are distressed, do not run from God. Come to Him with honesty, pray with persistence, and ask for His blessing. God can transform you in the midst of the struggle.
exp.48:0:
Jacob calls all of his sons and asks them to gather around him. He tells them he is going to declare to them what will happen to them "in the days to come," that is, in the future, in the times that would come after. The words "so that I can tell you" in the Berean wording are a way of saying "I am about to announce to you."

Jacob speaks as an old man, near his death, in Egypt. He wants to leave his sons, who will become the tribes of Israel, words of farewell and blessing. Some scholars understand this as a prophecy; others as a portrait of the character and destiny of each tribe. What follows includes both warnings and promises.

For today: Value the time you have with your family and speak to them with honesty and love while you can. Do not wait until the end of life to leave them words that encourage them, correct them with kindness, and point them toward God.
exp.4:21:
The explanation says that Enoch walked with God for three hundred years after he became the father of Methuselah, and that he also had other sons and daughters. To "become the father of" someone means to have a son. To "walk with God" is a way of saying that he lived in closeness, trust, and obedience to Him.

The author of Genesis is a narrator who tells the story of humanity through a list of generations. Almost everyone in the list ends with "and he died," but Enoch stands out for his relationship with God. The verse that follows says that God "took him," and gives no further explanation; the Bible does not give details of how it happened.

For today: faith is lived in everyday life. Enoch walked with God while raising his family. We can do the same if, in the midst of work and home, we seek God each day with prayer and simple obedience.
exp.27:4:
Isaac sent Jacob to Paddan-aram, a region north of Canaan. There lived Laban, the brother of Rebekah, who was the mother of Jacob and Esau. The word "Aramean" shows that Bethuel and his family belonged to that people.

It is the narrator who tells this, right after Isaac blessed Jacob. Isaac told him not to marry a Canaanite woman and instead to seek a wife among the relatives of his mother. According to the account, Rebekah also wanted to keep him safe from the anger of Esau, who was angry over the blessing Jacob had received. The blessing of Abraham thus passes to Jacob.

God often guides our steps even in difficult or confusing situations. When you have to make an important decision, seek counsel from people of faith and look for God's direction, trusting that He keeps His promises.
exp.10:2:
The explanation says that the people of Shinar encouraged one another to make bricks and bake them. So the brick served them in place of stone, and the tar, a sticky substance similar to asphalt, served them in place of mortar to hold the bricks together. Phrases like "Come, let us" are an invitation to get going, and "thoroughly" means fully and completely.

The people speaking at that time shared one language. In Shinar, a plain of Mesopotamia, there was no stone close at hand, so they made do with what they had. This practical step is the beginning of a larger project: the city and the tower. The text does not say the bricks were poor; what God examines afterward is their purpose, to make a name for themselves.

For today: ability and ingenuity are good gifts, but it is wise to ask what we use them for. Before starting a project, ask yourself whether you seek to honor God and serve others, or only to exalt yourself.
exp.2:19:
Here Adam gives his wife a name: Eve. He says the reason is that she would be the mother of all the living, meaning all of humanity. In Hebrew, the name Eve is related to the word for "life," although some scholars debate its exact origin.

The narrator tells us what Adam does right after God announced the consequences of sin, including death. Even so, Adam names his wife with a name that speaks of life and of the future. Many see this as a sign of faith that God would continue to care for humanity, and some connect it with the earlier promise about the woman's offspring. Others see it simply as an act of authority and of accepting reality.

For today: even in the midst of pain and difficult consequences, we can choose to speak and live with hope, trusting that God continues to work in favor of life.
exp.43:29:
This verse is part of a sentence that continues into the next one. It says that if the boy is not with Judah when he returns to his father, the old man will suffer greatly, because his life is wrapped up in the boy's life. "Boy" means a young man, "your servant" is the humble way Judah speaks of himself and his father, and "wrapped up in" expresses a very deep attachment.

Judah, brother of Joseph, is speaking before Joseph, whom he does not yet recognize and sees as the ruler of Egypt. Benjamin, the youngest, has been accused of theft. Judah pleads that he be set free and offers to stay as a slave in his place, so as not to cause more suffering to his father Jacob, who, as he believed, had already lost Joseph.

For today: true love shows itself when we are willing to bear the cost for others. Let us think today about who needs us to protect or accompany them, and take one concrete step of help.
exp.6:17:
The explanation says that the water kept rising higher and higher and covered the earth with great force. The waters "surged and rose" and kept growing stronger until they overwhelmed everything in their path. Yet the ark did not sink. It floated on the surface of the waters.

Genesis tells this as a flood account, and here the narrator is speaking, not a character. God had already warned Noah of the judgment that was coming because of the violence and wickedness on the earth, and had commanded him to build the ark. The previous verse says that the LORD shut him in, a sign that God was caring for Noah and his family.

For today: when problems rise like a flood, remember that God can sustain you. Obeying Him does not keep every storm away, but He keeps you safe in the midst of it.
exp.40:51:
Here Joseph gives his second son his name: Ephraim. That name sounds like a Hebrew word connected with "being fruitful" or "bearing fruit." Joseph says that God has made him fruitful in the land where he suffered. "Affliction" means prolonged pain or suffering.

Joseph speaks as a grateful father. He was sold by his brothers, made a slave, and unjustly imprisoned in Egypt. Now he is a man of authority, with a wife and children. In naming Manasseh he spoke of forgetting his pain, and with Ephraim he acknowledges that God blessed him right in the place of his suffering. He credits everything to God, not to his own merit.

For today: God can bring fruit even in the places where we have suffered most. We can recognize with gratitude the good He has done in the midst of difficulties, without denying the past pain, and give thanks for those blessings.
exp.46:27:
This verse says that Jacob lived seventeen years in Egypt, and that the length of his life was 147 years. It is a simple summary: how long he stayed there and how long he lived in all.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Jacob, also called Israel, had come to Egypt in old age, because his son Joseph ruled there and had saved him and his family from the famine. They enjoyed years of peace in Goshen, and the verse announces that his life is drawing near its end, as becomes clear shortly afterward when he asks to be buried in the land of his fathers.

For today: our days are numbered, and God can give us years of peace and rest even after very hard times. It is worth making good use of the time, caring for family, and leaving a faith that others can inherit.
exp.3:0:
Genesis 4:1 says that Adam "had relations with" his wife Eve, a discreet way of describing marital intimacy. She became pregnant and gave birth to Cain. Then she declared: "With the help of the LORD I have brought forth a man," meaning that with God's help she had given birth to a son.

The speaker is Eve. This is the first birth recorded in the Bible, after Adam and Eve had left the garden of Eden. Her words show gratitude to God. Some think she may have hoped that this son would be the fulfillment of the promise of a descendant who would defeat evil, but the text does not state this clearly. The name Cain sounds like the Hebrew word for "to acquire."

For today: recognize that children and every good thing are a gift from God. Thank Him simply, and pray that those He has entrusted to you will learn to follow Him.
exp.28:18:
Laban replies to Jacob that he prefers to give his daughter Rachel to him rather than to another man. Then he says, "Stay here with me." The phrase "stay here with me" means remaining to live and work in his household.

The speaker is Laban, Jacob's uncle. Jacob had come fleeing from his brother Esau and fell in love with Rachel. Since he had no money to pay a bride price, he offered to work seven years. Laban agrees, though his answer sounds practical and convenient for himself: he gained a worker. He says nothing clear about the plan he would later have, for he would later deceive Jacob.

For today: when you make an agreement, be clear and honest, and do not rely only on kind words. Put what is important in writing and act with integrity, even when others do not.
exp.33:22:
Here Hamor and his son Shechem speak to the men of their city. They say that if everyone agrees to be circumcised like Jacob's family, their livestock, their possessions, and all their animals will become ours. "Possessions" means goods or wealth. "Consent" means to come to an agreement.

Shechem had dishonored Dinah, Jacob's daughter, and now he wanted to marry her. Hamor proposes an alliance and a joining of the two peoples. To the men of the city he no longer speaks of love, but of gain: he offers Jacob's wealth as the attraction. That self-interested way of presenting the proposal has something of manipulation in it, and the narrative does not approve of it.

For today: be wary of decisions justified by gain while the true motive is hidden. Before committing to something, ask yourself whether it is moved by truth or only by convenience. And remember that the revenge of Jacob's sons was not righteous either.
exp.40:52:
This verse says that the seven years of abundance in Egypt came to an end. "Abundance" means having more than enough to eat. It is a short phrase that marks the close of one period.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks. Joseph is already a ruler under Pharaoh and has stored up grain, as God had made known to him through the dreams. Shortly before, Joseph named his two sons with gratitude for what God had done in his life. Now the account moves forward toward the time of famine he had foretold.

For today: good times do not last forever, so it is wise to live them with gratitude and wisdom. We can save, prepare, and trust God, without letting comfort make us forget him.
exp.48:12:
This verse says that the tribe of Zebulun would live by the seashore, in a place where ships come in and find shelter. A "harbor for ships" is a place where boats can take refuge. "His border" is the tribe's boundary, which would extend as far as Sidon, an ancient city on the northern coast.

Jacob, now old, blesses his sons and announces what the future will hold for each tribe. Here he speaks of Zebulun, his tenth son. Scholars debate whether the tribe's territory really touched the coast, since Joshua places it instead near the Sea of Galilee and the Mediterranean. For that reason some understand the phrase as nearness or commercial influence.

For today: God gives each person a different place and task. Ask yourself where he has placed you and how you can serve there, being a shelter and a help to those who come into your life.
exp.10:16:
The explanation says that Eber lived 430 years after he became the father of Peleg, and that he had other sons and daughters. The phrase "after he had become the father of Peleg" in your verse tells us that Eber's long life continued past the birth of his son Peleg.

These words are part of the genealogy that runs from Shem to Abram. The narrator, traditionally Moses, does not speak of great deeds but follows the family line through which the people of Israel would come. Some believe the ages are literal; others think they have a symbolic meaning or are shaped by the writer's style. The Bible does not fully make this clear.

For today: God cares for every generation, including people who barely appear in the accounts. Your everyday life, your family, and your faithfulness also matter to Him and can be part of something greater than you can see.
exp.11:0:
God tells Abram to leave his land, his relatives, and his father's household, and to go to a place that God has not yet shown him.

The one speaking is the LORD. Before this moment, the Bible says that Abram's family had left Ur and settled in Haran. Now God calls him to move on. With this call begins the story of Abram, whom God would later name Abraham, and the promise of blessing that follows in the verses after.

God often calls us to take steps of faith without showing us the whole path. Today we might ask ourselves: what comfortable or familiar thing is God asking me to let go of? Obeying one step at a time, trusting in his promise, is a simple way to live that faith.
exp.16:1:
God tells Abram that he will establish a covenant, meaning a solemn and firm promise between the two of them. He also assures him that he will multiply him greatly. The reader's wording "I will multiply you exceedingly" carries the same idea as the original: "exceedingly" means "in great abundance" or "abundantly."

The LORD, God Almighty, speaks when Abram is ninety-nine years old. Years earlier God had already promised him descendants, but Sarah's son had not yet come. Now God renews and confirms his promise, and asks Abram to walk before him and be blameless. Abram responds with reverence, falling on his face.

God keeps what he promises, even when it seems to us late or impossible. Today we can trust him when the waiting stretches on, and keep walking with honesty and obedience, without depending only on what we see.
exp.8:8:
God tells Noah and his sons that He Himself establishes a covenant, that is, a solemn promise, with them and with their descendants. The word "descendants" refers to the children and generations who would come after them.

God speaks after the flood, when Noah and his family come out of the ark. They have just lived through a terrible judgment and need security. God takes the initiative: He asks nothing in return, but commits Himself never again to destroy the earth with water. The promise also includes the animals.

For today: when you feel fear about the future, remember that God is faithful to what He promises. You can rest in His word, and also trust that His promises reach your family and the generations that come after you.
exp.18:23:
The explanation says that God rained down sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah from heaven. "Rained down" means it fell like rain. The phrase "the LORD... from the LORD" is repeated, and some understand it as a way of stressing that the judgment comes from God himself; others see in it a distinction between divine persons. It is not certain what the exact intention is.

Here the narrator of Genesis is speaking. Earlier, the angels had brought Lot and his family out, because the cities were very wicked. God waited for Lot to arrive safely in Zoar before acting. The judgment was serious, but God also rescued those he could.

For today: God is just, but also merciful. When he warns you or opens a way out, do not delay in obeying. Listen to his voice and take the step today, without looking back with longing.
exp.20:17:
God tells Hagar to get up, to lift up her son and take him by the hand. "Lift up the boy" means to pick him up and support him. "The boy" refers to Ishmael, and "a great nation" means a large nation. God promises that from this young man a numerous people will come.

The speaker is the angel of God, who calls to Hagar from heaven. She and her son had been sent away from Abraham's house and were lost in the desert, with no water. Hagar, in despair, moved away so she would not have to watch her son die. God heard the boy crying and answered with comfort and a promise.

For today: when you feel there is no way out, remember that God hears you even when you do not know what to say. He asks you to get up and take the next step, and often He opens your eyes so you can see the help that was already close by.
exp.28:11:
This verse tells us that Jacob told Rachel who he was: he was Rebekah's son, a relative of her father Laban. The phrase "told Rachel" means that he shared the news about himself with her. Rachel then ran to tell her father. Laban was Rebekah's brother, which made him Jacob's uncle, and the wording of the verse points to that close family tie.

Jacob had arrived after fleeing from his home and was looking for his mother's family. He met Rachel by the well, helped her with the flocks, and, moved with emotion, wept. Now he makes himself known. The Bible does not explain why he wept, but it is understood that he felt relief and emotion on reaching his kin.

For today: when God leads us to a new place, we can introduce ourselves with simplicity and honesty. And when someone comes into our life, we can hurry to welcome them and share the good news.
exp.41:8:
This verse tells us that Joseph, already ruler in Egypt, recognizes his brothers, but they do not recognize him. He remembers the dreams of his youth, in which they bowed down before him. Then he accuses them: "You are spies." The words "if our land is vulnerable" mean the weak or undefended places of Egypt.

Joseph is the one speaking. His brothers came from Canaan because of the famine to buy grain. Years earlier they had sold him as a slave. The commentators do not agree on the exact reason for the accusation: it may be a way of testing them, of learning news of their family, or of seeing whether they had changed. The text does not fully explain it.

For today: when someone has hurt us, God can give us time to act with wisdom and not in haste or revenge. Remembering what God has shown us helps us to seek truth and reconciliation with care.
exp.17:20:
It says that the Lord will go down to Sodom and Gomorrah to see whether their actions fully justify the outcry that has reached him. If not, he will find out. The phrase "fully justify the outcry" means that he will check whether their wickedness has truly reached the extent the reports describe. "I will find out" is human language, used to show that God does not judge lightly.

God is speaking with Abraham, whom he chose to teach righteousness to his family. Earlier he explained that the cry against those cities had grown and that their sin was very grave. After this verse, Abraham comes near and pleads for the righteous. Some think that "I will go down" does not point to any ignorance on God's part, but to his way of acting with justice and patience.

For today: God sees, hears, and examines everything truthfully. We can trust that he is not indifferent to injustice. And, like Abraham, we can pray for others instead of only criticizing them.
exp.29:19:
Leah says that God has given her a good gift, a valuable present of the kind a husband once gave a wife. She hopes that this time her husband will honor her and treat her as a cherished wife. For this reason she names her sixth son Zebulun, a name that sounds close to the Hebrew idea of honoring or dwelling with someone.

Leah speaks in the middle of a painful rivalry with her sister Rachel. Jacob loved Rachel more, and Leah longed to be valued. She sees in her children a sign of God's favor. The Bible does not say whether Jacob changed his treatment of her.

Today we can learn to see God's gifts even in the midst of pain and the desire to be loved. Even so, our worth does not depend on others recognizing us, but on God seeing us and caring for us.
exp.35:9:
This verse lists the first two sons of Esau named in this passage. Eliphaz was born to Adah, and Reuel was born to Basemath, both wives of Esau. The names are spelled as they appear in the Berean Standard Bible, with the spellings "Eliphaz" and "Basemath."

The author of the book (tradition attributes it to Moses) follows the family record of Esau, also called Edom. After telling the story of Jacob, the account shows how God fulfilled his promise to make Esau a nation. This lineage gave rise to the Edomites, neighbors of Israel.

God takes notice of families and of names, even of those who do not continue the main line of the promise. Today we can remember that every person matters to God. Pray for your family, including relatives who seem distant, and trust that God knows them by name.
exp.37:18:
Tamar got up and left that place. She removed the veil she had used to cover her face and put on her widow's clothes again. "Got up and departed" describes her leaving, and "widow's garments" refers to the clothing of a woman whose husband has died.

This is part of the story of Judah and Tamar. Tamar had been left a widow, and Judah did not give her his youngest son to carry on the family line, as was the custom. She disguised herself, and Judah, not recognizing her, spent the night with her. Here the narrator tells what she did afterward: she returned to her ordinary life, with Judah's pledges as proof of what had happened.

God sees what is hidden, and sooner or later the truth comes to light. This story invites us to act with justice and honesty toward vulnerable people, without taking advantage of them or leaving promises unkept.
exp.6:19:
The explanation says that the flood waters rose fifteen cubits above the mountaintops, covering them completely. The waters rose and took control of the land. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly 45 to 50 centimeters, so fifteen cubits would be about seven meters. Some think it refers to the height of the water above the mountains; others, to the depth the water reached so that the ark could float. The text does not fully settle this.

Here the narrator of Genesis speaks, recounting the flood. God had decided to judge the wickedness of the earth, but he had kept Noah, his family, and the animals safe inside the ark. This verse shows that the judgment was total and that no one could escape by their own means.

For today: God does what he says, and his care for those who trust him is firm. When everything seems covered by problems, trust that he can sustain you, as he sustained the ark above the waters.
exp.47:19:
Jacob blesses his two grandsons, Joseph's sons, on that same day. He says that when the people of Israel want to bless someone, they will say: "May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh." The Berean Standard Bible reads "By you shall Israel pronounce this blessing," so the blessing is one the people of Israel will speak using these two boys' names. The verse says that Jacob puts Ephraim before Manasseh, placing the younger boy ahead of the older.

Jacob speaks as an old man, near death, in Egypt. Joseph had brought his sons to him and placed Manasseh, the firstborn, at Jacob's right hand, but Jacob crossed his hands and put his right hand on Ephraim instead. He understood that God would make both of them grow, though Ephraim would become greater. In the Bible, God often acts outside the expected order.

For today: do not measure your worth by your place or by your turn. God does not depend on human positions. You can bless your children or other people by asking that they grow in the grace of God, and trust that He knows what He is doing.
exp.7:7:
This verse tells us that Noah sent a dove out from the ark to check whether the water had gone down from the surface of the ground. "Then Noah sent out a dove" means he released it from the ark, and the purpose is stated plainly: he wanted to know whether the water had receded.

Noah had already sent out the raven, which flew back and forth without giving a clear answer. Now he tries the dove. Inside the ark he could not see the ground, so he used the means he had to know when it was safe to leave. The text does not say why he chose these birds; that is only one possible conclusion.

For today: Noah did not rush or guess. He waited and went step by step. When you face an important decision, trust God, pray, and move forward with patience, without losing heart if the first answer is not the one you hoped for.
exp.35:6:
The explanation says that Esau and Jacob had so much wealth, especially livestock, that they could no longer live together. The land where they were staying could not support so many animals. The word "possessions" means property and belongings.

No one speaks here; it is the narrator of Genesis, who explains why Esau moved to the mountain country of Seir, where the people of Edom came from. The situation is similar to that of Abraham and Lot in Genesis 13, when they also separated for lack of pasture. The text does not mention any quarrel between Esau and Jacob, so the separation seems practical and peaceful.

For today: sometimes parting in peace is better than forcing a living arrangement that no longer works. If there is tension over money, space, or work, look for an orderly and respectful way forward, without resentment.
exp.24:16:
Ishmael, the son of Abraham and Hagar, lived a total of 137 years. Then he breathed his last and died, and was gathered to his people. This phrase is a way of saying that he died and was joined to his own family. Some read it as only a description of death, while others see in it a hint of hope beyond the grave. The Bible does not explain this in detail.

Here the narrator of Genesis speaks, closing the story of Ishmael. God had promised Abraham that Ishmael would have many descendants, and this is seen in the twelve princes of the earlier list. Afterward, the account returns to the line of Isaac, through whom the promise of the covenant would continue.

For today: life passes, but God keeps what He promises. Live thankful for the time God gives you, and trust that He cares for you and your family.
exp.26:37:
Esau asks his father whether he has only one blessing to give. He pleads with him to bless him too, and then he weeps aloud.

Isaac, already old, had given the main blessing to Jacob, believing he was Esau. Jacob pretended to be his brother with the help of their mother, Rebekah. Esau grieves what he has lost, though earlier he had sold his birthright for a bowl of food. Hebrews 12:17 mentions his tears, and the Bible does not make clear everything that was in his heart.

For today: hasty decisions have consequences that cannot later be undone. Value what God has given you and take care of it with wisdom. If you fail, God remains merciful to whoever comes to Him with sincerity.
exp.42:24:
The brothers of Joseph got the gift they had brought for him ready, while they waited for him to arrive at noon. They had been told that they were going to eat a meal there. A "gift" is what they prepared for him, and the meal is the reason they were expecting to stay.

The brothers are in Egypt for a second time, now with Benjamin, because of the famine. Joseph's steward has just calmed their fear and returned Simeon to them. They do not yet know that the ruler is their brother. They prepare the gift to win his favor, since they fear being accused over the money they found in their sacks.

When we are afraid or feel guilty, we may try to set things right with gifts or our own efforts. But God is often already working with kindness, even when we cannot see it. We can prepare ourselves with humility and obedience, trusting that He guides the outcome.
exp.28:32:
Leah became pregnant again and gave birth to another son. She says that the LORD has heard that she is unloved, that she is loved less than her sister, and so he has given her this son as well. She names him Simeon, a name that sounds like the Hebrew word for "hear."

Leah, Jacob's wife, speaks here. Jacob was given to her through a deception by her father Laban, since Jacob loved Rachel. Leah lives in pain and longs for her husband's affection. Here she sees that God attends to her suffering, although at this moment she still does not speak of receiving Jacob's love.

For today: when you feel ignored or undervalued, bring that pain to God honestly. He hears the one who suffers and can give you comfort and hope, even when people do not respond as you would wish.
exp.34:16:
It says that Rachel was going through a very hard and painful labour. The midwife, the woman who helped mothers give birth, speaks to her to calm her. The midwife tells her not to be afraid, and she assures her that she is having another son, meaning the baby will come into the world.

The midwife speaks while the family of Jacob is on the journey toward Ephrath (Bethlehem). Rachel had already longed for another son (Genesis 30:24). Her labour becomes complicated, and the midwife tries to encourage her. The verses that follow tell that Rachel died in giving birth to Benjamin.

For today: in moments of pain or fear, words of encouragement do matter. We can be like that midwife, who stays close and comforts, and we can also bring our fear to God, who is near to those who suffer, even when things do not turn out as we hope.
exp.25:22:
From there Isaac went up to Beersheba. This verse says that Isaac left the place where he had dug the well of Rehoboth and went up to Beersheba. The phrase "went up" indicates that he moved to a higher place in the terrain. The name Beersheba is the same one that appears in the verse.

The account tells what happened to Isaac, the son of Abraham, who lived as a foreigner among the Philistines. After many disputes over water, he finally found a place of peace. Even so, he did not stay there but continued on his way. Then, in Beersheba, God appeared to him that very night to encourage him and remind him of his promise.

After a season of conflict and relief, God knows what the next step in our life should be. Sometimes He moves us from a place of rest to another where He waits for us with words of encouragement. We can trust that He accompanies us in every move and every change.
exp.17:28:
Abraham continues speaking with God and asks what would happen if only forty righteous people were found in the city. God answers that he would not destroy it because of those forty. The words "once again" show that Abraham is making his request one more time, and "suppose" means "what if".

Here Abraham speaks with the Lord, shortly before Sodom is judged. Abraham knows that his nephew Lot lives there. With humility and respect, he gradually lowers the number of righteous people, and God answers him patiently each time. The passage shows that God is not impatient or harsh when someone brings him a sincere plea.

For today: pray with confidence for people and places that concern you, even if you feel your request is small or bold. Do so with humility, knowing that God hears you and is just and compassionate.
exp.23:34:
This verse says that God has blessed Abraham, the master the servant speaks of, very greatly. He has made him rich and has given him sheep and cattle, silver and gold, menservants and maidservants, camels and donkeys. The phrase "he has become rich" means that Abraham grew into a wealthy and important man.

The one speaking is Abraham's servant, probably the oldest servant in his household (Genesis 24:2). He had traveled far to look for a wife for Isaac. Upon arriving at the home of Rebekah's family, before eating, he presents his message. By listing Abraham's riches, he makes clear that everything comes from God and that his master is a man who can be trusted.

For today: when you speak of what you have or what you have achieved, acknowledge God as the one who gave it to you. A grateful life, which gives Him the credit, inspires trust in others.
exp.11:18:
Pharaoh confronts Abram because Abram had said Sarai was his sister. That deception nearly led Pharaoh to take her as his wife. "Putting me in a dangerous or mistaken position" describes the harm Pharaoh says he was pushed into. In the end he gives Abram back his wife and tells him to take her and go.

Pharaoh, king of Egypt, is the one speaking. Abram had gone there because of the famine and, out of fear, asked Sarai to say she was his sister. God struck Pharaoh's house with plagues, and in this way the truth came to light. It is striking that a pagan king rebukes the servant of God with justice.

For today: a lie, even one born of fear, ends up harming others and our testimony. When we are afraid, let us trust God and speak the truth, without resorting to deception to protect ourselves.
exp.22:5:
The people of Heth answer Abraham with great respect. They call him "my lord" and say he is "a mighty prince among us," which can be understood to mean someone powerful or greatly blessed by God. They offer him the finest of their tombs to bury his dead, and they assure him that none of them will refuse him a tomb for burying his dead.

Abraham is a foreigner in Canaan, and he has just lost his wife Sarah. He needs a place to bury her, but he has no land of his own. That is why he asks the Hittites, who are the inhabitants of the region, for a burial place. Their response shows that they respected him for his character and his faith. Some think their offer was generous and sincere; others think it was the opening of a courteous negotiation.

Today this reminds us that living with integrity and kindness earns the respect of others, even when we are strangers in a place. We can also tenderly accompany someone who is in mourning.
exp.41:2:
This verse says that ten of Jacob's sons, Joseph's brothers, traveled to Egypt to buy grain. "Went down" is used because Egypt lay to the south, and people spoke of "going down" to it.

The narrator tells what happened after Jacob, their father, noticed that his sons were sitting idle. There was famine in Canaan, and Jacob ordered them to go buy food so that they would not die. The brothers had no idea they would meet Joseph, whom they had sold years earlier. Benjamin stayed home because Jacob feared losing him too.

For today: when a need arises, do not simply stand "looking on." Take a concrete and sensible step, and at the same time trust that God may be at work in what you cannot yet see.
exp.40:25:
Here Joseph begins to explain the two dreams of Pharaoh. The seven good cows and the seven ripe heads of grain stand for seven years. With the words "The dreams have the same meaning," he says that both dreams carry one single message.

Joseph speaks before Pharaoh, who is troubled because no wise man of Egypt was able to interpret his dreams. Joseph makes clear that the interpretation does not come from his own cleverness, but from God, who shows Pharaoh what he is about to do. The seven good years will be followed by seven years of famine.

For today: God does not always give us everything clearly right away, but he can give us wisdom to prepare ourselves. Make use of good times with gratitude and prudence: save, serve, and take care of what you have. And when you do not understand something, ask God for light with humility, as Joseph did.
exp.4:20:
This verse says that Enoch was sixty-five years old when he became the father of a son named Methuselah.

No one speaks in this passage; the narrator of Genesis lists the generations from Adam onward. It is a family record that shows how the line of descent continued. What stands out comes next: the text says that Enoch "walked with God" after Methuselah was born. Some believe his life of faith deepened when he became a father, though the text does not explain this.

For today: the major changes in life, such as having a child or taking on a new responsibility, can be a good time to draw closer to God. Today you might set aside a few minutes to pray sincerely for your family.
exp.24:28:
This verse tells us that Jacob was cooking a thick stew, probably of lentils, as the text mentions later. At that moment Esau came in from the field, exhausted after hunting or working outdoors.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. He introduces two very different twin brothers: Esau, a man of the field, and Jacob, quiet and a man of the tents. Their parents had different favorites between them. This scene sets up the exchange that follows: Esau, hungry, will end up giving little value to his birthright, the special right of the firstborn son. The Bible does not justify all of Jacob's actions, but it shows how Esau acted without thinking.

For today: when we are tired or strongly longing for something, let us not make important decisions right away. Let us ask God for wisdom and value what is eternal above what is immediate.
exp.1:20:
This verse tells that the LORD God caused the man to fall into a deep sleep. While he slept, God took one of the man's ribs and closed up the area with flesh. The word for "rib" can also be understood as "side," since the Hebrew term is interpreted in both ways. "The man" is Adam, and "the LORD God" is the name of God.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks. Adam had just named the animals and did not find among them anyone suitable, that is, fitting for him. God responds to that need by creating the woman. Afterward, Adam receives her with joy.

For today: God sees our real needs and acts with care. We can trust that he provides what we need in his time. We can also value the people God places beside us, as companions on the journey, with respect and gratitude.
exp.39:14:
Here Joseph says that he was "kidnapped", that is, taken by force and carried away from the land of the Hebrews. He also states that in Egypt he has done nothing wrong to deserve being put in this dungeon. The word "that" here means "for the reason that" or "because".

Joseph speaks with Pharaoh's cupbearer, to whom he has just explained his dream with good news. He asks him to remember him and speak to Pharaoh. Joseph mentions his history because his brothers sold him and he was later imprisoned unjustly (Genesis 39). He tells the truth simply, without insulting anyone, and seeks help to get out of that situation.

For today: when you suffer an injustice, you can tell the truth calmly and ask for help without bitterness. Do what is within your reach, but trust that God works in his time, even when people forget you.
exp.23:64:
In this verse, Rebekah sees a man walking across the field toward them and asks the servant who he is. The servant answers, "It is my master," meaning Isaac. Then she takes her veil and covers herself.

The narrator describes the end of a long journey. Abraham's servant had been sent to find a wife for Isaac, and Rebekah agreed to go with him. Now she sees her future husband for the first time. The text does not say with certainty why she covered herself; many understand it as a gesture of respect, modesty, or preparation for marriage, according to the customs of that time.

For today: the moment of meeting someone important deserves respect and humility. Rebekah did not act with haste or carelessness, but with reverence. We can learn to begin our relationships with honor, and to trust that God guides the steps of those who seek him.
exp.18:8:
The men of Sodom push Lot aside with contempt. "Get out of the way!" they say. They accuse him of being a foreigner who came to live among them, and now he is acting like a judge over them. They threaten to treat him even worse than his visitors, they press in on him roughly, and they move to break down the door.

The crowd of Sodom, which had surrounded Lot's house, is speaking. He had just tried to protect his guests, who were angels, although his offer to hand over his daughters is very harsh, and the Bible does not present it as an example to follow. The people take offense because Lot, being a foreigner, calls them out for their wickedness.

For today: when someone corrects us, it is easy to respond with mockery or anger. Let us ask God for a humble heart to listen, and for courage to speak the truth with love, even when it costs us.
exp.38:6:
After some time, Potiphar's wife looked at Joseph with desire. "Cast her eyes upon Joseph" means she looked at him with interest and lust. Then she said to him plainly, "Sleep with me," that is, she proposed that they have sexual relations. It was an invitation to commit adultery.

Here the speaker is Potiphar's wife. Joseph was a young Hebrew slave, to whom his master had given authority over his entire household, and God was blessing him. The text says Joseph was handsome. She used her position of power to pressure him. Joseph then refused, because it would betray his master's trust and sin against God.

For today: temptation sometimes comes directly and in moments of trust. Decide your limits in advance, and if the test comes, say "no" firmly, thinking first of your faithfulness to God.
exp.5:15:
God gives Noah instructions for the ark. He is to make a roof for it and finish its walls a cubit (about 45 to 50 cm) from the top. He is to place a door in the side of the ark, and build lower, middle, and upper decks. The word translated "roof" is unclear; some think it refers to an opening for light and air, others to an open strip just under the top. It is not certain what the exact meaning is.

God is speaking, having already told Noah that a flood would come because of the great wickedness of the earth. He gives precise measurements so that the ark would serve its purpose: to save Noah, his family, and the animals. God also promises to establish his covenant with him.

For today: Noah obeyed the details without changing the plan. We can trust that God cares even for the small things when he guides us. Obeying him step by step, even when we do not understand everything, is a simple way to show faith.
exp.40:36:
It says the proposal pleased Pharaoh and all his officials, that is, his advisers and the men who served his court. The word "proposal" here means a plan or suggestion, not a business deal.

Joseph had just interpreted Pharaoh's dreams: seven years of plenty would come, followed by seven years of famine. Without being asked, Joseph proposed storing grain during the good years to have reserves for the bad ones. Pharaoh and his court heard him and approved the idea. That is why Pharaoh soon recognizes that Joseph has the "Spirit of God" in him.

For today: the wisdom that comes from God also shows itself in foreseeing and organizing with order. Saving, planning, and preparing ourselves with humility is a practical way of caring for our family and serving others.
exp.40:23:
Pharaoh recounts the last part of his dream: the thin, withered heads of grain were swallowing the seven plump, healthy ones. The word "magicians" refers to the wise men or diviners of Egypt. Pharaoh says he has already told all of them about the dream, but none of them could explain it to him.

Here Pharaoh speaks, troubled because his dreams disturb him. This is the moment when the cupbearer remembers Joseph, who was in prison. Egypt's experts fail, and then God uses Joseph to give the answer, as seen in what follows.

For today: there are questions and problems that no human wisdom can solve. When you find yourself with no way out, come to God with humility, asking Him for light, and trust that He can use unexpected people and circumstances to give you direction.
exp.24:23:
This verse tells us that the time came for Rebekah to give birth. "To give birth" means to bring a child into the world, and "twins" are two children born together. What God had told her is confirmed: there were two babies in her womb, not one.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Rebekah, wife of Isaac, had felt the children struggling inside her and had asked God what was happening. God told her that two nations would come from them, and that the older would serve the younger. After the verse we see Esau and Jacob being born.

For today: God keeps his word in his own time, even when months or years pass and we do not understand everything. Like Rebekah, when something troubles or confuses us, we can bring it to God in prayer and wait with confidence.
exp.18:32:
This verse tells that Lot's two daughters got their father drunk on wine. The firstborn went in and slept with him. Lot was so drunk that he was not aware when she lay down or when she got up. Here, "slept with" means having sexual relations.

Lot and his daughters had just escaped the destruction of Sodom and were living alone in a cave. The daughters believed that no man was left who could give them children, so they came up with this plan. The Bible recounts what happened without approving of it; it shows the bad decisions that come from fear and despair.

For today: when we feel afraid or see everything as lost, let us not take crooked paths on our own. It is better to trust God and ask for His guidance, because He cares for us even in the darkest moments.
exp.27:6:
