Here Laban and Bethuel tell Abraham's servant that Rebekah is standing right in front of him. They tell him to take her and go, so that she may become the wife of his master's son, Isaac. They acknowledge that this all comes from the LORD.

The family of Rebekah speaks. Abraham's servant had traveled far to find a wife for Isaac. He told them how God had guided him to Rebekah at the well. When they heard the account, they saw the hand of God and did not want to stand in its way. Afterward, the servant bowed down to worship God.

For today: when you see that God opens a door clearly, do not resist out of fear or self-interest. Recognize his work, respond with humility, and give thanks to him before moving forward.
exp.49:10:
The verse tells us that the Canaanites, the people living in that land, saw the mourning that took place at the threshing floor of Atad. A threshing floor is a flat piece of ground where grain was beaten out of the stalks. They said, "This is a solemn ceremony of mourning by the Egyptians." Because of this, the place across the Jordan was called Abel-mizraim, a name that sounds like "mourning of Egypt." Here the mourning refers to a public ceremony of grief.

Jacob had just died in Egypt, and Joseph was taking him to be buried in Canaan, as his father had asked. A large company of Egyptians went with him. The ones speaking are the Canaanites, outside observers who did not know the family. It is not known with certainty where Atad was; "across the Jordan" can be understood in different ways depending on where one looks from.

For today: grief is part of life, and honoring those we love is something good. When someone suffers a loss, accompany them with your presence, without rushing them or offering empty words.
exp.37:28:
When the baby who had first put out his hand pulled it back, his brother was born. The midwife said, "You have broken out first!" That is why he was named Perez, a name linked to the idea of breaking out or breaking through.

Tamar gave birth to twins, sons of Judah. The midwife had tied a red thread on the hand of the first one to appear, but the other one came out first. The one speaking is the midwife, surprised by the unexpected turn of events. Perez appears later in the line of David and in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:3). The Bible does not explain more; not everything is made clear here.

For today: God does not depend on our plans or on the orders that seem fixed. He can act in unexpected ways, and even in complicated stories he continues to fulfill his purpose. Trust him when everything seems disordered.
exp.42:29:
Here the account tells us that Joseph hurried out because he was moved to tears by his love for his brother Benjamin. The text says he was moved to tears for his brother, which means he felt a very strong, tender emotion at seeing him. He then went to a private room to weep.

This is the account of Joseph, already ruler in Egypt, when his brothers come to buy food. They do not recognize him. It is the first time he sees Benjamin, his brother from the same father and mother, after many years. Joseph has not yet revealed who he is, so he goes to a private room to weep without being seen.

God made us with emotions, and weeping is not weakness. Joseph shows that true love is felt deep within the heart. Today we can seek a quiet moment to weep and pray, and also let love for our family move us to forgive and to be reconciled.
exp.48:17:
Jacob says he confidently awaits God's salvation. In today's English, "salvation" means deliverance, rescue from danger or trouble, and not simply good health. The Hebrew word (yeshuá) speaks of liberation. The name of God used here is the LORD. It is a brief prayer in the middle of a long blessing.

Jacob speaks as an old man on his deathbed, blessing and foretelling the future of his twelve sons. He has just spoken about Dan, with images of danger and struggle. Many think that, thinking about those struggles, Jacob turns to God and places his hope in Him. The text does not explain exactly why he says it here, so it is understood in several ways.

For today: when you see conflicts or an uncertain future, pause and pray. Place your hope in God, not only in your own strength.
exp.30:23:
God comes to Laban the Aramean in a dream that night and warns him, "Be careful not to say anything to Jacob, either good or bad." The warning means not to speak to Jacob in extremes, whether harshly, violently or with crude threats. The phrase "be careful" is the same idea as "watch yourself."

Laban had been chasing Jacob with his relatives, because Jacob had left secretly with his wives, his children and his possessions. Laban felt deceived and had the power to do harm. The text does not say exactly what Jacob feared would happen, but God steps in before the meeting and protects Jacob. It is God who speaks, and he speaks to Laban in a dream.

For today: God cares for his own even when they do not see him at work. When you face a conflict or a fear, pray and trust that God works in quiet ways. And when you are angry, remember that God asks you to speak with self-control.
exp.26:0:
This verse tells us that Isaac was now very old and could no longer see. He called his older son Esau and said to him, "My son." Esau replied, "Here I am."

The phrase about Isaac's eyes, which in this translation says his eyes were so weak that he could no longer see, describes his blindness as the result of age.

Here the story of Isaac's blessing begins. The narrator presents an aging father who wants to pass the family blessing to his older son. Rebekah and Jacob will also play an important part later. The text does not explain everything Isaac was thinking, but it shows that the moment was approaching for him to hand on his spiritual and family inheritance.

For today: let us not leave what is important for later. If we have the opportunity, let us bless, counsel, and express love to our family with time, wisdom, and honesty, and seek God's direction.
exp.4:25:
It says that Methuselah lived 782 years after he became the father of his son Lamech, and that during those years he had other sons and daughters. The verse uses the phrase "became the father of," which means he had a son. The older forms of the names, which the explanation notes, are Mathusalam and Lamech. Adding the 187 years before, his years total 969.

This is part of the genealogy in Genesis 5, a third-person account with no character speaking. Its purpose is to show the line of descendants from Adam toward Noah, and how life continued even under the shadow of death. Earlier, Enoch is mentioned, who walked with God. Methuselah was his son. How to understand these very long lifespans is interpreted in several ways, and there is no single certain explanation.

For today: our life is much more than a name in a list. Methuselah raised a family over many years. We can use our time to form our own children in the faith, just as Enoch left an example of walking with God.
exp.20:32:
Genesis 21:33 says that Abraham planted a tamarisk tree in Beersheba and there called upon the name of the LORD, the Eternal God. The word for the tree can be understood as a tamarisk, a tree that gives shade; scholars do not fully agree on this. "The LORD" is the name of God, and "called upon" means that Abraham called on him in prayer and worship.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Abraham had just made a peace agreement with Abimelech over a well of water. After the agreement, Abraham was not only content with human peace, but worshiped God. It is the only time in Genesis that God is called "the Eternal God."

For today: when God gives you a breathing space, a solution, or peace in a conflict, do not forget to thank him. And in the midst of what changes, remember that God does not change.
exp.36:17:
Now Joseph's brothers saw him in the distance, and before he arrived, they plotted to kill him. "Plotted" means they thought through and arranged something on purpose.

Here the narrator of the story is speaking. Joseph, sent by his father Jacob, went to look for his brothers to find out how they were doing. They envied him and held a grudge against him because of his father's special affection for him and because of his dreams. That buried resentment now turns into a violent plan.

For today: resentment that is never faced grows quietly and can lead us to do harm. If you feel envy or anger toward someone, bring it to God in prayer and speak honestly before your heart becomes hard.
exp.31:31:
This verse explains a custom of the Israelites: they did not eat the tendon attached to the socket of the hip, the part where the thigh joins the hip bone. The explanation notes that the tendon is the one near the socket of the hip, and that the reason for avoiding it is that the socket of Jacob's hip was struck near that tendon. The memory recalled here is the moment Jacob was struck in that place.

The one who speaks is the narrator of the book. Earlier, Jacob wrestled all night with a mysterious man, who struck him on the hip, and Jacob was left limping. Afterward he recognized that he had seen God. The text does not say where or when this custom began, only that it continued "to this day" when it was written.

For today: sometimes God uses our struggles to leave a mark that reminds us we depend on Him. Today we can think about a past difficulty and give thanks for what it taught us, rather than being ashamed of it.
exp.9:23:
This verse is part of a list of families. It says that Arphaxad was the father of Shelah, and that Shelah was the father of Eber. Today many write these names as Arfaxad, Sala, and Éber.

We are in the "Table of Nations" in Genesis 10. The narrator, whom tradition identifies with Moses, reviews the descendants of Noah's sons after the flood. Here the text follows the line of Shem. This line leads to Eber, and later in Genesis it leads to Abraham. Scholars debate how direct each connection is, but the text shows how humanity spread out.

For today: God pays attention to every generation, even when some names seem to us to be only a list. Your life and your faith are also part of a larger story. Live with gratitude for those who came before you, and with the desire to pass on faith to those who come after.
exp.40:24:
Here Joseph tells Pharaoh that his two dreams, the one of the cows and the one of the ears of grain, are really one message. The words "The dreams of Pharaoh are one and the same" state this directly. Joseph adds that God has revealed to Pharaoh what He is about to do, meaning that the event comes from God and not from chance.

Joseph speaks at the court of Egypt, a Hebrew prisoner who has just been called before the king. Pharaoh's magicians had not been able to explain the dreams. Joseph does not claim the credit for himself but points to God as the one who reveals and the one who acts. He will go on to explain that seven years of plenty and seven years of famine are coming.

For today: when you have the chance to help others with your ability or knowledge, acknowledge with humility that everything comes from God. And if God warns you of something difficult that is coming, use it to prepare yourself with wisdom, not with fear.
exp.26:27:
Isaac blesses Jacob and prays that God will give him "the dew of heaven," the moisture that makes crops grow in dry land. He also prays that God will give him "the richness of the earth," the best and most fertile part of the soil, and "an abundance of grain and new wine," that is, plenty of bread and fresh wine pressed from grapes.

Isaac speaks as an old man who is nearly blind. He believes he is blessing Esau, his firstborn son, but Jacob has disguised himself as Esau, deceiving his father with the help of his mother Rebekah. In that culture, a father's blessing carried great weight and was understood as a word that God stood behind. The account shows the deception without approving it, and its consequences will come later.

For today: every provision comes from the hand of God, not from our schemes. We can trust that He cares for us and wait for his promises without resorting to lies or shortcuts.
exp.17:32:
This verse tells us that the Lord departed as soon as he had finished speaking with Abraham, and that Abraham returned home. The wording here is simple in the Berean Standard Bible, so there is no need to explain older terms.

Abraham had just asked God, again and again, not to destroy the city of Sodom if there were fifty, forty, thirty, twenty, and even ten righteous people in it. God answered patiently each time. Here the conversation ends. The text does not say why Abraham stopped asking; that is left unexplained. It also does not yet say what will happen to the city.

For today: we can pray with confidence and sincerity, even for other people, as Abraham did. And after praying, we learn to rest, leaving the outcome in God's hands, who is just and merciful.
exp.28:17:
Genesis 29:18 says that Jacob loved Rachel and proposed to Laban, her father, that he would work for him seven years in exchange for marrying her. The verse also identifies Rachel as Laban's younger daughter.

Jacob had arrived at the house of his uncle Laban, fleeing from his brother Esau. There he met Rachel and fell in love with her because of her beauty. At that time he had no money to offer as a bride price, so he offered his labor instead. He speaks directly to Laban, who accepts the proposal in the next verse.

For today: true love is willing to wait, to work hard, and to commit. Jacob saw the time as "a few days" because he loved. We can ask ourselves what we are willing to give with patience for the people and goals we truly value, including in our relationship with God.
exp.9:12:
This verse lists some of the descendants of Mizraim, which is the Hebrew name for Egypt. "Was the father of" means these names stand for the founders of peoples or tribes, which is how such lists are usually understood. The Ludites, Anamites, Lehabites and Naphtuhites are groups thought to have lived in northern Africa and nearby regions. Scholars do not know their exact locations with complete certainty.

This is part of the genealogy of the nations in Genesis 10. The narrator, traditionally identified with Moses, shows how after the flood the sons of Noah populated the earth. Mizraim was a son of Ham. The list continues with other peoples, including the Philistines.

For today: God knows the names and origin of every people. No person is a number to Him. Today we can treat everyone with respect, remembering that we come from one common origin and that God values us.
exp.30:54:
Early the next morning, Laban got up, kissed his grandchildren and his daughters, and blessed them. Then he left and went back home.

Jacob had fled from Laban, his father-in-law, with his wives, his children, and his possessions. Laban caught up with him, there was tension and accusations, and in the end they made a covenant of peace. This verse closes that story. Here the narrator tells us that the conflict ended without violence.

For today: even when there are wounds or disagreements within the family, we can seek a peaceful farewell. Blessing others, instead of holding on to resentment, helps us close conflicts with dignity and trust that God cares for everyone.
exp.13:6:
This verse tells how the eastern kings, after defeating other peoples, turned back and came to En-mishpat, which is Kadesh. There they conquered the whole territory of the Amalekites. They also attacked the Amorites who lived in Hazazon-tamar. The word "territory" here refers to the lands and settlements that belonged to the Amalekites. "Conquered" means that they overpowered these peoples and took control of their land.

Moses, the traditional author of Genesis, narrates a military campaign by Chedorlaomer and his allies. It describes how they advanced, conquering region after region. This prepares the scene for the war against Sodom and its neighbors, where Lot, Abraham's nephew, was living. Some scholars note that "Amalekites" here refers to a territory that later took that name, but this is interpreted in different ways.

For today: human power can seem unstoppable, but it is always passing. This story reminds us not to place our trust in strength, money or influence, but in God, who cares for his own even in the middle of conflicts that seem bigger than we are.
exp.18:28:
This verse sums up what happened to Sodom and Gomorrah. When God destroyed the cities of the plain, he remembered Abraham and brought Lot out of the catastrophe that wiped out the cities where Lot had lived. "Catastrophe" here means complete destruction, and "brought out" means he led Lot safely away.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not a character. After describing the smoke Abraham saw from a distance, the text explains why Lot was saved. It does not say this was because of Lot's merits, but because God remembered Abraham, who had pleaded for those cities (Genesis 18). In the Bible, to "remember" someone means to act on their behalf.

For today: our prayers for others matter. Pray for your family and friends, trusting that God cares for them with mercy, even when you cannot see how.
exp.31:7:
Jacob divides all his people into two groups, along with his sheep, cattle, and camels. He thinks that if Esau attacks one camp and destroys it, the other camp will be able to escape.

Jacob speaks after his messengers tell him that Esau is coming with four hundred men. Years earlier, Jacob had deceived Esau and fled from him. Now he is returning to his land and fears for his life. We do not know for certain what Esau intends; the text only shows Jacob's fear.

It is wise to make careful plans when facing danger. But Jacob does not stop at his strategy: right after, he prays and remembers God's promises. We can think carefully and act responsibly, but also bring our fear before God and trust in his faithfulness.
exp.42:13:
Jacob prays that God Almighty will grant his sons mercy from that man in Egypt, so that he will release their other brother, Simeon, along with Benjamin. Then he says that if he must lose his children, he will accept it. "Man" here means a man, and "mercy" refers to compassionate treatment.

Jacob speaks as an old man. There is famine in the land, and his sons must return to Egypt for food. Simeon was kept there, and the governor demanded to see Benjamin. Jacob does not know that this man is Joseph. After resisting, he gives in and sends Benjamin, along with double money and a gift.

For today: when you cannot control the outcome, do what is wise, entrust the matter to God in prayer, and rest in the knowledge that he cares for those you love, even when it hurts.
exp.20:12:
God tells Abraham that he will also make a nation of Ishmael, the son of Hagar. The BSB calls Hagar the slave woman, Sarah's servant. Ishmael is described as Abraham's offspring, meaning his own son. To make a nation means that God will make him into a great people.

God speaks. Sarah had asked that Hagar and Ishmael be sent away, and Abraham suffered greatly over his son. God comforts him: the main promise would continue through Isaac, but Ishmael would not be forgotten. Afterward Abraham sends them away, and in the desert God would again care for them.

For today: when a situation hurts us and has no easy solution, we can trust that God cares for the people who seem to be left outside the plan. Give Him your worries about those you love, and act responsibly toward them.
exp.49:19:
Genesis 50:20 says that Joseph's brothers intended to harm him when they sold him into slavery, but God intended that same act for good. The verse uses the words "what you intended against me for evil" and "God intended for good," so the explanation focuses on intention. The purpose of the good was to bring about a day like the one Joseph was living through, which was the preservation of the lives of many people.

Joseph speaks to his brothers after the death of their father Jacob. They feared that he would now take revenge for what they had done to him. Joseph, who was a ruler in Egypt and had stored up food during the famine, does not place himself in God's position to judge them. He answers them with forgiveness and comfort.

Today, this invites us not to live bitter because of the harm we have received. God does not approve of evil, but he can work even within it. We can hand our wounds over to him, forgive, and trust that he is still at work, even when we do not yet understand everything.
exp.1:12:
The explanation says that the second river that flowed out of Eden was called Gihon, and that it winds through the whole land of Cush. In Hebrew the region is named Cush, and today it is not known with certainty where that region was, since scholars have located it in different ways. "Winds through" means that the river twists and turns across the land.

The narrator of Genesis, traditionally associated with Moses, describes the garden of Eden as a real place, with a river that divides into four branches. He names rivers and regions so that the reader understands that God prepared a fertile and rich land for human beings, just before placing him there to work.

For today: God cares about the details of what he gives us. Give thanks for the concrete provisions of your life, such as water, food and work, and receive them as gifts from God that you should care for responsibly.
exp.24:12:
This verse begins the list of the sons of Ishmael, the son Abraham had with Hagar, the Egyptian servant of Sarah. The first four are named: Nebaioth, the firstborn of Ishmael, then Kedar, Adbeel, and Mibsam. The list is given in the order of their birth, and the families that came from each son are the people who descended from him.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, traditionally attributed to Moses. After recounting the death of Abraham, he records the story of Ishmael before continuing with Isaac. This shows that God kept his promise to make Ishmael into a great nation (Genesis 17:20). Kedar appears later in other passages of the Bible as a people of the desert.

For today: God remembers names and keeps his promises, even with those who seem to stand at the edge of the story. You can trust that he sees you and cares for your life and your family.
exp.5:11:
God looked at the earth and saw that it was morally ruined. "Corrupt" means spoiled, turned away from what is good. And "all living creatures," that is, all human beings, had bent their ways, or in other words, the way they were living. It was not an isolated case but something widespread.

Here the narrator of Genesis is speaking. Earlier it was said that the earth was filled with violence. God does not act blindly: he looked and saw the reality. Next, God announces the judgment to Noah and gives him instructions for building an ark. Some understand "all living creatures" to mean all of humanity; others debate how far the scope reached, but the text stresses the seriousness of the situation.

For today: God sees what we sometimes ignore. Let us ask him to examine our ways and to help us live with justice and peace, even when the atmosphere around us goes astray.
exp.29:4:
This verse tells the story in a simple way: Bilhah, Rachel's servant, became pregnant and bore Jacob a son. The words "conceived" and "bore" mean "became pregnant" and "gave birth."

Rachel could not have children and suffered because of it. Her sister Leah already had several. So Rachel offered Jacob her servant Bilhah, following a custom of that time that seems strange to us today. Rachel wanted to regard the child as her own. Afterward she interpreted the birth as an answer from God and named the boy Dan, which means "judge." The Bible recounts this without fully approving or condemning it.

For today: when something takes a long time to arrive, it is easy to take human shortcuts that bring complications. Before acting out of desperation, let us ask God for wisdom and wait on Him with patience.
exp.33:5:
This verse says that Hamor, the father of Shechem, came to speak with Jacob. "Came" tells us that he traveled to the place where Jacob was, so he could talk with him directly. It is a simple step, but it opens a negotiation after what happened with Dina.

Earlier, Shechem had defiled Dina, that is, he had dishonored her, and now he wanted to marry her. Jacob heard about it and kept silent until his sons came back from the field. Hamor, as a father, speaks on behalf of his son. The text does not explain why Jacob was silent; it may have been prudence, grief, or caution.

For today: when there is a serious offense, it is not enough to fix things with kind words. It is wise to seek justice, to listen to those who were affected, and to wait to act with a clear head, asking God for wisdom.
exp.28:27:
Genesis 29:28 says that Jacob did just what Laban proposed. He finished the week of wedding celebration with Leah, and then Laban gave him his daughter Rachel to be his wife as well. The words "finished the week's celebration" refer to those seven days of festivities. The celebration belonged to Leah, and Laban gave Rachel to Jacob in marriage.

Jacob had worked seven years for Rachel, but Laban deceived him and gave him Leah first. When Jacob protested, Laban justified himself by appealing to a local custom: the younger daughter was not to be married before the older. He asked Jacob to wait out the week and serve seven more years. Jacob agreed, and Rachel was given to him at the end of the week, before completing those years of service. The text does not explain all the legal details of the time.

Jacob, who had deceived others, now received a deception himself. This reminds us that our actions have consequences, and invites us to respond to injustice with patience, honesty, and faithfulness to our commitments.
exp.35:31:
This verse says that Bela, son of Beor, was the first king of Edom mentioned in this list, and that his city was called Dinhabah. The Berean Standard wording gives the city name as Dinhabah, so the note about the spelling of the name no longer applies here.

The narrator of the book of Genesis speaks here, reviewing the descendants of Esau, also called Edom. The list shows that Edom already had kings before Israel had one. It is not known with certainty where Dinhabah was. It is also unclear whether this Bela is the same person as others with similar names; it is better not to assert it. What is clear is that God was keeping his promise to make Esau a nation (Genesis 25:23; 27:39-40).

For today: God keeps his promises even in things that look like simple lists of names. Trust that He works faithfully in history, and also in your life, even when you cannot see the whole picture.
exp.10:4:
This verse says that the LORD came down to look at the city and the tower that the people were building. "The LORD" is the name of God, and "the sons of men" simply means people, the people of that time.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Earlier, the people wanted to build a city and a very tall tower so they could make a name for themselves and avoid being scattered. That God "came down" is a human way of speaking: the tower was enormous to them, but God sees it from his height. Some think there is a touch of irony; others think it simply shows that God examines what we do.

For today: God sees our projects and also the reasons of our heart. Before undertaking something big, ask yourself: am I doing it to honor God and serve others, or only to make a name for myself?
exp.49:17:
His brothers come to him in person, bow down low before him, and say, "We are your slaves!" "Bowed down" means they bent low until they touched the ground.

After Jacob's death, the brothers fear that Joseph will finally take revenge on them. They send him a message that they say comes from their father, asking for forgiveness. We do not know whether Jacob really said that or whether they added it out of fear; the text does not make this clear. Now they present themselves, and so Joseph's dream from Genesis 37 comes true, when his brothers bowed down before him.

When we have wronged someone, fear can lead us to hide or to beg without trusting. Joseph's response, which follows, invites us to ask for forgiveness with humility and to trust in the grace of God and of others.
exp.23:8:
The explanation says that Abraham's servant swore a solemn oath to his master. To do so, he placed his hand under Abraham's thigh, an ancient gesture of commitment. "Servant" is the word used for the man who made the oath, and "this matter" refers to the charge Abraham had given him.

Abraham, already old, asked his trusted servant to find a wife for Isaac from among his own relatives, and not among the Canaanites. He reminded him that God had promised that land to his descendants. About the exact meaning of the gesture of placing a hand under the thigh there are several interpretations; many connect it with family descent, but this is not certain.

Today we can learn from this servant: he took his word seriously and kept faith with it. Work to make your promises, great or small, firm, and entrust your important tasks to God, as Abraham did.
exp.44:17:
Pharaoh speaks to Joseph's brothers and tells them to bring their father Jacob and their families to Egypt. He promises them "the best of the land of Egypt," that is, the finest that the country has to offer. "The fat of the land" is an old expression meaning the richest and most abundant things, like the finest foods. "Pleased" in the sense of "agreed with" or "was good in his eyes" is the idea behind Pharaoh's words.

The one speaking is Pharaoh, glad that Joseph's brothers have arrived. Canaan was suffering a famine, and Pharaoh, because of the esteem he had for Joseph, wants to welcome his whole family and care for them. It is a gesture of generosity toward them.

For today: God often blesses others through people He has placed in positions of influence. Just as Joseph served faithfully and his family was welcomed, we can use what we have to help and give shelter to those in need, and receive with humility the help that is offered to us.
exp.27:20:
It says that if Jacob returns safely to his father's house, then the LORD will be his God. The phrase "return safely" means come back home unharmed and well. It is the final condition of a vow that Jacob makes.

Jacob is speaking as he flees from his brother Esau on his way to Haran. He has just dreamed of a ladder reaching to heaven, and God promised to be with him. Jacob responds with a vow. Scholars explain the phrase "then the LORD will be my God" in different ways: some see a promise of total loyalty, others a response still weighed down with conditions.

For today: trusting God is not enough when everything goes well. We can decide to follow him from now on, sincerely and steadily, remembering that he has already cared for us along the way and that his faithfulness does not depend on how we bargain with him.
exp.25:5:
This verse says that Isaac settled down to live in Gerar, a region where there were Philistines. "Settled" means that he made his home there, not that he was passing through as a visitor.

Here the narrator of Genesis is speaking. God had just renewed to Isaac the promises made to Abraham, and had told him not to go down to Egypt during the famine. Isaac obeys and stays in Gerar. But soon his fear shows: he says that Rebekah is his sister. The Bible does not explain everything he was thinking, but the text indicates that he feared for his life.

For today: you can obey God and still feel afraid. When God promises you his care, do not wait until you have no fear before you trust. Hand your fears over to him and stay where he told you to be, without resorting to deception to protect yourself.
exp.7:9:
Noah waited another full week after the dove came back without finding a place to land. When that time had passed, he sent it out from the ark again. The phrase "sent out" and "from the ark" simply means he released it once more. It is understood that the seven days before were also a time of waiting, though the text says so in few words.

The one speaking is the narrator of Genesis, recounting what Noah did. The flood had already begun to subside, but Noah could not see the ground well from the ark. So he used the dove as a way to check whether there was yet a safe place to live. He did not act in haste, but with patience.

For today: when you are waiting for an answer or a change, do not despair or give up. Take one simple step, wait calmly, and try again, trusting that God is still at work even when you do not yet see results.
exp.0:3:
God looked at the light he had just made and saw that it was good. Then he separated the light from the darkness and set a boundary between the two.

This is the account of creation, told in the third person; the narrator describes what God does. Before this, the earth was formless and empty, and darkness covered the deep. God speaks and brings order, step by step. Separating is part of that order: later will come the day and the night, and then other separations. Some read this literally and others as poetic language about God's order; Christians have understood it in several ways.

For today: God looks at what he does and calls it good. We can learn to recognize the good in our lives and give thanks for it. We can also ask him to bring order where there is confusion, separating what harms us from what does us good.
exp.17:13:
Is anything too difficult for God? The verse says no. "At the appointed time" refers to the date God had already set, and "in about a year" tells us when the promise would come to pass, when life returns to bloom. "I will return to you" is a direct promise that God will come back at that time. The promise is clear: Sarah will have a son.

The Lord speaks, visiting Abraham along with two companions. Sarah was listening from behind the tent and laughed in doubt, since she and Abraham were old. God does not humiliate her but answers her with a question meant to awaken her faith and reaffirm the promise he had already made.

For today: when a situation seems impossible to you, do not measure it by your own strength but by the power of God. Bring him your doubts honestly, as Sarah did, and ask him to strengthen your trust while you wait for his timing.
exp.23:11:
Here the servant of Abraham prays to God. He asks that God would grant him success today, and that God would show kindness to his master Abraham. By success he means that the day will go well for him and that things will turn out as they should.

The one speaking is the oldest servant of Abraham, sent to find a wife for Isaac among his master's relatives. He has just arrived at the city of Nahor, by the well. The Bible does not give his name in this passage. He depends on God for a very important task and does not want to do it alone.

For today: before making an important decision, speak with God simply and ask him for guidance. Then stay attentive, with a heart ready to see how he answers.
exp.37:9:
The passage says that God saw what Onan was doing as wrong, and for that reason put him to death. "Wicked in the sight of the LORD" means that God judged his actions to be evil and did not approve of them. "Put Onan to death as well" means that Onan died.

The narrator tells this after Onan's older brother Er had also died. According to the custom of that time, Onan was to give a child to Tamar, his widowed sister-in-law, so as to continue his brother's name. He agreed outwardly, but avoided fulfilling that duty so as not to lose the inheritance. The text points to his selfishness and his lack of responsibility toward Tamar and his brother. Some see another theme here, but the passage emphasizes deceit and abuse.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we fulfill our responsibilities with honesty, especially toward those who depend on us, or whether we seek only our own advantage. God looks at the heart and at justice toward others.
exp.34:15:
This verse tells that Jacob and his family left Bethel and were traveling toward Ephrath (another name associated with Bethlehem). They were still some distance from Ephrath when Rachel went into labor, and the birth was difficult. The text describes her labor as difficult, which means she was in the pains of childbirth and suffering greatly.

Here no character speaks; it is the narrator who tells the story. Jacob had just set up a stone pillar at Bethel to remember his encounter with God. The account moves from a moment of worship to a scene of pain. Afterward it is told that Benjamin was born and that Rachel died. The exact distance from Ephrath is not certain; the text only indicates that they were not yet there.

For today: real life mixes moments of closeness with God and moments of unexpected pain. God is not absent when sorrow comes. We can bring our burdens to him with sincerity and accompany with tenderness those who suffer a loss.
exp.13:21:
Abram answers the king of Sodom with a solemn oath. "Raising the hand" was an ancient way of swearing or making a promise before God. He calls on the LORD God Most High, the Creator of heaven and earth, to witness what he is saying.

Abram had just rescued his nephew Lot and the people of Sodom. Melchizedek, priest of God Most High, had blessed him, and Abram gave him a tenth of everything. Now the king of Sodom offers him the goods to keep for himself. Abram refuses the offer because he wants only God to receive the credit for his prosperity, not a wicked king.

For today: before accepting money, favors, or help, ask yourself whether they will compromise you or cloud your witness. Trusting that God is the Creator and owner of all things lets us live with integrity and without depending on someone who does not honor God.
exp.44:0:
Here, Joseph can no longer hold back his emotions. In front of the attendants and officials who surrounded him, he cries out that everyone should leave the room. He is left alone with his brothers and reveals who he is. In plain terms, he could no longer control his feelings, and "made himself known" means he revealed who he really was.

Joseph was second only to Pharaoh in Egypt. Years earlier, his brothers had sold him as a slave. Now they have come for food during a famine, not knowing that he is the ruler. Joseph had tested them, and at this moment he decides to show his identity. He asked for privacy, probably to protect both their dignity and his own.

When there are wounds from the past, it is wise to handle what is painful in private and with care, without exposing anyone. Ask God for wisdom to seek reconciliation with humility and tenderness.
exp.42:1:
This verse tells how Jacob's family had used up the grain their sons had brought back from Egypt. So Jacob asked them to go back and buy more food. The phrase "had eaten all the grain" means that the supply had already run out. "Go back" means return to Egypt.

Jacob, the father, is speaking to his sons. The famine was severe throughout the region, and the family depended on Egypt to survive. The problem is that the Egyptian governor, who was Joseph though they did not know it, had demanded that they bring Benjamin. Jacob did not want to send him, and that is why Judah answers him right away.

For today: when our resources run out, we must act with humility and without delay. Sometimes we postpone a difficult decision out of fear, but waiting does not resolve the need. We can pray, speak honestly, and take the step that is needed, trusting that God cares for us.
exp.11:5:
Abram traveled through the land until he reached the place of the Oak of Moreh at Shechem. The verse names the place as Shechem, and it describes the people already living there as the Canaanites. The words "at that time" show that the land was not empty when Abram arrived.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. God had already called Abram to leave his home and had promised him a blessing. This detail reminds us that Abram arrived in a land already occupied by others. That is why the next verse, where God promises that land to his descendants, shows that the promise called for trust, not for something already visible.

For today: sometimes God guides us onto a path where we still see obstacles. We can keep trusting his promise and take the next step, as Abram did, who worshiped God in the middle of waiting.
exp.18:20:
God, speaking through the angel who is talking with Lot, tells him that he grants his request. A "supplication" is a humble plea, and the word "accepted" here means that the request was granted. The small city Lot asked for will not be destroyed, so that he can take refuge there.

The one speaking is the messenger sent by God, who is leading Lot and his family out of Sodom before the judgment. Lot was afraid to flee to the mountain and asked to stay in a nearby city, later called Zoar, which means "little." Some think Lot's fear shows a lack of trust, but the text simply says that God was patient with him.

For today: you can speak to God honestly, even with your fears and limits. He is compassionate and listens. Still, it is good to also ask him for courage and confidence to continue on his path.
exp.38:14:
She tells the people of her household what happened. When she screamed for help, Joseph left his cloak beside her and ran out of the house. The phrase "I screamed for help" describes her crying out loudly, and "ran out of the house" means he left the building.

The one speaking is Potiphar's wife, and what she reports is false. Earlier she had insisted that Joseph lie with her, and he had refused out of faithfulness to God and to his master. Now, having been rejected, she changes the story to accuse him. She uses the cloak Joseph left behind when he fled as if it were evidence against him.

For today: sometimes we will do what is right and still be misunderstood or unjustly accused. Joseph fled from temptation and kept his integrity. We can do the same and trust that God sees the truth, even when others do not.
exp.25:13:
The explanation says that Isaac came to have many sheep, many cattle, and a great number of servants and workers in the field. The phrase "flocks and herds" refers to sheep and cattle, and "servants" refers to the workers who tended and managed his estate. As a result, the Philistines envied him.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Isaac was living as a foreigner in Gerar, in Philistine territory, during a famine. God had blessed him with a harvest of a hundredfold, and that prosperity stirred jealousy in his neighbors, who afterward stopped up the wells and asked him to leave.

For today: when God blesses you, do not be surprised if someone feels envy. Respond with humility and peace, as Isaac did, and do not let other people's jealousy take away your trust in God. And if envy arises in you, ask God for a grateful heart.
exp.42:0:
This verse says that the shortage of food was still very severe throughout the region. The word "famine" here refers to a true food crisis: there was not enough to eat. "Still severe" means that it had not eased and was continuing as before.

No person is speaking here; the narrator is describing the situation. Jacob's family in Canaan had already used up the grain that his sons brought back from Egypt. That is why Jacob tells them to go and buy more. But Judah recalls that the Egyptian ruler, whom they did not yet recognize as their brother Joseph, insisted that Benjamin go with them. So the need forces the family to face a difficult decision.

For today: sometimes our needs push us to face what we have been avoiding. Instead of running away, we can ask God for wisdom and trust that he can guide us even in hard times.
exp.6:4:
The verse says that Noah did all that the LORD had commanded him. The wording makes clear that he did not carry out only some of the instructions or change them to suit himself, but fulfilled each one exactly as it was given. "LORD" in capital letters marks God's personal name in the Old Testament.

God had just told Noah that in seven days he would send rain for forty days and forty nights. He also indicated how many animals Noah was to bring into the ark to preserve life. The verse is a brief conclusion to the account: faced with so great and difficult a command, Noah responded with obedience. The text does not record his words or his feelings, only his actions.

Obeying God sometimes means trusting without seeing the whole picture. Today we might ask ourselves: what specific thing do I know God is asking of me, and am I still putting it off? A simple step of obedience, taken in faith, is worth more than many good intentions.
exp.3:11:
God tells Cain that when he works the ground, it will no longer yield its produce to him, meaning its good crops. "Working" the ground means tilling and cultivating it. Cain will also become a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth: without a fixed home, moving from place to place, never feeling settled.

God speaks with Cain after Cain has killed his brother Abel. Cain was a farmer, so the punishment strikes directly at his work and his way of life. Cain then answers that the punishment is too heavy to bear and fears that he will be killed. Some read the ground "will no longer yield its produce" to mean a smaller harvest; others read it as a life of great hardship.

For today: our bad decisions leave real consequences. If we have harmed someone, the best thing is to acknowledge it with humility, ask God for forgiveness, and seek to repair the damage, rather than hiding it.
exp.34:1:
Jacob tells everyone in his household to get rid of the foreign gods they have, to purify themselves, and to change their clothes. The "foreign gods" are the idols of other peoples' false gods. "Purify yourselves" refers to a cleansing that prepares a person to come before God.

God has just told Jacob to return to Bethel, the place where he met God when he was fleeing from Esau. Jacob speaks as the head of the family. Before drawing near to God, he wants no one in the household to keep idols. Some of them probably came from Mesopotamia or from what they took in Shechem, though the Bible does not give the details. Washing and changing clothes were outward signs of a heart turning back to God.

Before seeking God with greater closeness, ask yourself what thing occupies the place that belongs to Him alone. Set it aside, ask for forgiveness, and begin again with sincerity.
exp.30:1:
Here it says that Jacob saw from Laban's face, that is, from his expression and the way he behaved toward him, that Laban's attitude had changed. "Countenance" refers to the face and its expression. Jacob noticed that Laban no longer treated him as he once had.

Here the narrator speaks. Jacob had been working for Laban, his father-in-law, for years. Laban's sons were saying that Jacob had grown rich at their father's expense. That envy seems to have shaped the atmosphere, and Jacob perceived it. Soon God speaks to him and tells him to return to his homeland, promising to be with him.

For today: sometimes changes in an environment, such as a job or a relationship, make us notice that a season has ended. Instead of responding with anger or fear, we can pray and ask God for direction, for he guides our steps faithfully.
exp.10:30:
This verse tells how Terah, the father of Abram, took his son Abram, his grandson Lot (son of Haran, who had already died), and his daughter-in-law Sarai, the wife of Abram, and set out with them from Ur of the Chaldeans. They were heading for the land of Canaan, but when they arrived in a place called Haran, they stopped and settled there. "Settled" means that they made their home there. A "daughter-in-law" is the wife of one's son.

This is a narrative passage; the author recounts the story of Terah's family. It does not say why they set out, although later in the Bible it is shown that God called Abram. Sarai had no children, and the family had already known loss. Here the way is being prepared for the story of Abram.

For today: sometimes we begin a journey with good intentions and stop halfway. Today you can ask God to help you finish what He has placed in your heart.
exp.28:4:
Jacob asks some shepherds whether they know Laban, the grandson of Nahor, and they reply that they do. Nahor was Abraham's brother, so Laban was a relative of Jacob's family. The question "Do you know Laban the grandson of Nahor?" is a plain request for information, and "We know him" means that they know who he is.

Jacob has arrived in Haran after fleeing from his home, and he is looking for his family. He speaks with shepherds who are waiting by a well. His question is direct and practical. He does not yet know that God is guiding him, but the story lets us see it: the first shepherd he meets confirms that he is in the right place, and soon Rachel will arrive.

For today: when you do not know where to go, take simple steps and ask questions with humility. God often guides through ordinary conversations and through the people we meet along the way.
exp.16:4:
God changes Abram's name, which means something like "exalted father," to Abraham, which is connected with "father of many." The phrase "a father of many nations" refers to a large number of peoples or nations. God says that the former name will no longer be used.

God himself speaks with Abram, who is lying face down on the ground as a sign of respect. This is the moment when God confirms his covenant with him, even though Abram and Sarah still did not have the promised son. The new name serves as a constant reminder of the promise.

For today: God knows how to call us by what He promises, not only by what we see now. When your situation seems barren or without a way out, you can hold fast to the word of God and live with confidence, taking steps of faith even when the fulfillment is delayed.
exp.11:16:
The explanation says that the LORD afflicted Pharaoh and his household with severe calamities, because Abram's wife Sarai had been taken into the palace. "Afflicted" means struck or punished. "Severe plagues" are hard blows or misfortunes. "Household" here means his family and his people.

The narrator speaks here. Abram had gone down to Egypt because of the famine and, out of fear, said that Sarai was his sister. Pharaoh took her, not knowing the truth. The text does not explain what the plagues were, so it is not right to invent details. What is clear is that the LORD acted to protect Sarai and his promise.

For today: God takes care of his own even when they fail out of fear. But this is no excuse for lying. Let us trust in him and act with truth.
exp.16:14:
In this verse God tells Abraham that he should no longer call his wife "Sarai," but "Sarah." It is a change of name. The two names are related to the idea of princess, though scholars do not agree on the exact difference in meaning.

God speaks with Abraham just after establishing circumcision as the sign of his covenant. Abraham is already ninety-nine years old, and God affirms that his wife will also have a part in the promise. She will not be a mere companion: God will bless her, and the promised son will be born from her.

For today: God knows us by name and can give us a new identity and a new purpose, even when it seems late or impossible to us. Trust in his promise, even though, like Abraham, sometimes it is hard for you to believe it.
exp.33:4:
This verse says that Jacob heard that Shechem had defiled his daughter Dinah. The word "defiled" means that she had been violated or wronged. Jacob's sons were out in the field with the livestock, so Jacob remained silent about it until they returned.

Here the narrator is speaking. Earlier the story tells how Shechem took Dinah and then said he loved her, asking his father to arrange her as his wife. The text does not explain why Jacob stayed silent. Some think it was prudence, others caution or weakness. His silence contrasts with the furious reaction of his sons afterward.

For today: when faced with injustice or painful news, it is wise to pause and think before acting. But silence should not become indifference. One should seek counsel, protect the one who was hurt, and act with justice and without revenge.
exp.37:3:
She became pregnant again and gave birth to a son. The text says she named him Onan.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is recording the history of Judah's family. Judah had separated from his brothers and had married a Canaanite woman. The text only notes the births of his sons: Er, Onan, and Shelah. These names will become important later in the story. The exact meaning of "Onan" is uncertain; some connect it with strength or vigor, but this is debated.

For today: God sees each life from its beginning, including names that may seem like mere details. Care for your family in prayer, and teach your children to walk with God, because their character is formed by what they see at home.
exp.33:0:
This verse tells us that Dinah, the daughter Leah had borne to Jacob, went out to visit the young women of the region. The Berean Standard Bible describes her as the daughter Leah bore to Jacob, which makes clear that she was Leah's child. "The land" refers to the land of Canaan, where the local people lived. It is a simple detail, but it opens a very painful story.

The narrator of the book of Genesis introduces Dinah here as the only daughter of Jacob who is mentioned. The family lived near Shechem. The text does not explain why she went out, nor does it say that she did anything wrong. What follows shows that she was the victim of a serious injustice. Some scholars see in this a contrast between God's people and the customs of their surroundings, although the text does not state this clearly.

For today: Let us care for the most vulnerable and never blame the victims. If someone suffers abuse, they deserve protection, a listening ear, and justice, and the church should be a safe place.
exp.26:33:
Esau hears his father's words and understands that the blessing has already been given to another. His reaction is a loud and bitter cry, full of pain. He pleads: "Bless me too, O my father!" The wording "loud and bitter cry" conveys intense weeping, and the word "loud" shows how deep his grief was.

Isaac, already old, had wanted to bless Esau, his firstborn. But Jacob, following the plan of his mother Rebekah, pretended to be his brother and received the blessing. Esau arrives late and discovers what happened. His pain is real, although the Bible also shows that earlier he had placed little value on his birthright (Genesis 25:29-34).

Today this verse reminds us that hasty decisions can bring painful consequences. It also invites us to value what God gives us and not to act with deceit, because deceit wounds families.
exp.5:16:
God tells Noah that He Himself is going to bring floodwaters upon the earth. This flood would destroy every creature under the heavens that has the breath of life, meaning people and animals. The phrase "under the heavens" refers to the whole earth as far as the eye can see.

God speaks in the middle of His instructions for building the ark. Just before this, the text tells us that wickedness and violence had filled the earth (Genesis 6:5, 11-13). Some believe the flood covered the entire world, and others that it was very wide but limited to a region. Either way, the text presents it as a massive judgment. Even so, God immediately offers a covenant and a way of rescue.

Today we can see that God takes evil seriously, but He also provides a way out for those who trust in Him. Ask yourself: what is God asking you to do in faith, as Noah did, even though you cannot yet see the result?
exp.11:9:
Now there was a famine in the land. So Abram went down to Egypt to live there for a while because the famine was severe.

The verse tells that a severe famine struck the land of Canaan. Because of it, Abram went down to Egypt to stay there for a while. "Live there for a while" here means to stay as a foreigner, without settling there permanently. The Berean Standard Bible says "to live there for a while," and that phrase carries this same sense of temporary residence as a stranger.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Genesis. Abram had just arrived in the land God had promised him, and there he worshiped the LORD. Now he faces a crisis. The Bible does not say that God commanded him to go to Egypt, and so some see it as a human decision made out of fear, while others see it as a prudent way out. What follows shows that this decision brought problems.

For today: when hard times come, before acting out of fear, stop to pray and seek God's guidance. He can care for you even in scarcity.
exp.29:2:
Rachel tells Jacob that she is giving him her servant Bilhah so that he may sleep with her. If Bilhah bears a child for Rachel, then through her Rachel can also build a family. The phrase "so that through her I too can build a family" shows that Rachel would count the child as her own.

It is Rachel who speaks. She could not have children and felt envy toward her sister Leah, who already had several. Jacob had been angered by her desperation. Rachel looks for a solution according to the customs of her time. The Bible recounts this event without expressly approving or condemning it, and we see that it brought tension into the family.

For today: when something hurts us and we are slow to receive an answer, it is tempting to force solutions on our own. It is better to bring our anguish to God in prayer, trust in his timing, and not compare ourselves with others.
exp.0:13:
God commands that there be lights in the expanse of the sky, that is, heavenly bodies placed above the earth. Their purpose is to separate the day from the night, to serve as signs, to mark the seasons, and to measure the days and years.

God himself speaks, on the fourth day of creation. He had already made light, the sea, and the plants, and now he sets in the sky the heavenly bodies that govern time. Some believe the text describes the fourth day in literal sequence, and others read it in a more symbolic way; the passage does not settle that debate.

God brought order to time, and this is no accident. Today we can receive each day and each season as a gift from him, and live them with gratitude, rest, and purpose.
exp.17:11:
Sarah laughs to herself, where no one can hear her, and wonders whether, at her age, she can still have this pleasure, meaning joy or delight, when her husband is old too. "To herself" means in her own heart, and "my master" is how she refers to Abraham.

Three visitors, one of them the Lord, have arrived at Abraham's tent. One of them promises that Sarah will have a son. She listens from the entrance of the tent. Since she is now worn out and has been unable to have children for years, the promise seems impossible to her. Her laughter sounds like doubt, although some think it also mixes wonder and pain over a long-held hope.

Today we can be honest with God about our doubts. He knows them, and still asks us: "Is anything too hard for the Lord?" You can entrust to him whatever seems impossible.
exp.21:18:
Abraham goes back to his servants, the young men who had waited for him at the foot of the mountain. Then everyone gets up and sets out together toward Beersheba, and there Abraham settles down to live. It is a simple, almost quiet ending, after a very intense scene.

The one who narrates is Moses, according to tradition. He has just told how God tested Abraham by asking him to offer Isaac, and how an angel stopped the sacrifice and renewed the promise. The text does not mention Isaac in this verse, and we do not know why; some see it as a narrative detail and nothing more.

For today: after great trials or moments of faith, God also calls us back to everyday life. Trusting Him does not end on the mountain; it continues at home, at work, and in our routines.
exp.27:10:
It says that Jacob arrived at a certain place and spent the night there, because the sun had already set. He took one of the stones from that spot, put it under his head, and lay down to sleep. The place is simply a particular spot on his journey, and the stone serves as his pillow as he rests.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks. Jacob is leaving home on the way to Haran, after the conflict with his brother Esau. He travels alone and without comforts, with only a stone beneath his head. What follows is very important: in that ordinary place, God speaks to him in a dream and renews the promises made to Abraham and Isaac.

There are moments when we feel alone, tired, or uncertain. This verse reminds us that God can meet us right there, even when we do not have everything figured out. You can speak to him honestly tonight, just as you are.
exp.0:14:
God commanded that there be lights in the expanse of the sky, meaning the space above the earth that we see as the heavens. Their purpose was to shine on the earth. The verse ends with "And it was so": what God commanded, happened.

The one speaking is God, on the fourth day of creation. In the verses before, He had already said that these lights would serve to separate day from night and to mark seasons, days and years. The text does not explain how it happened; it only shows that God commands and his word is fulfilled. Some Christians read it literally and others in a broader way, but all recognize God as Creator.

For today: each time you see the light of day or the stars, remember that God cares for and orders your life. You can thank him and trust that his plans are fulfilled.
exp.26:21:
Here Jacob comes close to his father Isaac, who is already old and blind. Isaac touches him and notices something strange: the voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau. "Came close" means moved near, and "touched" means felt with the hands.

Isaac wants to give the family blessing to Esau, his firstborn son. Rebekah and Jacob deceive Isaac: Jacob covers himself with goatskins and pretends to be Esau. Isaac hesitates, and that is why he examines him. Even so, the deception continues, and Jacob even uses the name of God to support his lie.

For today: a lie may seem like a shortcut, but it leaves wounds and consequences. The Bible does not hide the failures of its characters. Trust that God carries out his plans without needing us to help him with deceptions. Let us seek to be honest, even when it costs us.
exp.49:13:
This verse says that after Joseph had buried his father Jacob, he returned to Egypt. He came back with his brothers and with everyone who had traveled with him to the burial. The phrase about going up is not in this wording, so it is left out here. The fact it reflects is still true: Canaan lay to the north, in higher country, which is why the journey there is described as going up.

The narrator tells us that Joseph kept the promise he had made to Jacob to bury him in Canaan, in the cave of Machpelah. With the burial finished, the family goes back to its life in Egypt. But the next verse shows that the brothers were afraid, thinking that Joseph would now take revenge on them.

For today: keeping what we have promised to others, even when it costs us, is a way of honoring them. And if there are unresolved wrongs between us, let us not wait until fear grows; let us seek reconciliation with humility and trust in the grace of God.
exp.17:12:
Here the LORD asks Abraham why Sarah laughed. She had thought, "Can I really bear a child when I am old?" The word "bear" means to give birth.

Three visitors had arrived at Abraham's tent, and one of them is the LORD. Sarah was listening behind the entrance and laughed to herself, because she and Abraham were very old. God does not rebuke her harshly, but shows that He knows even her private thoughts. Then He reminds her that nothing is too hard for Him.

Today, we sometimes doubt God's promises when everything seems impossible. We can be honest with Him about our doubts, knowing that He already knows them. And we can ask Him to strengthen our trust in His power and His faithfulness.
exp.21:1:
God tells Abraham to take his son Isaac, his only son, the one he loves, and go to the land of Moriah. There Abraham is to offer him as a burnt offering, a sacrifice that is burned up completely, on one of the mountains God will show him.

God speaks after years of Abraham waiting for this promised son. The text presents it as a test. Abraham answers, "Here I am," meaning, "I am ready." That is why he obeys without argument, though the text does not say what he felt. Many read this story as foreshadowing Christ, though this is a Christian interpretation.

Today, this story invites us to ask ourselves what we love most and whether God holds first place in our lives. We can entrust our possessions, plans and relationships to God, trusting that he is faithful, even when we do not understand everything.
exp.9:13:
This verse continues the list of the descendants of Mizraim, a name that in Hebrew is also used for Egypt. It names the Pathrusites, the Casluhites and the Caphtorites, which are peoples or clans. It says that the Philistines came from the Casluhites, although it is not clear whether they descend from the Casluhites or from the Caphtorites. Other biblical texts connect the Philistines with Caphtor, which many believe is Crete, but there is no certainty.

It is part of the "Table of Nations," which tradition attributes to Moses. It shows how the lands were resettled after the flood. For the people of Israel, it also explained where their neighbors, such as the Philistines, came from.

For today: God knows the origin and the name of every people. This invites us to respect every person, regardless of their country, because we all come from one common origin and have equal worth before God.
exp.23:27:
The explanation says that Rebekah, the young woman, ran off and told her mother's household everything that had happened at the well. The word "girl" refers to a young woman. "Told" means she let them know, or related it. "Her mother's household" probably refers to the family members who lived in that home.

Abraham's servant had been sent to find a wife for Isaac. After Rebekah gave water to him and his camels, he worshiped God, giving thanks for guiding him. Now Rebekah, filled with excitement, runs to share the news. The text does not say everything she told them, but what follows shows that she spoke of the encounter and of the gifts she had received.

For today: when God shows us his goodness, it is good to tell our family about it soon. Sharing what God is doing encourages the faith of others and opens doors for them to come to know him too.
exp.10:5:
The explanation says that the Lord observes a united people: they all speak the same language and have already begun to build. According to God, nothing they devise will be beyond them, meaning nothing they set out to do will be out of reach. The phrase "beyond them" describes how far a human plan can go when nothing holds it back, and it does not speak of fear of God.

The Lord speaks after coming down to see the city and the tower. The builders wanted to make a name for themselves and not be scattered, even though God had commanded them to fill the earth. Their unity served pride and self-sufficiency. Interpreters explain the exact scope of the sin in different ways, but the text stresses that desire for their own glory.

For today: before launching into a project, let us honestly ask whether we seek to honor God and serve others, or only to make our own name great. Let us bring our plans to him in prayer.
exp.42:33:
The explanation says that Joseph had portions from his own table served to his brothers. Benjamin's portion was five times larger than any of theirs. A "portion" here is a serving of food, and "feasted and drank freely with Joseph" means they ate well, drank openly, and enjoyed themselves in Joseph's company. They still did not know he was their brother.

This is a scene from the account of Joseph in Egypt. The narrator tells how Joseph, now a ruler, receives his brothers, who had come for food during the famine. Joseph has been testing them without revealing who he is. Giving more to Benjamin, Jacob's youngest and favored son, may have been a way of seeing whether they would feel envy, as they once felt it toward him. The text does not explain this, so it is one possible interpretation.

Today we can learn to rejoice when others receive blessing, without envy or comparison. Let us ask God for a heart that celebrates the good of others, just as God gradually healed this family.
exp.36:5:
Here Joseph speaks to his brothers and asks them to listen to a dream he had. The word "dream" refers to what he saw while he was asleep. This is only the opening line, before he tells the dream itself.

The one speaking is Joseph, a young man whom his father Jacob loved more than the others. His brothers already hated him and could barely speak to him peacefully. Even so, Joseph tells them his dream. The Bible does not say why he did this: some think it was naivety, others that it was a lack of prudence. Whatever the reason, the account shows that this increased their hatred.

For today: not everything God shows us must be said right away or to just anyone. Before speaking, let us ask for wisdom to know when, how, and to whom to share it, always taking care of our relationships.
exp.27:16:
Jacob wakes from his sleep and feels afraid. "Awesome" here does not mean "horrible," but rather it describes a place that inspires respect and reverent awe. Jacob understands that this place is "the house of God" and "the gate of heaven," that is, a place where God is present and heaven touches the earth.

Jacob is the one speaking. He is fleeing from his brother Esau and is alone, far from home. In the dream, God promised to be with him and to watch over him. On waking, he realizes that God was there and he did not know it. That is why he sets up the stone as a sign and names the place Bethel, "house of God."

For today: God can be with you in places and moments that seem empty or difficult. Pause to recognize his presence, and respond with reverence, gratitude, and trust.
exp.48:27:
These are the tribes of Israel, twelve in all, and this was what their father said to them. He blessed them, giving each one a blessing that fit him.

Jacob, now old and near death, gathers his sons to tell them what would come upon them. Some of his words are blessings, others are corrections, as the ones addressed to Reuben, Simeon, and Levi. Here the text describes all of it as blessing, and scholars understand this in several ways. This is the origin of the tribes of Israel.

God deals with each person personally, not in a series. Let us ask God to speak to us according to our lives, and let us learn to bless our families with sincere words that encourage and also guide with love.
exp.36:19:
Joseph's brothers see him coming from a distance, and, filled with resentment, they decide to kill him. They propose throwing him into one of the pits, which was a dry hole used to hold water, and making up a story that a vicious animal devoured him. The brothers' plan is to say that a wild beast got him, and then to see what becomes of his dreams, which they mock because they want to find out whether those dreams will come true.

The speakers are Jacob's sons, at Dothan, far from home. They were jealous because their father loved Joseph more, and because he had dreamed that they would bow down before him. Reuben, the eldest, will soon step in to try to save his life.

For today: jealousy that is not confronted can grow until it becomes violence. If we feel envy or anger toward someone, it is better to bring that to God in prayer and seek an honest conversation before the heart hardens. God can carry out his purposes even when others try to hinder them.
exp.10:12:
It says that Arphaxad, after he had become the father of Shelah, lived 403 more years and during that time had other sons and daughters.

This is part of the family line of Shem, which runs from the flood to Abram. The narrator of Genesis, traditionally attributed to Moses, is not addressing any particular person here but records the family line through which God's promise continues. The very long lifespans are understood in several ways, and the Bible does not explain them.

God cares for the generations, even when no one remembers them. Every life counts in his plan. Today you can live with faith in everyday life, raising children, serving, and teaching others, trusting that God uses what is simple for something greater.
exp.26:17:
Jacob goes in to his father Isaac and says, "My father." Isaac answers, "Here I am," and asks, "Which one are you, my son?"

Isaac is old and can hardly see. Rebekah and Jacob have prepared a deception so that Jacob will receive the blessing that belonged to Esau, the firstborn. That is why Jacob carries the food, and why the goatskins are on his hands and neck. Isaac's question shows that he suspects something, and what follows is Jacob's lie.

This passage shows how a lie begins with a simple question and grows bigger and bigger. The Bible tells these events without approving of them, and then shows their consequences. Today we can learn to be honest, even when we want something good, and to trust that God keeps his promises without our having to force them through deceit.
exp.22:3:
Abraham calls himself a "foreigner and an outsider among you." He means that he is someone from another place who lives there for a while, with no land of his own. He asks for "a burial site among you so that I can bury my dead." "My dead" refers to Sara, and the request is for a place to lay her to rest with dignity.

Sara has just died in Hebron. Abraham, still in grief, stands up and speaks with the Hittites, the people of the region. He had been promised this land, but he did not yet own anything in it. For that reason he respectfully asks to be allowed to buy a place for burial.

For today: we can honor our loved ones with dignity and, at the same time, live with humility and hope, remembering that in this world we are all just passing through. Abraham wept, but he also acted with calm and respect.
exp.48:15:
The explanation says that the tribe of Dan will provide justice for its people, just as any other tribe of Israel does. "Shall provide justice" here means to lead and to defend what is right. There is a wordplay, because "Dan" in Hebrew is related to the word for "judge."

Jacob, now an old man, speaks here, gathering his twelve sons to tell them what will come upon their descendants. Dan was the son of Bilhah, Rachel's servant. For that reason, the phrase "as one of the tribes" stresses that Dan will have a full place in Israel. Some think of Samson, who was a Danite, although the text does not say so.

For today: God gives each person a place and a responsibility, regardless of their origin. Try to act justly in your family and at work, and do not feel less because of your history.
exp.26:20:
Isaac asks Jacob to come closer so that he can touch him. "Touch" here means testing something with the hands. Isaac is uncertain and wants to know whether this is really Esau, his firstborn son, or not.

Isaac is old and can hardly see anymore. Jacob pretends to be Esau, following the plan of his mother Rebekah, in order to receive the father's blessing. Isaac notices things that do not add up: how quickly the game was found and the voice. That is why he wants to check by touch. Jacob answers with a lie, even bringing God's name into it. The Bible recounts the deception without approving it, and later Jacob suffers its consequences.

For today: when something does not sit right with you, do not ignore that unease. Ask God for wisdom and seek the truth calmly. And remember that a deception, even when it seems to work, almost always brings consequences.
exp.41:4:
This verse says that the sons of Jacob, here called "the sons of Israel," went to Egypt to buy food along with other people who were also traveling there because of the same need. The word "grain" in the Berean Standard Bible refers to food in general, and in this context it means the supplies they needed to survive. The phrase "the famine had also spread to the land of Canaan" means there was a severe shortage of food there too.

The account is told by the narrator of Genesis. A severe famine was affecting Canaan, and Jacob sent ten of his sons to get grain in Egypt. He did not let Benjamin go, for fear of losing him as he had lost Joseph. Without knowing it, his sons were about to meet Joseph, whom they had sold years earlier.

For today: when times of need come, God can use those same difficulties to lead us to face what we have kept silent about. If there is something unresolved that you need to put right with someone, do not ignore it; ask God for the courage to seek reconciliation.
exp.18:2:
This verse tells that Lot urged the two visitors strongly, until they agreed to go with him. Once in his house, he prepared a meal for them, and they baked unleavened bread, that is, bread made quickly, without waiting for the dough to rise. Then they ate.

The phrase "insisted so strongly" conveys that he pressed them firmly.

The narrator is describing what Lot did. The visitors were two angels who appeared to be travelers, and they had said they would spend the night in the square. Lot knew that place was dangerous, and the text that follows shows the wickedness of the city. His insistence appears to be care and hospitality, although the text does not explain all of his reasons.

Today we can learn to be generous with those who need shelter, even when it costs us time or effort. A simple table, offered with a good heart, can be an act of protection and of love for our neighbor.
exp.7:13:
This verse says that by the twenty-seventh day of the second month, the earth was fully dry. The phrase "fully dry" means there was no longer any moisture or mud left on the ground. Earlier, in the first month, Noah saw that the surface was dry on top, meaning there was no water lying on it. By now the ground was already firm.

The narrator of the book recounts the dates of the flood with great care. Noah had waited a long time inside the ark. Although he could already see uncovered ground, he did not leave on his own. He waited until God spoke to him and gave the order to come out, as seen in the following verse.

For today: sometimes God makes us wait even when it seems that everything is ready. We can learn from Noah not to rush ahead, but to trust in God's timing and wait for his direction before taking the next step.
exp.26:38:
Isaac tells Esau that his home will be away from the richness of the land and away from the dew of heaven above. "Dwelling place" is the place where he will live, and "richness of the land" refers to fertile, productive ground. The dew represents the rain and care of God. The phrase "away from" means Esau's home will lie apart from the best land and its blessings, so it can be read as a blessing of a different kind or as something harder.

Isaac speaks here in his old age. Jacob had just received the main blessing, although Isaac had intended to give it to Esau. Esau weeps and asks for something for himself. Isaac answers with words that do not cancel what has already been given, but leave him a future with difficulties.

For today: when we do not receive what we hoped for, we can avoid bitterness. Esau was filled with hatred. Instead, we can ask God to help us trust in Him and to guard our hearts.
exp.29:25:
