Jacob asks his father-in-law Laban to let him leave with his wives and children. He says, "for whom I have served you," meaning that he worked fourteen years for them. Jacob appeals to what Laban already knows: his hard work.

Jacob speaks to Laban after Joseph, Rachel's son, was born. Jacob had worked for Laban for his two daughters, Leah and Rachel, and now he feels it is time to return to his own land. Laban answers that God has blessed him because of Jacob, and he offers wages so that Jacob will stay.

For today: when the time comes to take an important step, such as changing jobs or moving to another place, do it with clarity and respect. Remember your faithful service, speak honestly, and do not let the pressure of others turn you away from what God shows you.
exp.23:51:
This verse says that when Abraham's servant heard the response of Rebekah's family, he bowed down to the ground before the Lord. The phrase "bowed down to the ground" describes a deep, humble posture of worship and gratitude.

The servant had been sent by Abraham to find a wife for Isaac. He had prayed asking for guidance, and now Laban and Bethuel agree that Rebekah may go, acknowledging that this comes from the Lord. The account does not explain all the family background, but it shows that the servant saw the answer to his prayer.

Today we can learn to stop and thank God when we see that he answers. Before moving on with our plans, it is worth pausing, giving thanks, and recognizing that God was at work along the way.
exp.19:1:
Abraham said that Sarah was his sister, without making clear that she was also his wife. Then Abimelech, king of Gerar, had Sarah brought to him. The verse says he had her brought, which means he gave the order for her to be taken to his household.

The narrator tells us that Abraham was living as a foreigner in Gerar. Out of fear, he repeated what he had already done before in Egypt: presenting Sarah only as his sister. Chapter 12 and verse 11 of this same chapter make clear that he feared for his life. God intervened in dreams and protected Sarah and Abimelech, who had not yet come near her.

For today: fear can lead us to speak half-truths, and that hurts others. When you feel afraid, pray and be honest, trusting that God protects even when we fail.
exp.6:12:
This verse says that on that very day the flood began, Noah went into the ark along with his sons Shem, Ham and Japheth, his wife, and the wives of his three sons. In all there were eight people.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is recounting events. God had already warned Noah about the flood and had told him to build the ark. This verse shows that Noah obeyed, and that his whole family went in with him. The text stresses that all of this happened on that very day, the same day the great waters burst forth.

For today: obedience to God is not put off until later. Noah trusted God's word and acted on it. We can ask ourselves what God has asked of us that we are still postponing, and take one concrete step of faith today.
exp.26:3:
Isaac asks his son Esau to prepare a tasty dish, the kind he loves. A "stew" is a dish of cooked meat, and "venison" is the meat of wild animals. Isaac wants to eat this dish and then bless Esau before he dies.

Isaac speaks as an old man, nearly blind, who thinks his death may be near. In that time, a father's blessing was something very serious, because it shaped the future of the eldest son. Rebekah hears everything, and this leads to a plan to deceive Isaac. Some see in Isaac an excessive fondness for food; others see simply a custom of the time. The text does not fully explain this.

For today: do not put off the important words of blessing, and seek to do things with clarity and honesty, not with deception. God keeps his promises, but we must trust without manipulating.
exp.48:22:
The explanation says that Joseph was attacked harshly. The phrase "they attacked him with bitterness" means they caused him a great deal of pain. "They aimed at him in hostility" means they shot arrows at him with ill will, and "the archers" are the men who shoot with bows. Their hostility is pictured as an attack, which is figurative language that speaks of envy and enmity.

Here Jacob, now an old man, is blessing each of his sons before he dies. About Joseph he looks back: his brothers envied him and sold him, and later he lived in Egypt through injustices such as a false accusation and prison. Many understand that it also refers to the future tribes that would descend from him. This cannot be fully pinned down. What matters is that the next verse shows God sustaining him.

If envy or injustice wounds you today, you are not alone. As with Joseph, God can sustain you and give you strength. Give Him your pain and seek His help so that you do not respond with bitterness.
exp.24:17:
Ishmael's descendants lived across a wide area, from Havilah to Shur, a place near the border of Egypt on the way toward Asshur. The verse also says they lived in hostility toward all their brothers. Scholars do not agree on exactly what the phrase about their brothers means, so this line can be read in different ways.

The narrator closes the story of Ishmael before returning to the story of Isaac. In this way he shows that God kept what he promised Abraham about Ishmael: that he would have many descendants (Genesis 17:20). Earlier it had been said that Ishmael would live in hostility toward all his brothers (Genesis 16:12).

For today: God keeps his word and remembers everyone, even when a person is not at the center of the story. Trust that he also cares for you and your family.
exp.41:17:
This verse tells how, after three days in prison, Joseph speaks to his brothers and offers them a way out: "So do this and you will live." He also says: "I fear God." The wording is "said to them" and "you will live," not die. With that phrase, Joseph shows that he will act with respect toward God.

Joseph is now governor of Egypt. His brothers have come to buy food because of the famine, and they do not recognize him. He accuses them of being spies and tests them. Then he softens his decision: only one will remain imprisoned, and the others will take grain home. The Bible does not give all his reasons in detail; many think he wanted to know whether his brothers had changed.

For today: the fear of God helps us use power with justice and mercy. If someone owes us or has wronged us, we can seek the truth without revenge.
exp.35:17:
This verse lists the sons of Oholibamah, one of Esau's wives. Three chiefs came from her: Jeush, Jalam and Korah. Here the word "chief" means the head of a clan or family group, not a title of nobility.

The writer, traditionally recognized as Moses, includes this list to record how the descendants of Esau, called Edomites, took shape as a people in the land of Edom. Before the story returns to Joseph, the account closes the line of Esau. This shows that God kept his word to make Esau into a nation, even though the main promise continued through Jacob.

For today: God cares for every family, even those that do not carry the central thread of the story. Value your place and trust that God sees you. Live with gratitude, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.49:20:
Here Joseph tells his brothers not to be afraid. He will provide food for them and for their children. The Bible adds that he reassured them and spoke kindly to them, that is, with gentle and sincere words. "Provide" means to supply food and care.

After Jacob died, the brothers feared that Joseph would take revenge for having sold him years earlier. Joseph, already a ruler in Egypt, answers them that he is not in the place of God to judge them. He acknowledges that they acted wrongly, but that God used that story to save many lives.

Today we can learn to respond to those who have hurt us with kindness and not with revenge. If someone asks us for forgiveness, we can reassure them with sincere words, trusting that God can bring good even out of painful situations.
exp.26:30:
Esau prepares a meal from the game he hunted and brings it to his father Isaac. He asks his father to sit up and eat, so that Isaac will bless him. "Some tasty food" describes a prepared dish, and "so that you may bless me" asks for the blessing to be given sincerely.

Esau is the one speaking, the elder son. He does not know that Jacob, with Rebekah's help, has already received the blessing by pretending to be him. Esau arrives only minutes late, confident that the blessing of the firstborn still belongs to him.

For today: this passage reminds us that decisions have consequences and that deception leaves wounds. It also invites us to value in time what God gives us, without neglecting it, and to trust that his plans are fulfilled, even when people fail.
exp.46:0:
Here the text says that Joseph went to inform Pharaoh that his family had already arrived. His father Jacob, his brothers, their flocks and herds, and all they own had come from the land of Canaan, and now they were in Goshen.

Joseph is the one speaking in this moment, and he speaks as the governor of Egypt. There had been a great famine, and his family had come by Pharaoh's invitation. Joseph reports this respectfully, because Egypt was not his native land. Goshen was a fertile region, suitable for raising livestock. The following verses show that Joseph presented his brothers so that they would live there as shepherds.

For today: Joseph cared for his family with order and respect, without taking advantage of his position. We can help those we love by acting with honesty, humility, and good communication, without running over anyone.
exp.38:13:
She calls the household servants and tells them a false version of what happened. She says that Joseph, whom she calls "this Hebrew," has been brought in to make sport of them, and that he came to her so he could sleep with her, but that she screamed as loudly as she could. "To make sport of us" means to mock or humiliate them; "sleep with her" refers to sexual relations.

It is the wife of Potiphar who speaks. She has just been rejected by Joseph, and to protect herself from shame she falsely accuses him. By calling him "this Hebrew" she stresses that Joseph is a foreigner and a slave, so that the servants will believe her and not him. The garment he left in her hands serves her as supposed proof.

For today: when someone accuses us unjustly, let us remember that God sees the truth. And if we are tempted to blame others to hide our own wrongdoing, let us instead choose honesty, even when it costs us.
exp.15:7:
Here the angel of the LORD finds Hagar in the wilderness and speaks to her by name and by her role: servant of Sarai. He asks her two questions: where have you come from, and where are you going? She answers honestly that she is running away from her mistress Sarai. "Running away from" here means she is leaving her mistress's presence behind.

Sarai, the wife of Abram, had mistreated Hagar, and Abram did not step in. Hagar, alone and pregnant, escaped toward the wilderness. The angel does not scold her at the start; he seeks her out and asks her questions. Some think this angel is a special appearance of God himself, though the text does not fully make this clear.

For today: God sees the one who suffers and asks with tenderness. When you are running from a problem, be honest with him, because his questions are not meant to accuse you, but to help you think and find a way forward.
exp.43:4:
The explanation says that Joseph's steward is to accuse the brothers of having taken his lord's cup. "Divination" here refers to consulting or trying to learn hidden things. It is debated whether Joseph really used the cup this way or said it only as part of his plan. The text does not make this clear.

The steward speaks, following Joseph's orders. Joseph, already governor in Egypt, had had his silver cup hidden in Benjamin's sack. He wanted to test whether his brothers had changed, and whether they would abandon another brother as they had done to him years earlier.

Today, this reminds us that God can use difficult trials to bring to light what is in the heart. Let us ask him to give us faithfulness and love for others, especially when it is costly.
exp.45:11:
This verse lists the descendants of Judah, the fourth son of Jacob. His sons were Er, Onan, Shelah, Perez, and Zerah. It is noted that Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan, before the family traveled to Egypt. Then the sons of Perez are named: Hezron and Hamul.

The book of Genesis presents a list of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt during the time of the famine. Tradition holds that Moses wrote the book. The list shows that God cared for this family, which would become the beginning of the people of Israel. Perez is important because, later on, from his line would come King David and, according to the New Testament, Jesus.

For today: God pays attention to each person and each family, even with imperfect stories. Trust that He can work through your story.
exp.22:7:
Abraham answers the Hittites by asking for their help. He tells them that, if they agree to let him bury his dead wife, Sarah, they should listen to him and speak on his behalf to Ephron, the son of Zohar. To approach someone on another person's behalf means to speak to them for that person.

Sarah had just died, and Abraham was a foreigner in Canaan. The Hittites had offered to let him bury her for free in their tombs, but Abraham wanted to buy a plot of land of his own. So he bowed respectfully and asked that they speak up for him with Ephron. Some think he was looking for a secure and legal possession; the text says nothing more about his reasons.

For today: when you face a difficult moment, ask for help with humility and respect, and act with honesty and clarity. Abraham, even in his grief, treated those around him with dignity and sought to do things properly.
exp.5:2:
God says that his Spirit will not keep contending with human beings forever, because they are mortal, frail and bound to die. For that reason he sets a limit: their days will be 120 years. The phrase "the LORD" in the Berean Standard Bible is the personal name of God, the one who speaks in this verse.

God speaks in the middle of a land that was filling up with wickedness. Readers have understood the "120 years" in different ways: as a period of time before the flood, or as a limit on the length of human life. The text does not fully settle this. In either case, God gives time before he acts.

Today, let us not take God's patience lightly. If you sense that he is calling you to change something, respond with humility today, without putting it off for later.
exp.4:10:
This verse closes the account of the life of Enosh, grandson of Adam through his son Seth. It says that he lived a total of 905 years, and then he died. In this verse, the wording is simple and direct, with no special terms to explain.

The narrator of Genesis (tradition points to Moses, though it is not known how the text was brought together) presents a list of generations. The same pattern repeats: a man is born, has children, lives many years, and dies. This shows how humanity continues and, at the same time, how death remains present after the fall of Adam. About Enosh, the text gives no further details of his life.

For today: our life is brief, even if it is very long. We should live it with purpose, teaching the faith to the next generation and trusting in God, who is the one who gives meaning to our days.
exp.23:54:
Here the family of Rebekah, her brother and her mother, asks that she stay with them ten days or so before she leaves. A "girl" here means a young woman, and the request is for more time to say goodbye.

Abraham's servant had come to seek a wife for Isaac. He had already given gifts, and the family had accepted the proposal. But at dawn, he wants to leave at once. Her brother and mother respond with this request, probably because it was hard for them to part with her so soon. The text does not explain their reasons in detail; it could be affection, custom, or a wish to prepare.

Acting with haste or with delay can both be reasonable, but it is wise to recognize when God is already opening a path. We can say goodbye with love without holding back what God is doing.
exp.2:22:
This verse says that the LORD God banished the man from the Garden of Eden. He could no longer live there, and now he had to work the ground, that is, cultivate it. "Work the ground" means to farm the soil, and "taken" refers to the fact that he had been taken out of it. This recalls that the man was formed from the dust of the earth.

The one acting is the LORD God, and the account is traditionally attributed to Moses. Adam and Eve had disobeyed by eating the forbidden fruit. God clothed them with garments of skins and then sent them away, so that they would not eat from the tree of life in that state. Many see here both judgment and care.

For today: our decisions have consequences, but God does not abandon us in them. Even as he sent them out, he clothed them. If you have failed, you can return to him with humility, and your daily work, though it is hard, can be done with confidence in his care.
exp.28:26:
Laban tells Jacob to finish the wedding week with Leah, and after that he will also give him Rachel. In return, Jacob would have to work for him another seven years. "Finish this week's celebration" refers to the week of wedding festivities. "The older one" is Leah, and "the younger one" is Rachel.

Laban, Jacob's father-in-law, is the one speaking. Jacob had worked seven years to marry Rachel, but Laban gave him Leah, his older daughter. When Jacob complained, Laban justified himself by local custom. His proposal guaranteed himself another seven years of work. The Bible does not explain all the details of the custom, but it shows that Laban acted with cunning.

For today: when we are deceived or things do not turn out as we expected, it is wise to act with patience and honesty, without repaying deceit with deceit. God can work even in unjust and difficult situations.
exp.22:16:
This verse describes what Abraham received when he paid Ephron: the field at Machpelah, near Mamre, with the cave in it, all the trees, and everything within the field's boundaries. "Deeded over" means the property was formally transferred to him. "Boundaries" means the limits of the field. Everything was recorded in careful detail.

Sarah had died, and Abraham, who lived as a foreigner in Canaan, needed a place to bury her. He negotiated openly with the sons of Heth and paid four hundred shekels of silver. In this way the purchase was clear and recognized by all. This was the first piece of the promised land that Abraham owned, even though it was only a tomb.

For today: Abraham acted with honesty, order, and openness, even in the midst of grief. We can imitate him by keeping our agreements with clarity and fairness, and by trusting that God keeps his promises with patience.
exp.44:13:
This verse says that Joseph threw his arms around his brother Benjamin and wept, and that Benjamin also wept as they embraced. Holding someone this closely and crying openly is a clear expression of deep affection.

Joseph has just revealed himself to his brothers, the ones who had sold him years earlier. Benjamin is his brother through their mother and the only one who did not take part in that betrayal. After so many years apart, Joseph cannot hold back his emotion. That is why his words about bringing his father to Egypt come with tears and embraces.

For today: do not be afraid to show your feelings to the people you love. If there is a broken relationship in your family, take the first step toward reconciliation. A sincere embrace and some tears can begin to heal wounds of many years.
exp.45:29:
Here Jacob, also called Israel, tells his son Joseph that he can now die in peace, because he has seen him alive. "Finally I can die" is not an expression of sorrow, but of fullness. The words "now that I have seen your face and know that you are still alive" show that his greatest longing has been fulfilled.

For many years Jacob had believed that Joseph was dead. Now he arrives in Goshen, in Egypt, and is reunited with him in tears. After so much pain, seeing his son alive brings deep rest to his heart. The Bible says nothing more about his feelings, but the scene conveys joy and relief.

For today: God can restore hope where we thought all was lost. When we wait for something difficult, we can keep trusting in Him. And if there is a broken relationship in your life, take steps toward reconciliation while there is still time.
exp.7:2:
The verse says that the waters of the flood were steadily receding from the earth. The phrase about the waters moving back and forth suggests a constant movement, like a tide slowly going out. The word for the waters pulling away describes them receding, and "had gone down" means they dropped. After 150 days, the level of the water had dropped noticeably.

The one telling the story is the author of Genesis, recounting what happened after God remembered Noah. That does not mean He had forgotten him, but that He acted on his behalf. God sent a wind, closed the fountains of the deep, and stopped the rain. The account shows that God cares for those under His protection.

Today, this text reminds us that God works with patience. Sometimes trials do not end all at once, but little by little. We can keep trusting that He has not forgotten us.
exp.48:14:
He says that Issachar saw that his resting place was good and that his land was pleasant. For that reason he bent his shoulder to the burden, like someone carrying a load, and submitted to labor as a servant. The word "burden" refers to heavy work he took on, and "pleasant" means agreeable, lovely.

Jacob, now old, blesses his sons and speaks of what each tribe will become. Here he describes Issachar as a strong donkey that lies down to rest. Many understand that he preferred comfort and fertile land, though in exchange he was placed under others. Others see it in a more positive light, as diligent work. The text allows both readings.

For today: comfort is good, but it is wise to ask what price we pay for it. Let us ask God for wisdom so that we do not trade our freedom or our calling for ease, and so that we work faithfully wherever we are.
exp.31:20:
The explanation says that the gifts Jacob prepared for his brother Esau went on ahead of him. Jacob, by contrast, spent that night in the camp. "Gifts" means presents offered to show goodwill, and "camp" refers to the place where he and his household stopped for the night.

The narrator tells us that Jacob was afraid of meeting Esau, whom years earlier he had deceived. For that reason he sent animals in groups, with servants who would say that he was coming behind them. He wanted to calm his brother's anger. Shortly afterward, that same night, he would get up, cross the river Jabbok, and wrestle with God. Some see in that quiet night only a brief moment before the great trial, although the text gives no further details.

For today: doing what is ours to do to be reconciled, such as asking forgiveness or taking a humble step, is good. But afterward we must hand the outcome over to God and rest in Him, without living ruled by fear.
exp.9:2:
This verse names the three sons of Gomer, who was a son of Japheth and a grandson of Noah: Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah. It is part of a list of families.

It is a narrative text, and the narrator, traditionally attributed to Moses, explains how humanity spread out after the flood. This list, sometimes called the "Table of Nations," presents Japheth as the ancestor of peoples to the north and west. Scholars do not fully agree on locating each people precisely, so it is wise to be cautious with identifications.

For today: God knows the names and stories of families, even though to us they may seem like dull lists. If He cares for every generation, He also knows you and values you. Give thanks for your family and pray for it.
exp.1:23:
This verse says that a man will leave his father and mother, will be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh. In plain modern English: the word translated "be united" means to draw close to someone and stick to them firmly. "One flesh" speaks of a deep union: shared body, life, and purpose.

After Adam exclaims with joy when he sees the woman, the text shifts to a comment from the narrator. It is no longer Adam speaking, but the one telling the story, and he explains why marriage has been this way from the beginning. Jesus quoted this verse when he spoke about marriage (Matthew 19:5).

For today: if you are married or plan to marry, loyalty to your spouse should come first among your human relationships. Honoring your parents remains important, but the new home needs its own center.
exp.24:2:
This verse is part of a family list. It says that Jokshan, son of Abraham and Keturah, was the father of two sons: Sheba and Dedan. It then names three descendants of Dedan: the Asshurites, the Letushites, and the Leummites, which seem to be names of groups or tribes.

Here it is not a character speaking; it is the narrator of Genesis. After Sarah, Abraham had another wife, Keturah, and from her came many peoples. This shows God keeping his promise to make Abraham the father of many nations. Even so, the text makes clear right away that Isaac received everything Abraham had. As to the exact location of these peoples, scholars do not have complete certainty.

For today: God pays attention to families and to names that seem small to us. Remember that your life and your inheritance of faith matter to Him; live today in a way that blesses those who come after you.
exp.31:14:
This verse continues the list of the gift that Jacob prepared for his brother Esau. Here it mentions thirty female camels with their young, forty cows, ten bulls, twenty female donkeys, and ten male donkeys. The phrase "milk camels" refers to camels that were giving milk, that is, nursing females, and "young" here means their offspring.

Jacob is returning to his land with fear, because years earlier he deceived Esau and took away the blessing. Now he knows that Esau is coming to meet him, and he is not sure how he will be received. For that reason he sets apart valuable animals in groups, to send ahead as a gift that will soften the encounter.

For today: when a relationship has been broken through our own fault, it is not enough to wish it could be repaired. Jacob prayed and also acted with humility and generosity. We can look for concrete gestures of reconciliation, trusting that God works in hearts.
exp.18:16:
Once the men had brought Lot and his family out of the city, one of them gave him an urgent command: "Run for your lives!" That means flee to save yourselves. "Do not look back" means do not turn around to look at the city. "Do not stop anywhere on the plain" means do not pause anywhere in the low country. "Or you will be swept away" means you will be destroyed.

It is one of God's messengers who speaks. Sodom was going to be destroyed because of its wickedness, and Lot had hesitated to leave. The angels had taken him by the hand out of the mercy of the LORD. Now they ask him to obey without delay and without being distracted, and they point to the mountains as the place of safety.

For today: when God rescues you from something that is harming you, do not keep looking back or searching for excuses. Take the next step of obedience, trusting that his help is real and that he is caring for you.
exp.20:15:
Hagar moves away from her son Ishmael, about as far as an arrow shot from a bow would travel. She sits down nearby, but not close to him, because she says, "I cannot bear to watch the boy die!" Then she lifts up her voice and weeps.

The narrator describes what happens in the desert of Beersheba. Abraham had sent Hagar and her son away with bread and water, and now the water has run out. Hagar, in despair, believes her son is going to die of thirst and cannot bear to watch him.

When we feel that we can no longer do anything, God is not far away. What follows in the text shows that He hears the weeping and responds. We can bring Him our pain honestly, without pretending to be strong, and trust that He listens.
exp.20:9:
Sarah is the one speaking here. She asks Abraham to drive out Hagar, the servant, and her son Ishmael. Her words make clear that she does not want the son of the servant to share in the inheritance with Isaac. The word "expel" means to send someone away, and "slave woman" refers to a woman who serves as a slave in the household.

Isaac had just been weaned, and at the feast Sarah saw Ishmael mocking. Her reaction is harsh and jealous, and she asks Abraham for something that grieves him deeply. Then God tells Abraham to listen to Sarah, because the promise would pass through Isaac. Even so, God would also care for Ishmael.

For today: when family conflicts wound us, we can ask God for wisdom before we react. He can guide even painful situations and care for those who are left hurt.
exp.19:13:
The explanation says that King Abimelech gave Abraham sheep, cattle, male servants and female servants, and also returned his wife Sarah to him.

Abraham had said that Sarah was his sister, and Abimelech had taken her into his household. God warned him in a dream not to touch her, and now the king corrects the mistake. The gifts show his desire to repair the harm and make peace. Some understand that it was also a way of publicly acknowledging that Abraham was under God's protection.

For today: when we make a mistake or affect others, saying "I'm sorry" is not enough. Acknowledging the wrong and repairing the harm, as far as we can, is a concrete way to live with honesty and humility.
exp.20:31:
Here is what the verse says: Abraham and Abimelech made a peace agreement at Beersheba. Afterward, Abimelech and Phicol, the commander of his army, got up and returned to the land of the Philistines. A "covenant" is a solemn agreement, and the commander is the one who leads the army.

The narrator tells of the end of a dispute over a water well. Abimelech, a king of the region, recognized that God was with Abraham and wanted to secure peace. Abraham gave him seven ewe lambs as proof that the well was his. This is where the name Beersheba comes from, which is commonly understood to mean "well of the oath" or "well of the seven."

Conflicts can be resolved through clear and honest agreements, without fighting. If you have a disagreement with someone, seek to speak with sincerity, put things in writing if needed, and pursue peace, trusting that God cares for you.
exp.36:34:
All of Jacob's sons and daughters tried to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted. He said, "No. I will go down to Sheol mourning for my son." He is saying he will go down to Sheol in grief, full of sorrow, to the place of the dead. His father wept for him.

Jacob's sons had shown him Joseph's bloodied coat, and he believed a wild beast had killed him. Jacob speaks out of deep pain. He does not know that Joseph is alive, as the following verse shows. The sons who try to comfort him are the same ones who deceived him, although the text does not say this directly.

For today: when someone suffers a loss, do not rush them to feel better. Accompany them with patience, listening and presence. And if the pain is yours, remember that God can work even in what you cannot see.
exp.36:26:
Judah proposes to his brothers that they sell Joseph to some Ishmaelite traders, rather than killing him. He says "let us not lay a hand on him," so that they themselves would not be the ones who harm him, and he reminds them that "he is our brother, our own flesh," that is, of the same blood. "And they agreed" means that his brothers accepted the plan.

Judah is one of Jacob's sons and the speaker here. The brothers were jealous of Joseph and resentful toward him, and they had already thrown him into a pit. Judah sees a way out that avoids shedding blood, but it is still a cruel act: they sell their own brother. The following text also mentions Midianites, and there have been several explanations of how they relate to the Ishmaelites.

For today: be careful not to justify wrongdoing by saying it is "less bad." Recognizing our bond with another person should lead us to protect them, not merely to avoid the worst. God can work even through our failures, but that does not erase our responsibility.
exp.0:20:
God created the great sea creatures, every living thing that moves in the waters, and every winged bird, each one according to its kind, that is, in their various classes. "Created" is the word used here, and "great sea creatures" can also be rendered as great sea monsters. At the end, God looks at what He has made and declares that it was good.

The narrator of Genesis tells what God did on the fifth day. God had commanded that the waters and the sky be filled with life, and here that command is carried out. Right away God blesses them so that they may multiply. Here we see a God who gives life with order and purpose.

For today: if God calls His creation good, we can care for it with respect and gratitude, without despising it or using it selfishly. Today you can thank God for something living that you see.
exp.1:4:
It says that, at the beginning, there were still no shrubs or plants of the field on the earth, and none had sprouted. That was so because the LORD God had not yet sent rain upon the earth, and there was no man to cultivate the ground. "Cultivate" means to work or tend the soil, and "sprouted" means to come up out of the ground and begin to grow.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is speaking, not a character. It begins a second account of creation, which focuses on the relationship between God, the earth, and the man. Some see it as a more detailed look at the sixth day; others see it as a complementary account. The following verses show that God provides water and then forms the man from the dust.

For today: life depends on God, and human work is also part of his plan. We can cultivate, study, and serve with effort, while recognizing that God is the one who gives the rain, the growth, and the breath. Work with diligence and give thanks with humility.
exp.27:0:
Isaac calls Jacob, blesses him, commands him, and says to him: "Do not take a wife from the Canaanite women." The Berean wording gives the command directly, so the explanation follows it.

Isaac, now an old man, speaks to Jacob. The Canaanites lived in the land where Abraham's family dwelt as strangers, and they had other beliefs and customs. Isaac wanted the family to remain united to the faith of Abraham and to God's promise. For this reason, in the verses that follow, he sends Jacob to find a wife among his mother's family.

For today: when making big decisions, such as marriage or close friendships, it is good to think about what will strengthen our faith and the faith of our family. Seeking advice from people who are mature in faith also helps.
exp.38:10:
One day, however, Joseph went into the house to attend to his work, and not a single household servant was inside. This verse tells us that at that moment none of the other servants were there. "Work" here means his labor or his daily duties. He was left alone in the house, and that set the stage for what follows.

It is part of the story of Joseph in Egypt, where he was the steward in Potiphar's house. Potiphar's wife pressed him every day, and he always refused, saying that to yield would be to sin against his master and against God. Here the narrator, that is, the one telling the story, shows us that this time the pressure comes in a moment of solitude.

For today: when temptation keeps insisting, it is not enough to say no just once. It is wise to decide ahead of time what we will do, to guard the places where we are alone, and, like Joseph, to get out quickly from whatever leads us into sin.
exp.23:14:
This verse tells us that Rebekah arrived just before Abraham's servant had finished praying. It identifies her as the daughter of Bethuel, who was the son of Milcah and of Nahor, Abraham's brother. She was going out to the well with her jar of water on her shoulder.

The verse picks up right after the servant's prayer. Abraham had sent him to find a wife for his son Isaac from among Abraham's relatives. The servant asked God for a sign, and Rebekah appeared before he had finished speaking. Her family connection to Abraham was exactly what the servant had been looking for.

For today: we can bring our important decisions to God in prayer, trusting that he listens. He may answer in his own time and in his own way, sometimes sooner than we expect. In the meantime, it is good to stay attentive and faithful.
exp.0:4:
God gives a name to the light: he calls it "day." The darkness he calls "night." Then the text says, "there was evening, and there was morning—the first day," and this is how the first day of creation ends.

Here the narrator of Genesis describes how God orders everything by his word. After creating and separating the light, God names what he has made, showing that he rules over time. Christians understand the length of these "days" in different ways, and the Bible does not require one single reading.

For today: God orders time in cycles of work and rest. You can begin and end your day by giving God your morning and your evening, trusting that he sustains your life.
exp.34:19:
Jacob set up a monument over Rachel's tomb. The word "pillar" here refers to a stone marker, something raised to mark an important place. The text says that this marker still stood "to this day," that is, up to the time when the account was written.

It is the narrator who tells us what Jacob did. Rachel died while giving birth to Benjamin, on the road to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem. Jacob, in the midst of his grief, did not want her tomb to go unmarked. The text gives no further details about what the marker was like, so we should not imagine more than it says.

For today: grief is real, and remembering with affection those we love is healthy. You can honor their memory with a simple gesture, such as visiting a place, writing a few words, or telling their story. And as you remember, keep walking, as Jacob did, trusting that God sustains those who suffer.
exp.22:18:
This verse tells us that after these events Abraham buried his wife Sarah in the cave of the field at Machpelah, near Mamre, which is Hebron, in the land of Canaan. The field is the piece of ground where the cave was located. "Buried" means that he laid her to rest there.

Here no character speaks; it is the narrator who tells what happened. Sarah had died, and Abraham, who lived as a foreigner in Canaan, had no land of his own. For that reason he negotiated with the sons of Heth and bought the field and the cave. In this way he had a legitimate place to bid her farewell. Many see here a first piece of the promised land in Abraham's hands, although the text does not explain this directly.

For today: saying farewell with dignity to those we love is an act of love and faith. Abraham did not act in haste or carelessly. We can honor our loved ones with respect, and even in grief continue to trust in God's promises.
exp.29:0:
This verse tells how Rachel, seeing that she was not bearing any children for Jacob, became jealous of her sister Leah, who was bearing him sons. She then made a demand of Jacob: "Give me children, or I will die!" The word "envied" here refers to the pain and resentment over what another person has and one does not. "Or I will die" expresses her desperation.

Rachel and Leah were sisters and both were wives of Jacob. Leah already had several children, while Rachel, whom Jacob loved more, still had none. In that culture, having children gave a woman great value and security. Jacob responds with anger, saying that he is not in the place of God. Rachel then proposes using her servant Bilhah, a practice of the time.

For today: when you compare yourself with others and feel pain over what you lack, bring that desire to God in prayer, instead of venting it on the people you love.
exp.41:28:
This verse says that Jacob's sons arrived back at their father's home in the land of Canaan and described to him everything that had happened to them in Egypt. The reader will notice that the verse itself gives no details of the report; it simply introduces what they said.

The narrator tells us that Joseph's brothers were returning from Egypt, where they had gone to buy grain because of the famine. There they dealt with Joseph, but they did not recognize him. They were frightened because the money had appeared in a sack, and they wondered what God was doing. Now they must give an account to Jacob, their father. Let us note that their report does not tell everything in detail; the Bible does not say here that they explained everything that had happened in the past with Joseph.

For today: when we go through confusing moments, it is good to tell someone we trust what we are going through, and also to bring it to God in prayer. Speaking about it honestly helps us think more clearly and keeps us from carrying the fear alone.
exp.25:25:
This verse tells us that Abimelech, king of Gerar, came to Isaac. He was accompanied by Ahuzzath, his adviser, and Phicol, the commander of his army. The phrase "came to Isaac" means he came to the place where Isaac was. The word "commander" refers to the military leader in charge of his soldiers.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Isaac was in Beersheba, and God had just promised him that he would be with him and bless him. Earlier, these men had driven him out of their land. Now they arrive with authority, and then they explain that they saw that God was with Isaac and want to make a covenant of peace.

For today: when you live with faith and without revenge, God can change the hearts of those who rejected you. You do not have to force reconciliation; trust God and keep doing good.
exp.35:23:
These are the sons of Zibeon: Aiah and Anah. Anah is the one who found the hot springs in the wilderness while he was pasturing the donkeys of his father Zibeon. The Hebrew word here is unclear, and some translate it differently, so its exact meaning is not known with certainty.

The verse is part of a long list of the families of the Horites, a people who lived in the mountains of Seir, in the land of Edom. The narrator is generally understood to be Moses, who records these family lines. The detail about Anah is included so that he can be clearly identified among several people with similar names.

For today: God notices the everyday. Anah was doing a simple job, caring for his father's animals, and yet he was remembered. Pay careful attention to the small things you have today, because valuable things can come from them.
exp.26:28:
This verse is the blessing Isaac pronounces over his son. It says that peoples and nations will serve him and bow down before him, and that he will be master over his brothers, meaning he will have authority over them. The Berean Standard Bible reads "master" here, which conveys the idea of ruling or having dominion. The verse also says that those who curse this son will be cursed, and those who bless him will be blessed.

Isaac speaks as an old man who is nearly blind. He believes he is blessing Esau, his firstborn son, but Jacob has disguised himself as Esau and deceived his father with the help of Rebekah. This blessing recalls the promise God gave to Abraham. The Bible shows the deception clearly, without approving of it.

For today: God keeps his promises, but he does not need our tricks to bring them about. We can trust his timing and act with honesty, even when waiting is hard.
exp.43:15:
Judah speaks on behalf of all his brothers. He asks what they can say, or how they can plead, or how they can justify themselves, and he admits that they have no defense. He says, "God has exposed the iniquity of your servants," meaning that God has uncovered a guilt. He offers himself along with all of them as slaves to Joseph, including Benjamin, in whose sack the cup was found. Here "justify ourselves" means to prove that one is innocent.

Joseph had put his cup in Benjamin's sack in order to test his brothers. Judah does not know this. Perhaps he is speaking of the guilt they had carried since they sold Joseph, although the text does not say so clearly, and some readers interpret it that way.

Today, Judah teaches us to set aside excuses and take responsibility with humility. When we acknowledge our faults before God and others, the way opens to reconciliation and change.
exp.19:16:
This verse tells us that Abraham prayed to God on behalf of Abimelech, and God healed him, his wife, and his female servants, so that they could again bear children. "Maidservants" were the women who worked in the household.

Abimelech, king of Gerar, had taken Sarah, thinking she was unmarried, because Abraham had said she was his sister. God intervened and warned the king in a dream. After returning her, Abimelech made amends for the wrong. The next verse explains that God had closed the wombs of his household. Here Abraham acts as a prophet and intercessor, although earlier he had failed out of fear.

For today: God can use an imperfect person to bless others. Pray also for those who have caused you trouble, even if they did not mean harm. Prayer can open the way to healing and reconciliation.
exp.29:8:
Leah saw that she had stopped having children, so she gave her servant Zilpah to Jacob as a wife. "Having children" means giving birth, and "gave her servant to Jacob as a wife" is the plain meaning of the verse.

The narrator tells this in the middle of the rivalry between Leah and her sister Rachel. Rachel had just celebrated that her servant Bilhah had a second son. Leah responded in the same way: she used her servant to add children to the family. In that culture, having children brought honor and security. The Bible records the event, but it does not present it as an example to imitate.

When we compare ourselves with others, it is easy to make hasty decisions so that we do not fall behind. Before acting, stop to pray and ask whether you are trusting God or only competing.
exp.20:16:
God heard the voice of the boy, who is Ishmael. Then the angel of God spoke to Hagar from heaven. He asked her what was wrong, told her not to be afraid, and assured her that God had heard the boy right where he lay.

Hagar and her son had been sent away from Abraham's house and were lost in the wilderness of Beersheba. Their water ran out, and she, in despair, moved away so she would not have to watch him die. The account says that God heard the boy's voice, and then opened Hagar's eyes to see a well.

When you feel you have no resources and no way out, do not think that God does not see you. Cry out to Him sincerely. He hears the pain, and often He helps us discover the provision that was already close by.
exp.27:21:
Jacob says that the stone he set up as a pillar will be God's house, a place dedicated to God. He also promises that from all that God gives him, he will surely give God a tenth. "Pillar" here means a sign or monument, and "tenth" means one part in ten.

Jacob speaks after his dream at Bethel, where he saw a ladder reaching between heaven and earth and God promised to be with him. He was running away from his brother Esau and leaving home with very little. His vow sounds like a thankful response, though some readers see in the "if" of his earlier words a faith still growing. The Bible does not explain this in detail.

Today we can share that attitude of recognizing that everything we have comes from God. One practical way is to decide ahead of time, in prayer, how much you will give to the church or to help those in need, and to do it with gratitude, not out of obligation.
exp.15:6:
This verse tells that the angel of the LORD found Hagar beside a spring of water in the desert, on the road that leads toward Shur. The word "found" means that he came upon her, and "spring" here refers to a source of water. Hagar was fleeing and was alone, tired, and without direction.

The narrator relates what happened after Sarai mistreated her servant Hagar. She fled into the desert, probably toward Egypt, her homeland, although the text does not say this clearly. Some understand "the angel of the LORD" to be a messenger of God, while others see God himself speaking there; the text allows both readings.

For today: when you feel hurt, lost, or without a way out, remember that God sees you and comes out to meet you, even in your own desert. You can speak to him honestly, as Hagar did, and listen for his guidance.
exp.29:39:
Jacob set apart the young animals, and he made the rest of the flock face the streaked and dark-colored sheep in Laban's flocks. Then he set his own animals apart and did not put them with Laban's animals. This means he built his own separate flock and kept it apart from Laban's.

This verse is part of the account of how Jacob worked for his father-in-law Laban. The two had agreed that the spotted and speckled animals would be Jacob's wages. Jacob used peeled rods, but the text does not say that these rods had any power in themselves. Later, Jacob recounts that God saw Laban's unfair dealing and took care of him (Genesis 31:9-12).

For today: when you find yourself working in an unjust environment, do your part with diligence and resourcefulness, but trust that God is the one who ultimately sustains and cares for you.
exp.1:22:
Here Adam says that the woman is part of his very own nature: "bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh." The word "woman" in the verse above is the ordinary word for a female human, and "man" is the ordinary word for a male human. In Hebrew there is a word play similar to this: ish (man) and ishah (woman). The phrase "out of man she was taken" describes how she was formed from the man, and it appears in the verse above in its modern wording.

Adam, the first man, is the one speaking. Before this moment he had been alone, and no animal was a companion equal to him. When God presents the woman to him, he joyfully recognizes that she is equal to him. Some see here the first poem in the Bible.

For today: value the people close to you, especially in marriage, as equals before God. Treat them with respect, gratitude, and joy, not as someone inferior or as a possession.
exp.33:21:
Here it is stated that the men of Shechem would agree to let Jacob's family live among them and become one people, but only on one condition: that all their males be circumcised, just as Jacob's family was. The phrase "will agree" means they would accept the arrangement, and the verse's wording "if all our men are circumcised as they are" makes clear that the requirement applied to every man in the city.

Hamor and his son Shechem speak to the men of their city at the gate, which was the place where public decisions were made. Shechem had dishonored Dinah, Jacob's daughter, and now wanted to marry her. Dinah's brothers had set circumcision as the condition. Hamor presents the arrangement as something peaceful, but he also lets it be seen that he is interested in the wealth of Jacob's household.

For today: before accepting an agreement, it is wise to ask what motives lie behind it, both in others and in ourselves. Kind words can hide selfish interests, and God calls us to act with truth and justice.
exp.23:62:
Isaac went out into the field early in the evening. The original word here is unusual, and some translations render it as "pray" while others say he went out to meditate or walk and think. When he looked up, he saw the camels approaching.

The narrator describes the moment just before Isaac and Rebekah meet. Abraham's servant had traveled a long way to find a wife for Isaac, and now he was bringing Rebekah back with him. Isaac lived in the south, near the well where God had earlier cared for Hagar.

Today we can set aside a quiet moment of the day to speak with God and think about what we hope for. While Isaac was praying and meditating, God was already guiding what he was waiting for. Trusting and waiting in peace is also a way of prayer.
exp.27:17:
Early the next morning, Jacob took the stone he had placed under his head and set it up as a pillar. Then he poured oil over the top of it. In this verse, "pillar" means a marker set up to remember something, and the stone was the one he had rested his head on.

The story picks up right after Jacob's dream at Bethel. He was running away from his brother Esau and traveling alone, far from home. God had promised him his presence and his blessing. When Jacob woke, he felt awe and reverence, and he marked the place. Pouring oil over the stone was a way of setting it apart for God. Scholars understand this as a dedication, though the Bible does not explain every detail of the act.

When God meets us, it is good to respond and not to forget. We can create a simple reminder: write down in a notebook what God has done today, and read it again on difficult days.
exp.47:12:
Joseph took his two sons and brought them close to his father Jacob, who is called Israel here. He placed Ephraim in his right hand, toward Israel's left hand, and Manasseh in his left hand, toward Israel's right hand. This arrangement shows how Joseph presented his sons to his father to receive the blessing.

Israel, already old and nearly blind, is about to bless his grandsons. Joseph wants the elder, Manasseh, to receive the main blessing, so he positions him toward his grandfather's right hand. But Israel will cross his hands, and the text does not hide it: he did so on purpose.

We can make plans with good intentions, as Joseph did, but God sometimes works in a different way. Today we can present our family before God in prayer and trust that his ways are better than ours.
exp.33:23:
All the men who went out of the city gate listened to Hamor and his son Shechem, and every male of the city was circumcised. "Listened" here means that they heard the proposal and accepted it. "The men who went out of the city gate" refers to the men who belonged to the community and took part in the city's decisions.

Hamor and Shechem spoke at the city gate, which was the place of meetings and decisions. They had persuaded the men with a promise of gain: the goods of Jacob and his household would become theirs. Earlier, Shechem had dishonored Dinah, and Jacob's sons demanded circumcision with deceit. The text does not approve of the violence that follows.

For today: before following the majority or a leader, examine their motives. When selfish interest is involved, ask God for wisdom so that you are not carried away.
exp.29:7:
Rachel says she has struggled hard with her sister Leah, and that she has won. That is why she names her son Naphtali, a name connected with the idea of wrestling or struggling. "Won" means that she has come out ahead in the contest between them. The phrase "in my great struggles" can be understood in more than one way: as an intense, long-running conflict, or as a struggle in which she sensed God's involvement.

The speaker is Rachel, the wife of Jacob. She could not have children, while Leah could. So she gave her servant Bilhah to Jacob, and Bilhah bore this second son. It was a painful rivalry between sisters, and Rachel reads the birth as a victory. The Bible recounts this without approving every decision the family made.

For today: when you feel pain or comparison with others, take care that your identity does not depend on "winning." Bring your pain to God with honesty, and ask him for healing and peace in your relationships.
exp.17:25:
It says that the LORD agrees to Abraham's request. If there were fifty righteous people within the city of Sodom, God would spare the whole place on their account.

The verse uses the phrase "on their account," which means "because of them" or "out of consideration for them."

The LORD answers Abraham directly. The divine visitors had told him they were going to examine the wickedness of Sodom. Abraham, concerned for the righteous and for his nephew Lot, who lived there, prays with reverence and asks whether the Judge of all the earth will not do what is just. God shows patience and a willingness to listen.

Today we can pray with confidence for our city, family, and country, appealing to God's justice and mercy. Our prayer matters, and the presence of faithful people can be a blessing to others.
exp.35:39:
This verse begins a list of chiefs who descended from Esau, the brother of Jacob. Here the first names appear: Timna, Alvah, and Jetheth, listed according to their families, their regions, and their names.

The author of the book, traditionally identified as Moses, reviews the history of Edom, the people who came from Esau. Earlier, the text spoke of Edomite kings, and now it presents the chiefs of their clans. This shows that God fulfilled his promise to make Esau a nation, even though the main promise passed through Jacob. It is not known with certainty why such detailed lists are included, but they show that the Bible rests on real history.

For today: God knows names and families, even those that seem unimportant to us. Remember that you are not anonymous to Him either, and treat every person with that same value.
exp.45:24:
This verse closes the list of the sons of Bilhah, the servant whom Laban gave to his daughter Rachel. Bilhah had children with Jacob: Dan and Naphtali, and from them came seven in all.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, listing the family of Jacob as he goes down to Egypt with Joseph. Names and numbers are recorded because God was forming the people of Israel, and every family counted. Some scholars explain in different ways how the totals of 66 and 70 are added up, so it is not wise to force a single explanation.

For today: God pays attention to each person, even to those whom the story could have passed over, like Bilhah. You are not an anonymous number to Him either. Today you can thank Him that He knows you by name and value those who usually go unnoticed.
exp.13:11:
The explanation says that the victorious kings carried off Lot, Abram's nephew, along with all his possessions. Lot was living in Sodom, and for that reason he was caught up in the defeat of that city. The word "possessions" means his belongings, and "was living" means that he had settled there.

It is part of Moses' account of a war between several kings of the region. Here the narrator simply reports what happened, without speaking to anyone. Earlier, Lot had chosen to settle near Sodom (Genesis 13). Now he suffers the consequences of being in the middle of a city in danger. The verse sets the stage for the scene in which Abram will step in to rescue him.

Our decisions can lead us to places we later find hard to leave. It is wise to think carefully about where we place our hearts and our lives. And if someone close to us is in trouble, as Abram was, we can help them with love, even when they have made mistakes.
exp.37:23:
About three months later, Judah was told that his daughter-in-law Tamar had prostituted herself and was now pregnant. The phrase "prostituted herself" means she had had sexual relations outside of marriage. The word "told" means that someone informed him. Judah, without investigating, orders her brought out and burned to death.

The one speaking is Judah, the head of the family. Tamar had been a widow of his sons, and he had not given her his son Shelah, as was due. She still belonged to the family, which is why Judah feels entitled to condemn her. He did not know the pregnancy was his own. Some scholars note that he judges harshly, even though he himself had acted wrongly.

For today: before condemning others, let us examine our own lives and seek the truth with humility. Jesus invites us to judge with mercy, remembering that we too need forgiveness.
exp.22:0:
Sarah lived to be 127 years old, and the verse tells us her full span of life. The wording stands out because it gives the total so plainly, and the number is written out in a single clear statement.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks. He opens the account of Sarah's death, the wife of Abraham, which took place in Hebron, in Canaan. Right after, it is told that Abraham mourned for her and looked for a place to bury her. The text does not explain why it gives her age; many think it wants to honor her whole life.

For today: God counts and values every life, and we can do the same. Honor those you love while they are with you, and when loss comes, allow yourself to weep, as Abraham did, without haste or shame.
exp.27:8:
Esau went to the family of Ishmael, his uncle, and married Mahalath, Ishmael's daughter and the sister of Nebaioth. He already had other wives, and now he added this one to them.

Here the narrator of Genesis speaks. Esau saw that his father Isaac was not pleased with the Canaanite women, and that Jacob had been sent away to find a wife among the relatives. So Esau tried to please his father by marrying a descendant of Abraham. The Bible does not explain his motives further, so we do not know whether it was a sincere gesture or only a late arrangement.

For today: Correcting a mistake is good, but God looks at the heart. Let us seek to obey sincerely, not only to look good before others.
exp.26:43:
Rebekah tells Jacob to stay with her brother Laban for "a while," meaning only a short time. The phrase "until your brother's fury subsides" means that Esau's anger would gradually fade and calm down.

The speaker is Rebekah, Jacob's mother. She learned that Esau, furious that Jacob had received their father's blessing, planned to kill him. She wants to protect her son's life, so she proposes that he flee to Haran. She believed it would be only a short time, but the Bible shows that Jacob was away for many years.

For today: when there is a serious conflict, giving it time and distance can sometimes help emotions settle. But this is no substitute for honesty or reconciliation. Ask God for wisdom to repair what you have damaged.
exp.42:6:
Joseph's brothers explain to their father Jacob (Israel) why they told the governor of Egypt that they had another brother. They say that the man questioned them in detail about their family: whether their father was still alive and whether they had another brother. They simply answered him truthfully. The phrase "in detail" reflects the closeness of his questioning, and "the man" is Joseph, whom they still do not recognize. Then they defend themselves: how could they possibly have known that he would tell them to bring Benjamin down?

Context: There is famine in the land, and they need to return to Egypt for food. Jacob grieves because he fears losing Benjamin, the son left to him by Rachel, after believing Joseph was dead. The brothers try to justify themselves in the face of his pain and his reproach.

For today: When something goes wrong, it is easy to defend ourselves or blame circumstances. It is better to listen with humility to the one who is suffering, acknowledge their pain, and seek a solution together, as Judah will do later.
exp.36:7:
Joseph's brothers answer him with anger: "Do you intend to reign over us?" "Will you actually rule us?" And they hated him even more because of his dream and his statements. To "reign" or "rule" means to hold authority over others, and "hated" means to despise and resent him.

The older brothers of Joseph are speaking, right after he has told them his dream of the sheaves bowing down to his sheaf. They already felt jealousy, since their father Jacob loved him in a special way. They understood the dream as a promise that Joseph would rule over them. The text does not say that Joseph spoke with bad intent, but his words increased the envy.

For today: jealousy can harden the heart and make us reject the one God wants to use. Let us ask God to help us rejoice for others instead of competing with them. It is also wise to speak with humility and wisdom when we share what we believe God is showing us.
exp.4:12:
This verse says that Kenan lived 840 years after he became the father of Mahalalel, and during those years he had other sons and daughters. The wording "became the father of" is the plain meaning here, so the phrase simply describes the birth of his son.

This is not a speaking character; it is the narrator of the book of Genesis, who records a list of generations from Adam. His purpose is to show how humanity continued, generation after generation, after the fall. The pattern repeats: a son is born, life goes on, other children are born, and finally the person dies. The very long numbers of years are understood in different ways, and there is no single certain explanation.

For today: our daily life, though it may seem ordinary, has value before God. We can use our years raising, teaching, and blessing those who come after us.
exp.39:8:
So the chief cupbearer told Joseph his dream: "In my dream there was a vine before me." The cupbearer was the official in charge of serving wine to the pharaoh, and "chief cupbearer" means the head of all those who poured drink for the king.

The pharaoh's cupbearer and baker were in prison together with Joseph, and both of them looked sad because of their dreams. Joseph had told them that God is the one who gives interpretations, and he invited them to tell him what they had dreamed. So the cupbearer speaks first, and Joseph listens closely.

For today: when someone is worried, it is worth stopping to ask how they are and to listen to them. Joseph, even while in prison, noticed the sadness of others and helped them, trusting that God is the one who gives true light.
exp.38:12:
This verse says that Potiphar's wife realized that Joseph had left his cloak in her hand and had run out of the house. The cloak she held was an article of clothing, probably a cloak or tunic.

The one who narrates is Moses, the traditional author of Genesis. Joseph was a young Hebrew slave, in charge of Potiphar's house. The woman had pressed him several times, and he had refused out of loyalty to God and to his master. When she saw that he had run away, she felt humiliated and soon invented a false accusation against him.

For today: when temptation is strong, there is no need to hesitate or argue at length; sometimes the wisest thing is to get away quickly. Joseph chose to lose his clothing rather than lose his integrity, although that brought him injustice for a time.
exp.37:8:
It says that Onan knew the child born would not be considered his. For that reason, when he was with his dead brother's wife, he would spill his seed on the ground so that he would not produce offspring for his brother. The word "offspring" in the Berean wording makes clear that the issue was children, and "sleep with" means have sexual relations with her.

The text tells what happened after the death of Er. Judah asked Onan to fulfill the custom of raising up an heir for the deceased brother, so that his brother's line and family would continue. Onan agreed in appearance, but acted out of selfishness. The passage says that the LORD was displeased with what he did. Many understand that the sin was refusing to fulfill his duty to Tamar and his brother.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we fulfill our responsibilities to others or seek only our own benefit. God looks at the heart behind our actions.
exp.38:20:
This verse says that the LORD was with Joseph even in prison. "Kindness" here means faithful, loving care. The phrase "granting him favor in the eyes of the prison warden" means that God caused the warden to look upon him with appreciation and trust.

It is part of the story of Joseph in Egypt. The narrator tells that, after being falsely accused by Potiphar's wife, Joseph was imprisoned. Even so, the text emphasizes that God did not abandon him. Soon the warden entrusted to him the prisoners and everything that was done there.

For today: when you are in an unjust or difficult situation, remember that God's presence does not depend on your circumstances. Keep doing your work with honesty, and trust that God can give you favor and care for you even in unexpected places.
exp.45:14:
This verse closes the list of Leah's children. It says that she bore these sons to Jacob in Paddan-aram, the region where Jacob lived with his uncle Laban. It also names his daughter Dinah. The verse counts everyone in this group, Jacob's sons and daughters, and the total comes to thirty-three. Some scholars explain in different ways how that number is reached.

The account, which tradition attributes to Moses, lists Jacob's family who go down to Egypt. This shows that God was beginning to fulfill his promise to make this family a great nation.

For today: God does not see people as a faceless crowd. Every name matters. Today you can value the members of your family, pray for them one by one, and trust that God cares for their story.
exp.39:12:
Within three days, the pharaoh of Egypt will restore the cupbearer to his position. "Lift up your head" means that he will bring him out of prison and honor him again. "Restore your position" means to return him to his former role, and a cupbearer is the one who served the king his cup. The phrase "just as you did when you were his cupbearer" means the cupbearer will go back to doing the same job he did before.

Joseph speaks from prison. The cupbearer had told him a dream about a vine with three branches, and Joseph interprets it as three days. He says this as an interpreter, but makes clear that the interpretation comes from God (v. 8). Right after, he asks the cupbearer to remember him, because he is imprisoned unjustly.

Today we can learn to be faithful and to serve with love even in difficult places, as Joseph did. It is also healthy to ask for help with humility, while trusting that God works in his own time, even when others forget us.
exp.30:30:
Jacob tells Laban that he left secretly because he was afraid. He believed Laban would take his daughters away from him by force. The phrase "by force" means taking them by violence, so that Jacob would be unable to stop it.

Laban caught up with Jacob and accused him of leaving without telling him and of stealing his gods, that is, his household idols. Jacob first answers the complaint about his departure. About the idols he knew nothing, because Rachel had taken them without his knowledge. That is why he later says that whoever has them should die.

When we are afraid, it is easy to act in secret instead of speaking plainly. Jacob explains his fear, but his flight created more conflict. Today we can seek honest conversation, ask for wise counsel, and trust that God cares for us, even in difficult conversations.
exp.23:47:
This verse says that Abraham's servant bowed his head to the ground, worshiped the LORD, and gave thanks. He recognizes that God led him on the right road, that is, the correct path, to find the granddaughter of Abraham's brother and bring her back to marry Isaac. "Blessed" here means "praised" or "gave thanks." "Worshiped" means "bowed down in worship."

Here the servant speaks, although the Bible does not give his name in this passage. He is in the house of Bethuel, telling Rebekah's family how he came to them. He explains that his prayer was answered at the well. With this account he wants them to see the hand of God in everything and to give an answer about the marriage.

For today: when you see that God guides or answers you, stop to thank Him. Before moving forward, acknowledge that it was He who opened the way.
exp.29:22:
Genesis 30:23 says that Rachel became pregnant and gave birth to a son. Then she declared that God had taken away her shame. The word "shame" here carries the sense of something humiliating, a mark that other people could see and that weighed on her heart.

The one speaking is Rachel, Jacob's wife. For years she could not have children, while her sister Leah, the other wife of Jacob, had many. In that culture, not having children was often experienced as a heavy burden and a great dishonor. The text says that God remembered her and heard her. She recognizes God as the one who lifted that shame from her. Afterward she names the boy Joseph, and asks for another son.

For today: when you carry a shame or a long wait, bring it to God honestly. And when he answers, don't forget to thank him, as Rachel did.
exp.17:23:
Abraham asks God whether he would sweep the city away even if there were fifty righteous people in it. He asks that, for the sake of those righteous people, God would not destroy the place but spare it. The word "perhaps" introduces his question, and "righteous" refers to people who live uprightly before God.

Abraham is the one speaking. Two of the visitors were already on their way to Sodom, but he remained standing before the LORD. God had told him about the judgment coming on the city. Abraham pleads, perhaps thinking also of his nephew Lot, who lived there, although the text does not mention him at this point. His concern is that God not treat the righteous and the wicked alike.

Today we can pray with confidence for our city, our family, and others, appealing to God's justice and mercy. Abraham teaches us to come near to God with reverence, yet with sincerity.
exp.40:43:
Pharaoh tells Joseph that he remains the king, but that no one in all of Egypt will move a hand or foot without Joseph's permission. "Lift up his hand or foot" means to move or act. In other words, Joseph stands as the highest authority after the king.

Pharaoh speaks after Joseph interpreted his dreams and advised him to prepare for seven years of plenty and seven years of famine. Impressed, Pharaoh appoints him ruler and gives him a ring, fine clothes, and a gold chain, signs of authority. Joseph was thirty years old and coming out of years of slavery and prison. The Bible presents this moment as a promotion that God made possible.

For today: God can use hard times to prepare a person. Be faithful and honest where you are, even when no one notices. And when you receive responsibility, use it to serve and protect others, as Joseph did.
exp.35:16:
These are the sons of Esau's son Reuel: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah. They are the chiefs who descended from Reuel in the land of Edom, and they were the grandsons of Esau's wife Basemath.

The word "chief" here means a leader of a tribe, not a noble in a European sense. Edom is another name for Esau, and also the name of the land where his descendants lived.

The narrator of Genesis is the one recording the family line of Esau. This list shows that God kept his promise to make Esau into a nation, even though the line of the promise passed through Jacob. Scholars believe these records were preserved to document the origin of Edom, Israel's neighbor.

For today: God remembers families and people, including those who seem less important in history. Your life and your family have value to Him, even when no one mentions them.
exp.4:18:
Genesis 5:19 says that after he had become the father of Enoch, Jared lived 800 years and had other sons and daughters. The verse simply records the next stage of his life: the birth of his son Enoch, followed by many more years and more children.

The account in Genesis 5 repeats a family history from Adam to Noah. Each life is summed up in the same pattern: a person was born, had children, lived, and died. The very large numbers are understood in different ways. Some readers take them literally, while others see them as a way of describing a very ancient period. The exact intention is not certain.

For today, Jared's life is not remembered for great achievements but for his family and the course of his years. We can use our own days with purpose, caring for those closest to us and passing on a living faith, trusting that God carries history forward.
exp.31:17:
Jacob tells the servant who leads the first group of animals what to say if Esau asks him. He must say that the animals belong to Jacob, whom he calls "your servant," and that they are a gift sent to Esau, whom he calls "my lord." He must also let Esau know that Jacob himself is coming behind. "Gift" is the plain meaning here, and calling himself "your servant" is a gesture of humility.

Jacob speaks after years of running from his brother, whom he had deceived to obtain the blessing. Now he knows that Esau is approaching with four hundred men, and he fears for his life. For that reason he sends gifts in stages, hoping to calm Esau's anger before they meet. The text shows his fear, but it does not say how Esau would have reacted without the gifts.

For today: when there is an unresolved offense, taking the first step with humility and concrete actions can open the door to reconciliation, without ceasing to pray and to trust in God.
exp.15:12:
Hagar, Sarai's servant, gives God a name: "You are the God who sees me." She is amazed that she has seen, there in the wilderness, the One who was seeing her.

Hagar was running away from Sarai, who treated her harshly, and she was alone beside a spring in the desert. The angel of the Lord spoke to her, promised her a son, and told her to name him Ishmael, which means "God hears." Many understand that this angel represented the Lord himself, since Hagar speaks of "the LORD who had spoken to her." She was a foreigner and had no power, yet God took notice of her.

For today: when you feel alone, overlooked, or hurt, remember that God sees you and hears you. You can speak to him honestly, knowing that your pain matters to him.
exp.42:3:
What it says: Judah is speaking to his father Jacob. He tells him that if he lets Benjamin, the youngest brother, go with them, they will go down to Egypt and buy food for the family. The word "send" means "let go" or "allow to travel," and "go down" means traveling south into Egypt.

Context: The family is going hungry because the grain they brought back earlier has run out. Jacob wants them to return to Egypt, but the ruler, who is Joseph without them knowing it, demanded that they bring Benjamin. Judah speaks with firmness and respect, and explains that without Benjamin the journey will be of no use.

For today: When a difficult decision has to be made, speaking clearly and honestly helps a great deal. Judah does not hide the problem or demand anything harshly; he presents the truth and proposes a solution. In this way we can face the fears of others: with calm, sincerity, and a willingness to take responsibility.
exp.23:1:
Abraham calls his chief servant, the one who manages all he owns, and asks him to place his hand under his thigh. The gesture was a solemn way of making an oath, and the verse shows Abraham treating the matter with great seriousness.

Abraham is now an old man, and God has blessed him in everything. He wants to make sure that his son Isaac marries someone who does not worship the gods of Canaan. So he asks his trusted servant for a serious promise. Scholars believe the gesture is connected with descendants and with the importance of the promise, but the text does not explain it with certainty.

For today: the important decisions of life, such as marriage, deserve prayer, wise counsel, and trustworthy people. Abraham did not act carelessly, but with faith and responsibility.
exp.48:31:
The field and the cave that is in it were purchased from the Hittites, ancient inhabitants of Canaan. It was not a gift or a questionable piece of property. It was a real, legitimate purchase.
