For today: when a difficult decision causes us pain, we can bring it to God with sincerity. He understands our suffering, guides our steps, and cares for the people we do not fully understand.
exp.9:21:
This verse lists the five sons of Shem, one of the three sons of Noah: Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud, and Aram. Some of these names are spelled in an older style, such as Asshur and Arphaxad. They are names of people, and over time they also came to be associated with peoples and regions.

The narrator, traditionally identified with Moses, presents what is often called the Table of Nations. It shows how the earth was resettled after the flood. Here the list of Ham's line ends and the list of Shem's line begins. From this line will come Eber and, later, Abraham. Scholars debate how exactly each people should be placed, so it is wise not to claim more than the text itself says.

For today: God knows every name and every family. You are not a number to Him. Remember to thank Him, because He cares for your story and for your people, even when you cannot see the whole picture.
exp.42:25:
This verse tells us that Joseph arrived home at midday. His brothers presented him with the gifts they had brought and bowed down to the ground before him.

The narrator is describing the brothers' second journey to Egypt. They had come back with Benjamin and with gifts to win the governor's favor. Without knowing it, they were fulfilling the dreams Joseph had as a young man, when his brothers bowed down before him (Genesis 37). They still did not recognize him.

God can carry out His plans even when we do not understand them. If you are living through a long wait or a confusing situation today, remember that God is still at work behind what you cannot see. Trust in Him and act with humility and honesty.
exp.9:15:
This verse continues the list of the sons of Canaan. It names three peoples who descend from him: the Jebusites, the Amorites, and the Girgashites. The final "-ites" in words like "Jebusites" indicates that the text speaks of a whole people, not just a single person. The spelling "Amorites" is the one used today.

Genesis 10 is the "Table of Nations." No one is speaking in it; the narrator, traditionally identified with Moses, sets out the origins of the peoples after the flood. Many of these peoples appear later in the history of Israel, for example the Jebusites in Jerusalem. Scholars debate some details of these identifications, but the general purpose is clear.

For today: God knows each people and each person, even when history forgets them. Today you can treat everyone with respect, remembering that they have value before God.
exp.45:30:
Here Joseph tells his brothers and all of his father's household that he will go up and inform Pharaoh. He says he will tell him: "My brothers and my father's household from the land of Canaan have come to me." The words "go up" and "inform" in the Berean wording correspond to the original, and his plan to report this to the king is the central point of the verse.

Joseph, already ruler of Egypt, speaks just after being reunited with his father Jacob (also called Israel) in Goshen. He wants to present his family before Pharaoh with order and respect, and to prepare them for what the king might ask them. In this way he makes sure they can remain in that land.

For today: Joseph used his position to care for his family with prudence and not with carelessness. We can learn to prepare things well and to use with humility the influence that God has given us to bless and protect those we love.
exp.23:17:
The explanation says that Rebekah answered kindly: "Drink, my lord." She then quickly lowered her jar to her hands so the man could take water, and gave him a drink. The phrase "quickly lowered" shows she acted without delay. A "jar" is a vessel for carrying water. A "maiden" is a young woman.

Abraham's servant, sent to find a wife for Isaac, had prayed asking for a sign. He arrived at the well, saw Rebekah, and asked her for water. She responds with respect and generosity. She will then offer to draw water for the camels as well, which was heavy work. Many understand that this shows her character, and that the account presents this scene as the answer to the servant's prayer.

Today we can imitate her attitude: to help quickly and kindly anyone who has a need, even a stranger. A simple gesture, done willingly and without complaint, can show a great deal of our heart.
exp.29:23:
Rachel says that when her son was born, she named him Joseph. The name sounds like the Hebrew word for "add," which is why she says: "May the LORD add to me another son." In other words, she gives thanks for this child and asks God to give her one more.

It is Rachel who speaks. She was the beloved wife of Jacob, but she had been childless for years and bore that situation as a shame. Now God hears her and gives her a son. His name expresses both gratitude and hope. Afterward, Jacob decides to return to his land, and so a new chapter of his life begins.

For today: when God answers a prayer of yours, thank Him sincerely and keep trusting Him for what is ahead. Giving thanks and continuing to hope do not oppose each other; they go together in a simple faith.
exp.14:6:
God reminds Abram who he is: "I am the LORD", the one who brought him out of Ur of the Chaldeans. And he tells him why he did it: to give him this land to possess. The word "possess" here means to have the land as his own, given to him as a gift and not earned by him.

God speaks with Abram right after promising him descendants as numerous as the stars, and Abram believed him. Now God adds the promise of the land, grounding it in what he has already done for him. Abram responds by asking for a sign, and God answers him with a covenant, through the animals he asks Abram to prepare.

For today: when you doubt the future, remember what God has already done for you. His faithfulness in the past gives you reasons to trust his promises, and it is fine to speak honestly with him about your doubts.
exp.0:23:
This verse tells that God commanded the earth to bring forth living creatures. "Kinds" refers to groups or types of creatures. "Livestock" means domesticated animals, the "beasts of the earth" are wild animals, and "land crawlers" are creatures that move along the ground. "And it was so" means it happened just as God said.

Here God speaks on the sixth day of creation. A day earlier He had filled the sea and the sky with life. Now He fills the land. It is the step just before the creation of human beings, which comes next. Some believers understand these days as literal days, and others as longer periods; the text does not fully settle the question.

God creates with order, purpose, and variety, and what He made is good. Today we can care for nature with gratitude, treating animals and the earth with respect, because they are the work of God.
exp.30:12:
Here the angel of God speaks in God's name and says, "I am the God of Bethel." He reminds Jacob of two things: that at Bethel he anointed the pillar, a stone set up as a sign, and that he made a solemn vow there. Then he gives him a clear command: get up, leave this land at once, and return to your native land.

Jacob tells Rachel and Leah about it. About twenty years of work for Laban have passed, during which Laban deceived him several times. God says he has seen all of that. Bethel was the place where, fleeing from his brother Esau, Jacob had dreamed of the ladder and God promised to be with him (Genesis 28).

For today: God sees what we suffer and remembers his promises and ours. If we have promised something to God, it is worth reviewing it with sincerity. And when God points us to a step, we can trust and obey.
exp.40:2:
After them, seven other cows, sickly and thin, came up from the Nile and stood beside the well-fed cows on the bank of the river. This verse tells that in Pharaoh's dream, seven more cows rise out of the river after the first ones. But these are sickly and thin, and they stand beside the well-fed cows on the bank.

The contrast between the healthy cows and the sickly ones is the key detail here. The thin cows stand right next to the fat ones, which makes their poor condition all the more striking.

The narrator of Genesis recounts Pharaoh's dream, which came to the king of Egypt two years after Joseph had been imprisoned. The contrast between the well-fed cows and the thin ones prepares what follows: the thin cows devour the fat ones. Later, Joseph will explain that God was announcing seven years of abundance and seven years of famine.

For today: good times do not always last, and difficult times can come. This passage invites us to be prudent, to save wisely, and to trust in God, who sees the future and cares for us in every season.
exp.7:3:
It says that on the seventeenth day of the seventh month, the ark came to a stop and settled on some mountains. "Came to rest" means it stopped moving and stayed firmly in place. "Ararat" is the name used in this verse; the original text names a mountainous region in the north. No one knows for certain which exact mountain it was.

The narrator tells of the moment when the flood begins to recede. God had stopped the rain, and the waters were slowly going down. After months afloat, the ark finally comes to rest. The text marks dates carefully, showing that God carried everything out in order and did not forget Noah or those who were with him.

When you are waiting for an answer, remember that God works in his own time, even when it is slow. Noah still had to wait several more months before he could leave. Trust that God has not forgotten you, and take the next step today with patience.
exp.48:3:
Here Jacob tells Reuben that he is uncontrolled like the waters, and for that reason he will no longer excel. He went up to his father's bed, onto Jacob's couch, meaning he had relations with one of his father's wives, and in this way he dishonored Jacob. The verse says he defiled the bed, which means he degraded it.

Jacob, now an old man, blesses and warns his twelve sons before he dies. Reuben, the eldest, was to receive the birthright, but his sin, which is recorded in Genesis 35:22, took that privilege away from him. Interpreters understand "uncontrolled as the waters" as a lack of self-control or steadiness.

For today: our impulsive decisions can cost us more than we think. Let us ask God for self-control, and if we have failed, let us turn to his forgiveness, even though some consequences may remain.
exp.44:9:
Here Joseph tells his brothers that their father Jacob will be able to settle in the region of Goshen, near him. There the whole family will be together: the children, the grandchildren, the flocks, and everything they own. "Flocks" refers to the sheep and goats, and "settle" means "live."

Joseph speaks to his brothers after revealing who he is. Egypt is suffering a famine, and five more years of it remain. He no longer blames them for having sold him, but sees the hand of God in everything. Goshen is usually placed in the east of the Nile delta, although its exact location is not entirely certain. It was good land for pasture.

Today we can learn from Joseph to offer forgiveness through concrete actions. He does not merely say that he forgives, but cares, provides, and brings his family close. Let us consider who needs from us not only words, but help and closeness.
exp.26:11:
Jacob tells his mother that he is afraid. He worries that his father Isaac might touch him and find out that he is not Esau. In the Berean Standard wording, Jacob asks, "What if my father touches me?" He fears that if he is discovered, he will be seen as a deceiver and will bring a curse on himself instead of a blessing.

Jacob speaks with Rebekah. She plans for him to pass himself off as Esau in order to receive Isaac's blessing, since Isaac was old and could barely see. Jacob does not object to the deception itself, but to the risk of being caught. Rebekah tells him that any curse will fall on her. The text narrates this without approving it, and painful consequences for the family follow.

For today: when a plan worries us more because of the punishment than because of what is right, it is wise to stop and reflect. God keeps his promises without our needing to use tricks.
exp.14:0:
God spoke to Abram in a vision, after these events. He tells him not to be afraid and makes two promises: to be his "shield," that is, his protector, and to be his "reward." The text describes this reward as "very great," that is, enormous.

The one speaking is God, and He speaks to Abram soon after Abram rescued his nephew Lot and turned down the riches of the king of Sodom (Genesis 14). Abram probably felt fear and doubt, since he still had no children, and that is why he answers in worry about his heir. God assures him that He Himself will take care of him.

Today, when you feel fear or uncertainty about the future, remember that God offers Himself as your protection and your greatest treasure. You can pray honestly, telling Him your fears, and trust that He cares for you.
exp.45:5:
This verse tells us that Jacob and his whole family went down to Egypt, taking their livestock and all the possessions they had acquired in the land of Canaan. The word "possessions" here refers to their belongings and property. The phrase "Jacob and all his offspring" refers to his descendants: his children, grandchildren, and other relatives. They left nothing important behind; they moved together, complete.

The passage is narrative, and the one telling the story is the writer of Genesis. Jacob, now an old man, was traveling to be reunited with his son Joseph, who was governing in Egypt. Before setting out, at Beersheba, God had told him not to be afraid, that he would go down with him to Egypt, and that he would bring him back again. So this journey was not merely a move because of the famine, but a step guided by God's promise.

For today: when God calls you to a major change, you can move forward in peace if you rest on his promise to go with you. Before deciding, pray and seek his guidance; then take the step with your family, trusting that he goes with you.
exp.19:15:
Here Abimelech speaks to Sarah. He tells her that he is giving a thousand pieces of silver to your brother, meaning Abraham, whom Sarah had presented as her brother. The words "It is your vindication before all who are with you; you are completely cleared" show that the gift is meant to clear her name publicly before everyone around her.

Abimelech, king of Gerar, had taken Sarah believing she was unmarried, because Abraham had said she was his sister. God warned him in a dream, and he returned her. Now he repairs the harm with gifts and with this public gesture.

For today: when we cause harm, even unintentionally, it is wise to acknowledge it and repair it with action. Honesty also prevents bigger problems.
exp.24:31:
Esau comes in exhausted and very hungry, and he says he is about to die. Then he asks what good the birthright is to him, that is, the special right of the firstborn son, which included honor, leadership in the family, and a double portion of the inheritance. "I am about to die" sounds exaggerated, and many read it as a way of expressing his desperation in that moment.

Esau is the elder brother of Jacob. Jacob had prepared a reddish stew of lentils, and he takes advantage of his brother's hunger to ask him for the birthright. Esau agrees and even swears to it. The text concludes that in this way he treated that right as something of little value.

For today: when we face an urgent need, let us ask God for calm before deciding. A quick satisfaction can cost us something valuable and lasting, such as faith, family, or integrity.
exp.37:11:
After a long time, Judah's wife, the daughter of Shua, died. When Judah had finished mourning, he went up to Timnah with his friend Hirah from Adullam, to the place where his sheep were being sheared, that is, where the wool was cut from them.

Here the narrator is speaking, not a character. Earlier, Judah had promised his daughter-in-law Tamar that she could marry his son Shelah, but he did not keep his word, out of fear that Shelah would also die. This verse shows that Judah has already returned to his life and his work, while Tamar keeps waiting, forgotten. That prepares what she will do afterward.

For today: comfort after grief is healthy, but it does not free us from keeping what we have promised. Let us check whether there is someone waiting for something we owe them, and keep our word.
exp.31:21:
It says Jacob got up during the night and took his family across the Jabbok River: his two wives (Leah and Rachel), his two maidservants, and his eleven sons. A "ford" is a shallow place in a river where a person can cross on foot. The verse says Jacob "got up," which is the plain sense of the wording.

The narrator tells us that Jacob was returning to Canaan and would soon meet his brother Esau, whom he had deceived years earlier. Jacob was afraid, so he sent gifts ahead to calm Esau's anger. That night he moved his family across, and afterward he was left alone. There follows the struggle with "a man," whom many understand as a divine being, though it is interpreted in different ways.

For today: when you feel fear about an unfinished matter, do what is yours to do with wisdom, as Jacob did, but do not stop seeking God in private prayer.
exp.31:6:
Genesis 32:7 says that Jacob was filled with great fear and distress. In response, he divided the people who were with him, along with the flocks, herds, and camels, into two camps.

Jacob was returning to his homeland after many years away. Long before, he had deceived his brother Esau, and now his messengers brought word that Esau was coming to meet him with four hundred men. It is not known for certain whether Esau was coming in peace or in anger, and Jacob feared the worst. Splitting his camp into two was a plan to save at least part of what he had. Right after this, Jacob prayed to God.

When we feel fear, it is wise to do what we can to act with care, as Jacob did. But the most important thing is to bring that fear to God in prayer and to remember his promises, instead of trusting only in our own plans.
exp.11:12:
Abram asks Sarai to say that she is his sister. "Please say you are my sister, so that I will be treated well for your sake, and on account of you my life will be spared" means that Abram hopes to be treated well because of her, and that his life will be spared.

Abram speaks with his wife as they enter Egypt, where he had gone because of a famine. He fears that he will be killed so that the Egyptians can take her, because she is very beautiful. Later, Sarai is in fact Abram's half-sister through their father (Genesis 20:12), so it was not a complete lie, but it was a half-truth that put her in danger. The Bible does not approve of his plan here; it shows his fear and its consequences.

For today: when we feel afraid, it is easy to look for escapes that seem clever but put others at risk. Before acting, let us pray and trust that God protects, even when we cannot see how.
exp.32:11:
Esau tells Jacob to set out on the road, and says that he himself will go on ahead, as a guide and companion. "Let us be on our way" is an invitation to travel together. "I will go ahead of you" means that Esau will lead the way.

Esau and Jacob are speaking after years of hostility. Jacob had fled out of fear that Esau would kill him, but now they meet again in peace. Esau accepts the gift and offers to accompany him, which shows his good will. Jacob, however, answers with caution and prefers to go more slowly because of the children and the flocks. Interpreters do not agree on whether this was sincere prudence or a lack of full trust.

For today: when God opens the door to reconciliation, receive with gratitude the hand that is extended. And even when you seek peace, be wise and honest about your limits.
exp.46:1:
Joseph chose five of his brothers and brought them before Pharaoh. The phrase "from the last" is not in this verse, so it is left out here. The verse says he chose them, and it does not say they were the least important among the brothers.

The passage tells how Jacob and his family came to Egypt because of the famine. Joseph, who was already a ruler under Pharaoh, announced their arrival and presented some of his brothers. It is not known with certainty why there were five or why these particular ones were chosen; some think it was so as not to overwhelm the king, or that they were the most suitable to speak. The text does not explain this.

Today, Joseph teaches us to act with order and respect, caring for family while remaining prudent. If you have to help others in an important matter, do it with humility, prepare well, and trust that God can open doors.
exp.13:3:
This verse says that the kings of the cities of the valley, including those of Sodom and Gomorrah, had been subject to Chedorlaomer for twelve years. In the thirteenth year they broke away and rebelled. "Subject to" here means being under his rule, probably paying tribute, that is, a payment made to a more powerful king.

No one speaks in this passage; it is the narrator of Genesis who recounts the events. It explains why a war breaks out among the kings of the region. The rebellion of these cities provokes the military response of the fourteenth year. This account sets the scene in which Lot, Abram's nephew, is taken captive.

For today: the decisions of others can affect us, even when we do not make them ourselves. This invites us to think carefully about where we live and with whom we align ourselves, and to pray for wisdom. God cares for his people in the midst of conflicts he did not cause.
exp.3:3:
Abel also brought an offering to God: the best portions of the firstborn of his flock. The phrase "the best portions" in the Berean Standard Bible points to the choicest part of the animals he offered.

Here the narrator of Genesis is speaking. Cain and Abel, the sons of Adam and Eve, bring offerings to God. The text does not clearly explain why God looked with favor on Abel and his offering but not on Cain. Some think the attitude of the heart mattered; others, the quality of the offering. Hebrews 11:4 says that Abel offered "by faith."

God deserves the best of us, not the leftovers. Before giving time, money or service, ask yourself honestly: am I doing it with gratitude and trust in God, or only to fulfill an obligation?
exp.30:39:
Here Jacob describes how hard his work as a shepherd was. During the day the heat wore him out, and at night the bitter cold, the frost, struck him. Also, "sleep fled from my eyes" means that he could hardly sleep, because he had to look after the flock.

The speaker is Jacob, and he is addressing his father-in-law Laban. After twenty years of service, Laban pursued him and accused him. Jacob defends himself and reminds Laban of his faithfulness: he took good care of the sheep, took responsibility for the losses, and worked without rest. Then he says that God saw his effort.

For today: God sees the quiet, sacrificial work that no one recognizes. Do your work with integrity, even when it costs you or no one thanks you, and trust that God knows what you go through.
exp.8:23:
Noah woke up from his drunkenness and learned what his youngest son had done to him. The verse says "drunkenness," not "wine," so the explanation should refer to the drunkenness itself rather than to the wine's effects. The text does not say in detail what Ham did. Some think he only saw it and told about it, while others believe there may have been something more. This is not known for certain. It is also not certain who "his youngest son" is: it could be Ham or, in a broader sense, his descendant.

The narrator of Genesis tells what happened after the flood. Earlier, Ham saw his father uncovered and told his brothers, while Shem and Japheth covered him with respect. Now Noah reacts, and in the following verses he pronounces a curse on Canaan and a blessing on Shem.

Today we can learn to cover the weaknesses of others with respect, rather than exposing them or talking about them without need.
exp.20:10:
This verse says that Sarah's request caused Abraham great distress. "Matter" here refers to what she asked for, and "greatly distressed" means deeply painful and hard to bear. "Concerned his son Ishmael" refers to the boy Abraham loved as his own son.

Sarah saw that Ishmael, the son of Hagar, was mocking, and she asked that Hagar and her son be sent away from the house to protect the inheritance meant for Isaac. Abraham suffered because he had to be separated from a son of his own. Then God comforted him: Isaac would carry on the promise, and Ishmael too would become a nation, because he was a descendant of Abraham.

For today: when a difficult decision hurts us, we can bring it to God in prayer. He understands our pain, guides us with wisdom, and cares for those we love, even when we cannot see how.
exp.8:13:
This verse says that whenever God forms clouds over the earth, the rainbow will appear in them. "Whenever" means "every time," and "I form" means "I will cause to form." The rainbow is the sign God chose.

God speaks, after the flood, addressing Noah, his sons, and all living creatures. He promises that he will never again destroy the earth with water. The rainbow is the visible reminder of that covenant, and God says he will remember it. Some understand this as a human way of speaking about God's faithfulness.

For today: when cloudy times come into your life, remember that God keeps his promises. Pause, look calmly, and give thanks for his faithfulness.
exp.12:13:
God tells Abram to lift up his eyes and look out in every direction: north, south, east, and west.

Abram and his nephew Lot had just gone their separate ways. Lot chose the well-watered plain and began moving toward Sodom, a city of wicked people. Abram, for his part, had allowed Lot to choose first. Right after that parting, the Lord renews his promise: the land Abram sees will be given to him and his descendants. Some believe God meant to comfort him after the separation; the text does not state this exactly.

When we let something go for the sake of peace, we can trust that God takes care of us. If today you are the one who has to give way in a situation, pray and look ahead with faith: God can give you more than you imagine.
exp.4:13:
This verse sums up the life of Kenan: in total he lived 910 years, and then he died. It is the sum of the 70 years before he became the father of Mahalalel and the 840 years after. The phrase "became the father" means that he had a son; "then he died" closes his story, just as it does for the other names in this chapter.

Here it is not a character speaking: it is the narrator of Genesis, who presents a list of generations from Adam. This list shows how humanity continued and how God's promise was passed on from one generation to the next. About why these lifespans are so long, there are several interpretations, and the text does not explain it.

For today: our life also has an end, and that invites us to live with purpose. Kenan raised sons and daughters over many years. We can ask ourselves what we leave to those who come after us: faith, affection, and a good example.
exp.30:32:
Laban went through the tents of Jacob's camp, searching for the household gods. He first entered Jacob's tent, then Leah's, then the tents of the two maidservants (Bilhah and Zilpah), but he found nothing. When he left Leah's tent, he went into Rachel's tent. The words "but he found nothing" build suspense before the outcome of the search.

Laban had chased after Jacob once Jacob secretly left with his family. He accused him of stealing his gods. Jacob, not knowing that Rachel had taken them, declared that whoever had them should die. Without realizing it, he put at risk the person he loved most.

Today it reminds us that speaking without knowing the whole truth can bring serious consequences. Before accusing others or making strong promises, it is wise to know the facts well and to know our own family. It also invites us to let go of any "idol" hidden in the heart.
exp.12:2:
He traveled little by little, from place to place, from the Negev toward Bethel. He arrived at the very spot where he had pitched his tent before, between Bethel and Ai. Each stretch of the journey was a stage covered as the days passed.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is speaking. Abram had come from Egypt, where he had gone because of the famine, and there he made mistakes (Genesis 12). Now he returns to the place where he had built an altar and worshiped God. The text does not explain his feelings, but many understand this return as a fresh start with God.

For today: if you have drifted away or made mistakes, you can return step by step to the place where your relationship with God was simple and sincere. Take up prayer, the Word, and fellowship with other believers again. No great leap is needed; it is enough to take the next step back.
exp.21:12:
Abraham looked up and saw a ram caught by its horns in a thicket. He went, took the ram, and offered it as a burnt offering, a sacrifice presented to God, in place of his son. The phrase "behind him" means behind Abraham, that is, behind his back. A thicket is a tangle of bushes with thorns.

God had tested Abraham by asking him to offer Isaac. Just as he was about to do it, the angel of the Lord stopped him from heaven. Then Abraham saw the ram. The account shows that God himself provided the sacrifice. Afterward Abraham named that place "The Lord will provide." Many Christians see here a shadow of Christ, although the text does not say this directly.

For today: when you feel you see no way out, keep trusting and obeying God step by step. He knows your need and often shows his provision when you take the next step of faith.
exp.43:5:
The explanation says that Joseph's steward caught up with the brothers as they were leaving the city and passed on to them the words that Joseph had ordered him to say. "Overtook" means that he reached them and came up to them. "Relayed these words to them" means that he told them what he had been instructed to say.

Here the narrator tells how Joseph's order is carried out. He had placed his silver cup in Benjamin's sack, and now he sends his steward to accuse them of theft. Many understand that Joseph wanted to test whether his brothers had changed, and whether they would abandon Benjamin as they had once abandoned him. The Bible does not explain this in detail, so it is an interpretation.

For today: when someone accuses us, even unjustly, it is wise to listen calmly before we respond. God can also use difficult situations to bring to light what is in the heart and to lead us to a sincere change.
exp.3:7:
This verse tells us that Cain said to his brother Abel, "Let us go out to the field," and that while the two of them were in the field, Cain rose up against his brother and killed him. The simple words carry a heavy weight: a quiet invitation became the first murder the Bible records.

God had just warned Cain, who was angry because his offering had not been accepted. He told him that sin was crouching at the door, like a force ready to seize him, but that he could master it. Cain heard the warning and gave in anyway.

For today: when you feel anger or envy, do not ignore it. God warns us in time. Speak with Him, seek peace with the other person, and do not let that anger grow until it becomes harm.
exp.40:14:
Pharaoh tells Joseph that he has had a dream and that no one has been able to explain it. He also tells him that he has heard Joseph can interpret dreams when he hears them.

The phrase "when you hear a dream you can interpret it" means that Joseph is able to explain a dream as soon as he hears it. The word "But" at the start of the second sentence sets up the contrast between the failure of others and the reputation Joseph has.

Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, is troubled because his wise men gave him no answer. Joseph has just come out of prison; he has been shaved and given clean clothes so that he can appear before the king. The cupbearer, who had been imprisoned with Joseph, told Pharaoh about his gift. Joseph answers at once, however, that the interpretation does not come from him but from God.

For today: when others recognize a gift or talent in you, learn from Joseph. Serve with willingness, but give the credit to God and not to yourself. Humility reminds us that everything good we can offer comes from Him.
exp.4:8:
This verse says that Enosh was ninety years old when he became the father of Kenan. In plain terms, Enosh had a son named Kenan when he was ninety.

The verse is part of the list of Adam's descendants in Genesis 5. No one is speaking in it; the narrator simply records one generation after another. This list shows how humanity continued after Adam, passing from fathers to sons. The very long ages are understood in several ways: some take them literally, and others see them as a way of speaking in that time. We do not know for certain which explanation is right.

For today: God notices every life, even those that seem like just a name on a list. Your faith can be the thread that connects your family to the next generation. Teach your children, and those around you, to know God through your daily example.
exp.25:14:
This verse tells us that the Philistines took dirt and stopped up all the wells that Abraham's servants had dug years before. They blocked each one with earth so that it could no longer be used. In that dry land, water meant life for people and for animals.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Isaac is living in Gerar, and God has blessed him greatly. The Philistines envy him, and for this reason they destroy what his father had left behind. Shortly afterward, Abimelech asks him to leave. Some think they stopped up the wells to harm him or to drive him out of the region. The text does not state this clearly.

For today: sometimes others can damage the good things we receive, out of envy or selfishness. We should not respond with violence. Isaac remained at peace and kept trusting in God.
exp.31:29:
Jacob gives the name Peniel to that place, which means "face of God." He says, "Indeed, I have seen God face to face, and yet my life was spared." Jacob reports that he has seen God directly and has come through the encounter alive.

Here Jacob speaks after wrestling all night with a mysterious man, whom the text presents as God himself. Jacob was about to meet his brother Esau, whom he had cheated years earlier, and he was afraid. There he received the name Israel and a blessing. Some think it was an angel; others think it was God in human form.

For today: when you are distressed, do not run away from God. Draw near to Him with sincerity, even if you come away with wounds, because there He can give you a new identity, blessing, and peace.
exp.2:23:
God drove the man out of the garden of Eden. Then he stationed cherubim, which are heavenly beings, on the east side of the garden, along with a whirling sword of flame that guarded the way to the tree of life. Its purpose was to block the path to that tree.

The narrator of the account tells what happened after Adam and Eve disobeyed. God had already said that it was not fitting for the man to eat from the tree of life in that state of sin. Scholars explain the meaning of the cherubim and the sword in several ways, but all agree that they show that access was closed off.

For today: sin brings real consequences, yet even in sending them out, God acted with care and did not abandon them. We can approach God with honesty, trusting that he continues to open paths of restoration.
exp.18:31:
Here the elder daughter of Lot proposes to her sister that they get their father drunk with wine so they can sleep with him and preserve his line.

The elder daughter speaks. After the destruction of Sodom, she and her sister live with Lot in a cave, isolated and afraid. They think there are no men left and fear that their family will disappear. The Bible recounts the event without approving of it; it is a deceitful and sinful plan, born of desperation and of a mindset shaped by Sodom.

For today: when we feel fear or scarcity, it is easy to justify crooked decisions with "good reasons." Before acting, let us stop to pray and trust God, who can care for us without our having to do what is wrong.
exp.30:2:
God tells Jacob to go back to the land of his fathers and to his family. He promises him: "I will be with you." The phrase "go back" points to returning home, and "family" refers to his relatives.

Here the Lord speaks. Jacob has spent years working for his uncle Laban, and now the atmosphere has become tense. Laban's sons accuse him, and Laban no longer looks at him kindly. God gives him clear direction in the middle of that pressure. Jacob later shares this with Rachel and Leah.

For today: when a situation becomes uncomfortable or difficult, do not act only out of fear or impulse. Ask God for direction and trust his promise to be with you. He can guide you step by step, and his presence is worth more than any safe place.
exp.7:1:
This verse tells how God stopped the flood. The springs of the deep are the waters that had burst up from beneath the earth, and the floodgates of the heavens are the openings from which the rain fell. Both were closed. "Were restrained" means that the rain stopped.

Here no character is speaking; it is the narrator of Genesis. The verse before says that God remembered Noah. That does not mean he had forgotten him, but that he acted on Noah's behalf, in keeping with his promise. In this way the water begins to go down, and the close of the judgment is set in motion.

For today: even when a trial seems endless, God knows when to set a limit to it. Trust that he remembers you and cares for you, and wait for his timing with patience.
exp.45:31:
This verse says that Joseph's relatives are shepherds, because they raise livestock. It also tells us they have brought their flocks and herds and all that they own to Egypt. The phrase "raise livestock" refers to their work of caring for animals.

Joseph speaks to his brothers and to his father's household before presenting them to Pharaoh. He explains what they should say about their occupation. According to the text that follows, he wanted them to live in the land of Goshen, because the Egyptians looked down on shepherds. The text does not explain why the Egyptians felt that way, so it is best not to invent reasons.

Today we can learn to be honest and straightforward about who we are and what we do, without being ashamed of our work. We can also ask God for wisdom to act with prudence in settings where what we do is not always valued.
exp.41:7:
Joseph recognized his brothers right away, but they did not recognize him. Here the verse is describing what each side knew in that moment. Although the brothers were standing in front of him, they had no idea that this Egyptian ruler was the brother they had sold.

This is part of the account in which a famine brought Joseph's brothers to Egypt to buy grain. Joseph was already a powerful official by then. About twenty years had passed, and he looked like an Egyptian, spoke through an interpreter, and dressed like a high official. That is why they did not recognize him. The text does not tell us everything Joseph was thinking; it only shows that he recognized them and remembered his dreams.

For today: sometimes God works in our lives without our noticing it, and only later do we understand what He was doing. We can trust that He continues to care for the story, even when we cannot yet see the whole picture.
exp.42:26:
Here Joseph, who has not yet made himself known to his brothers, greets them and asks if they are well. Right away he asks about his father: how is the elderly man you told me about, and is he still alive? The question "is he well" means "is he well in health and in spirit?"

Joseph speaks as governor in Egypt. His brothers have returned with Benjamin and with a gift, and they treat him with respect without knowing who he is. His question concerns Jacob, his own father. Some think Joseph shows sincere affection, even though he hides his identity; the text does not explain everything he was feeling.

For today: power and success should not dull interest in family. Asking sincerely about someone, especially the elderly, is a simple way of showing love. Today you could call an older relative and listen patiently.
exp.25:24:
Isaac built an altar in Beersheba and there prayed to God, calling on him by name. Then he pitched his tent, which means he decided to settle down and live in that place. His servants began to dig a well. "Calling on the name of the LORD" means praying and worshiping God. "Seed" refers to his descendants.

The narrator tells what Isaac did after God appeared to him that same night. God had told him not to be afraid, that he was with him, and that he would bless him for the promise made to Abraham. Isaac was coming out of a time of conflict over wells and of being rejected in Gerar. A well was vital for life in that dry region.

When God gives us reassurance, the first response is to worship him. Before taking care of his needs, Isaac set himself to pray. If you are in a new or difficult place, begin by seeking God and then work with confidence.
exp.16:6:
God tells Abraham that he will make a covenant with him and with his descendants, generation after generation. It is an "everlasting" covenant, meaning it has no end. The central promise is that God will be Abraham's God and the God of his descendants after him.

God Himself is speaking, when Abram is ninety-nine years old. He has just been given the new name Abraham, "father of many." God promises him children, nations, and land, even though he does not yet have the promised son. The covenant does not depend on Abraham's own strength, but on God's faithfulness.

For today: if God promises to be your God, you can rest in the fact that He keeps what He says, even when you do not yet see results. Trust Him today, and pass that trust on to your children or to those who come after you.
exp.20:28:
Abimelech asks Abraham why he has set apart these seven ewe lambs from the flock. Ewe lambs are young female sheep, and the question shows that Abimelech does not understand the gesture, so he asks for an explanation.

Abimelech, king of Gerar, is speaking. He and Abraham have just made a covenant, and earlier Abraham had a dispute with the king's servants over a well. By setting apart the seven ewe lambs, Abraham prepares a visible sign. He then explains that, by accepting them, Abimelech would acknowledge that Abraham dug that well. This is where the name Beersheba comes from, which is commonly understood to mean "well of the oath" or "well of the seven."

For today: when there is a misunderstanding, it is better to clear things up honestly and peacefully, leaving agreements clear, rather than letting tension grow from assumptions.
exp.20:6:
Sarah says in amazement: "Who would have told Abraham that Sarah would nurse children?" She adds that she has now borne him a son in his old age. To nurse means to feed a baby at the breast, and to bear means to give birth. Although she says "children," she means that she is now able to nurse a baby herself.

Sarah speaks here. She had waited for years and had laughed in doubt when God promised a son (Genesis 18:12). Now Isaac has been born, whose name is connected with laughter, and she rejoices. Her joy comes from seeing that God has fulfilled what seemed impossible. Abraham was a hundred years old.

For today: If you are waiting for something that seems impossible, do not lose hope. God can fulfill his promise in his own time, and when he does, remember to give thanks and tell others, as Sarah did.
exp.43:21:
Here Judah repeats what the brothers had told the governor of Egypt. "The boy" refers to Benjamin, the youngest. Judah explains that the boy cannot leave his father, because if he were to leave, his father, who is old, would die of grief.

Judah speaks before Joseph, whom he does not yet recognize. Joseph asked that Benjamin be brought to him and is holding him on a charge of theft. Judah intercedes with a moving speech to keep his father from suffering another loss. He himself had taken part in selling Joseph; now he offers to remain as a slave in Benjamin's place.

For today: when there is conflict, let us think about the pain of others and not only our own. Judah teaches us to take responsibility and to care for those who depend on us, even at personal cost.
exp.41:15:
Here Joseph, speaking as the ruler of Egypt, sets a test for his brothers. One of them must go and bring back your brother, while the rest of you stay confined. In this way it will be shown whether your words are true. "As surely as Pharaoh lives" was an oath sworn by the king. If you fail the test, he declares that you are spies.

Joseph is second in rank after Pharaoh. His brothers do not recognize him; they had sold him years earlier. He accuses them of being spies and demands to see Benjamin. The Bible does not explain his full purpose here. Many think he wanted to know whether they had changed and whether his father and Benjamin were well.

For today: truth is shown by deeds, not only by words. If you have failed someone, do not wait until you are pressed; acknowledge your wrong honestly and seek to make right what you can.
exp.30:42:
Laban tells Jacob that everything he sees belongs to him: the daughters, the sons, and the flocks. Then he asks what he could do today to his own daughters and to the children they have borne.

Laban, Jacob's father-in-law, speaks after he has pursued him and caught up with him. Jacob had just reproached him for twenty years of work and changed wages. Laban admits no guilt and keeps speaking as if he owns everything. Yet he recognizes that he cannot harm his family, and for that reason he proposes making a covenant. Probably God, who spoke to him the night before, influenced this change (Gen 31:24).

For today: when we believe we have a right over everything, we tend to harden ourselves. Acknowledging limits and seeking peace, rather than imposing ourselves, protects the family and honors God.
exp.20:3:
This verse tells us that when Isaac was eight days old, Abraham circumcised him. He did it because God had commanded him. "Circumcise" means to cut away the skin that covers the tip of the male organ. The phrase "when his son Isaac was eight days old" tells us the child's exact age at the time.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not a character in the story. He reports that God kept his promise by giving Abraham and Sarah a son in their old age. In Genesis 17 God had established circumcision as the sign of his covenant with Abraham and his descendants, and in that passage he also indicated that it should be done on the eighth day. Abraham simply obeys what God had already told him.

For today: God kept his promise, and Abraham responded with simple and punctual obedience. When God shows you something clearly in his Word, do not put it off for later. Obeying with joy is a beautiful way to thank him for what he has done in your life.
exp.43:2:
At daybreak, Joseph let his brothers set out for home, with their donkeys loaded with the grain. The phrase "sent on their way" means they were allowed to go; they were sent back home. The donkeys were the pack animals they used for the journey.

The narrator tells this moment in the middle of the test Joseph is preparing for his brothers. Without their knowledge, his silver and the silver cup are hidden in the sacks. Everything seems to be going well, but it is the calm before they are overtaken. Scholars understand Joseph's purpose in different ways: many think he wanted to know whether his brothers had changed.

For today: sometimes life seems calm just before a trial. We can trust that God is at work even when we do not see the whole picture, and live with integrity, since character is revealed when trial comes.
exp.34:24:
This verse names the two sons that Jacob had with Bilhah, Rachel's maidservant: Dan and Naphtali. A "maidservant" is a female servant who works in the household. With this detail, part of the list of Jacob's twelve sons is completed.

The narrator is the author of Genesis, who gives a family summary right after Rachel's death and the birth of Benjamin. According to the earlier account, Rachel gave Bilhah to Jacob so that he could have children through her, which was a common practice in that time. Here the list closes one stage: the children born in Padan-aram, and Jacob's return to his father Isaac.

For today: God works through imperfect and complicated families to carry out his plans. If your family story carries wounds or mistakes, do not think that God cannot work in it. Entrust your home to him with confidence.
exp.35:22:
This verse lists the five sons of Shobal: Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho, and Onam. Shobal was one of the sons of Seir the Horite.

The narrator of the book, traditionally identified with Moses, records here the families of the Horites, the people who lived in the region of Edom before the descendants of Esau settled there. This list appears within the genealogy of Esau. Scholars do not fully agree on how the two peoples came to mix, and the text does not explain this in detail.

For today: the Bible names people that almost no one remembers, and this shows us that God knows each one by name. Today you can treat with respect the "unimportant" people around you and pray for them by name.
exp.24:13:
This verse continues the list of the sons of Ishmael: Mishma, Dumah, and Massa. They are only names, but each one was a real person within a family.

The narrator of Genesis closes the story of Ishmael here, the son of Abraham and Hagar, the Egyptian servant of Sarah. At the end of the list, twelve princes are mentioned, which recalls God's promise to Abraham to bless Ishmael too and make him into a great nation. About the exact origin of these peoples, scholars know little, and they do not all agree.

For today: God remembers each person by name, even when the world does not take them into account. Today you can thank him for knowing you personally, and also treat with courage and respect those who seem "minor" around you.
exp.43:26:
In this verse, Judah repeats what Jacob, their father, told them. Jacob reminds them that his wife Rachel bore him only two sons: Joseph and Benjamin.

Judah speaks before Joseph, whom he does not yet recognize as his brother, and who is governor of Egypt. He wants to persuade him to let Benjamin go free. To do so, he explains how much their father would suffer if he lost this son, since he already believes Joseph is dead. Rachel was Jacob's most beloved wife, and for that reason their two sons were very dear to him.

For today: when we ask something on behalf of others, let us speak with humility and empathy, showing the pain a decision may cause. Thinking about the hearts of others helps us act with compassion and seek the good of the family.
exp.38:18:
This verse tells how Potiphar, Joseph's master, reacted when his wife told him her story: "This is what your slave did to me." When he heard it, he burned with anger, meaning he was filled with rage. The phrase "the story his wife told him" reminds us that he reacted to what he was told, not to what he himself saw.

Joseph was a slave in the house of Potiphar, an Egyptian official. Potiphar's wife had pursued Joseph and, when she was rejected, falsely accused him to protect herself and take revenge. Potiphar heard only one version of events. We do not know for certain whom his anger was directed at; some think it fell on Joseph, and others suggest he may have doubted the story, since the usual penalty for that offense was more severe than prison.

For today: before we grow angry or judge someone, let us take time to hear all the sides. And when we suffer an injustice, let us remember that God remains present, as He was with Joseph.
exp.15:8:
Here the angel of the LORD tells Hagar to return to her mistress, Sarai, and to submit to her authority. The phrase "submit to her authority" is the reader's wording, and it means accepting Sarai's authority over her. The earlier comment about old verb forms does not apply to this verse, so it has been left out.

Hagar, the Egyptian servant of Sarai, had fled into the wilderness because Sarai was treating her harshly. The angel finds her beside a spring and speaks to her with care. Some understand this "angel of the LORD" as speaking on God's behalf, and others see in him a divine presence. His command comes with promises: God will see her affliction and will bless her son.

For today: this text does not justify mistreatment or call us to endure abuse. It shows us that God sees the one who suffers and gives direction and hope. When running away does not solve anything, we can trust that God is with us as we face the situation with help and wisdom.
exp.25:32:
Here the text says that Isaac named the well his servants had just dug "Shibah." That is why the city is called Beersheba to this day, meaning up to the time the account was written. "Named it" means "called it." "Shibah" sounds like the Hebrew word for "oath" and also like the word for "seven," so the name recalls the covenant. "Beer" means "well."

The narrator tells that Isaac made peace with Abimelech, king of Gerar, after tensions over the wells. They made an oath and parted in peace. That same day the news of the water arrived. Something similar happened with Abraham in that place, and the texts tell it differently, but the name remained tied to the oath.

For today: when you seek peace with others, even after conflict, God can give you rest and provision. Name his blessings and remember them with gratitude.
exp.31:11:
Jacob reminds God of what He promised him: that He would make him prosper and that his offspring would be as numerous as the sand of the sea, too many to count. The word "offspring" means descendants, that is, children, grandchildren and all the generations to come.

The one speaking is Jacob, who is returning to his land after many years away. He learns that Esau, his brother, is coming to meet him, and he feels great fear because years earlier he had deceived him. So he prays, acknowledges that he is small, and relies on God's promise, not on his own merits.

For today: when you feel afraid, pray honestly and remind God of His promises, as Jacob did. Then do what is in your hands, as he did when he prepared a gift for his brother. Trusting God does not remove the responsibility to act wisely.
exp.26:4:
This verse tells us that Rebekah was listening when Isaac spoke to his son Esau. After hearing her husband's request, Esau went out into the field to hunt game and bring it back to his father.

Isaac, now old, wanted to bless Esau, his firstborn son, before he died. Rebekah listened to the conversation and, as the account that follows shows, decided to act so that Jacob would receive that blessing. The Bible does not justify everything the characters do; it simply tells what happened, and some readers see here a family divided by favoritism.

Today we can learn to be careful about what we hear and what we do with it. Before acting, it is good to pray and ask God for direction, rather than taking control with our own means.
exp.33:10:
Shechem spoke to Dinah's father and her brothers. He asks them to show him favor and promises to give whatever they ask. The payment of a bride-price and gifts was what a man offered when he wanted to marry a woman.

Shechem had just wronged Dinah, Jacob's daughter. Now, together with his father Hamor, he tries to set things right through marriage and a family agreement. He seems willing to pay whatever is asked, but what he did cannot be undone with money. Jacob's sons answer with deceit, and the story ends in violence. The Bible shows deep pain here without approving everything the characters do.

For today: when we have hurt someone, it is not enough to offer gifts or kind words. We need to acknowledge the harm, ask forgiveness humbly, and seek justice. And if we have been hurt, let us ask God for wisdom so that we do not respond with revenge.
exp.40:17:
Genesis 41:18 says that in Pharaoh's dream, seven cows came up out of the river Nile. They were well fed and sleek, and they came up to graze among the reeds by the water. Their appearance is what the verse emphasizes: they looked healthy and attractive.

Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, is the one speaking. He is telling his dream to Joseph, who had been brought out of prison to interpret it. Earlier, Joseph made clear that he could not interpret dreams by his own power, but that God would give the answer. No Egyptian wise man had been able to explain the dream, and Pharaoh was troubled.

For today: Joseph did not take the credit for himself, even though he stood before the most powerful man of his time. When someone asks you for advice or recognizes your talent, learn to say with humility that every gift comes from God, and to seek his direction first.
exp.45:23:
This verse names the four sons of Naphtali, one of Jacob's sons: Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer, and Shillem. Naphtali was a son of Bilhah, Rachel's servant.

The narrator of Genesis gives a list of Jacob's family who go down to Egypt during the time of the famine. The verses that follow say that Bilhah's descendants add up to seven. This list shows how the people who would later become Israel grew. The total of sixty-six is counted in different ways, and scholars explain it in several ways.

God cares for people one by one, even those who seem less important in the story. Today you can remember that your name and your family's name are precious to Him. Thank Him for your family and pray for each person close to you.
exp.30:21:
On the third day, someone informed Laban that Jacob had escaped. The words "was informed" mean "was told," and "had escaped" means "had gotten away." Jacob left without telling anyone, and Laban found out three days later.

Here the narrator is describing what happened, not quoting anyone speaking. Jacob had worked for years for Laban, his father-in-law, and the relationship had become strained. Jacob left secretly with his family and his possessions. When the news reached Laban, he set out to chase him down with his relatives. As we see in what follows, God stepped in and warned Laban in a dream not to treat Jacob harshly.

For today: when there is a conflict, running away or hiding things rarely resolves it, since what is hidden tends to come to light. It is better to speak honestly and respectfully, and to trust that God cares for those who seek him, even in difficult situations.
exp.33:2:
This verse says that Shechem felt a strong attachment to Dinah. "His soul was drawn to Dinah" means that his heart was bound to her. "He loved the young girl" means that he grew fond of her. "Spoke to her tenderly" means that he spoke to her gently, trying to comfort her and win her affection.

It is part of the story, told by the narrator. Before this, Shechem had taken Dinah by force and dishonored her. That is why these tender words appear right after a serious abuse. The Bible does not present them as a justification; some interpreters see here a selfish or possessive love, and others see only a description of his feelings.

Today it reminds us that pleasant feelings do not erase the harm done. If we have hurt someone, kind words are not enough: we need to acknowledge the wrong, ask for forgiveness, and act with respect.
exp.47:11:
Joseph removed his two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, from their grandfather Jacob's knees, also called Israel. Then he bowed facedown. The boys had been sitting on the old man's lap, and Joseph's bowing was a sign of respect and gratitude.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Jacob, nearly blind with age, had just embraced and kissed his grandsons. He was about to bless them. Joseph moved them away out of respect, recognizing that what was coming was a solemn moment. Jacob had said that he never expected to see Joseph again, and now God had allowed him to see even his grandchildren.

For today: when God gives you more than you expected, respond with humility and gratitude. Bowing down, praying, and giving thanks is a good way to acknowledge his goodness.
exp.43:0:
Here Joseph gives an order to the man in charge of his household, the steward. He was to fill his brothers' sacks with food, "as much as they can carry," that is, as much as they were able to bear. He was also to put each man's silver back in the mouth of his sack, that is, in the opening at the top.

Joseph speaks here as governor of Egypt. His brothers had come a second time to buy grain, and he had not yet told them who he was. The verse that follows shows that he was preparing a test: he put his silver cup in the sack of the youngest. The Bible does not explain this here, but many think he wanted to know whether they had changed and whether they would protect Benjamin.

For today: Joseph's generosity invites us to bless others even when they have been unfair to us. And when the truth is tested in difficult moments, it is good to ask God for a sincere and faithful heart.
exp.25:16:
Isaac left that place and set up his camp in the Valley of Gerar and settled there. "Encamped" means he pitched his camp, since he lived as a nomad, moving with his household and living in tents. "Settled there" means he made his home in that place for a time.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is speaking. Abimelech, king of the Philistines, had asked Isaac to leave, because Isaac had become very powerful and they felt fear or envy. Moreover, the Philistines had filled with earth the wells that Abraham, Isaac's father, had dug. Isaac does not fight; he simply withdraws.

For today: when someone rejects you or closes doors on you, you do not have to answer with a quarrel. You can step away calmly, trust that God takes care of you, and continue on, seeking the good that He has prepared.
exp.42:28:
He looks up and sees Benjamin, his own mother's son. He asks his brothers whether this is the youngest brother they told him about. Then he says to Benjamin, "May God be gracious to you, my son." The phrase "be gracious" here works like a loving blessing: may God care for you and show you favor.

Joseph is the one speaking. He is a ruler in Egypt, but his brothers do not yet know that he is the same man they sold years earlier. Benjamin is the only one who did not take part in that betrayal. Joseph sees him after a long time, and that is why the next verse says he was so moved that he went out to weep in private.

For today: when you feel strong emotions, such as gratitude or affection, do not hold them back out of pride. You can express them with a blessing or a prayer for the person you love, as Joseph did.
exp.2:15:
He says that God speaks to the woman after the fall. He announces that the pains of pregnancy and childbirth will increase. He also says that her desire will be for her husband, and that he will rule over her, meaning he will have authority over her. Scholars debate what that "desire" means: some see it as longing or dependence, others as a desire to control.

The LORD God speaks just after Adam and Eve ate the forbidden fruit. These words describe the consequences of sin, not an ideal that God intended from creation. Earlier, God spoke to the serpent, and afterward he will speak to the man.

For today: this verse describes a broken world, not a command to dominate others. We can seek relationships of respect and mutual service, asking God to heal pride and selfishness in our homes.
exp.44:16:
Here the pharaoh speaks to Joseph and asks him to pass an order on to his brothers. He tells them to load their animals, and the word "animals" here refers to donkeys or beasts used to carry things, and to return to the land of Canaan.

Joseph had just made himself known to his brothers and had been reconciled with them, with tears. The news reached the palace, and the pharaoh and his servants rejoiced. The pharaoh, grateful for what Joseph had done for Egypt, wants to bless his family. For that reason he sends them to bring Jacob, their father, to live there.

For today: when God restores a broken relationship, joy should move us to act. If there is reconciliation in your family, take concrete steps to care for and gather your loved ones.
exp.47:0:
Someone told Joseph that his father Jacob was ill. Then Joseph took his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, and went to see him. The words "some time later" only show that a while had passed since the events before this verse. "Ill" suggests that Jacob was already very weak because of his age.

The narrator is Moses, according to tradition. The scene takes place in Egypt, near the end of Jacob's life. Joseph, who was a ruler, sets aside his duties to visit his father. Bringing his sons is no accident: the account that follows shows that Jacob will bless them. The text does not say who gave the warning.

For today: when someone dear to you is weak or ill, make time to visit them, even if you are very busy. And if you can, bring the younger ones with you, so that they may receive their blessing and their words of faith.
exp.2:13:
The Lord God speaks to the serpent and tells it that it will be cursed above all the animals. "Livestock" and "every beast of the field" refer to both tame animals and wild ones. Going "on your belly" means crawling, and eating dust is an image of humiliation and defeat. The word "because" points to the cause of the curse: "Because you have done this."

The Lord God speaks after the man and the woman have eaten the forbidden fruit. First He questioned them, and now He pronounces judgment on the serpent, which had deceived the woman. Many understand that the serpent was an instrument of God's enemy, although the text does not say this in those words. Christians often see in the following verse a first promise of victory.

For today: evil does not have the last word. Even in the midst of the consequences of sin, God acts with justice and leaves hope open. We can trust that He takes care of us.
exp.35:10:
This verse gives the names of five sons of Eliphaz, who was the firstborn son of Esau: Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam, and Kenaz.

No one speaks in this passage. The narrator of Genesis carefully records the family of Esau, also called Edom, who lived in the mountain region of Seir. These lists show that God kept his promise that Esau too would have a great line of descendants. Some of these names, such as Teman, appear later in the Bible as places or clans of Edom. Scholars do not always agree on every detail of those connections.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those whom the story hardly mentions. Remember this when you feel overlooked, and value the "unnamed" people around you as well.
exp.4:7:
This verse sums up the life of Seth: he lived a total of 912 years, and then he died. "Seth" is Set, the son of Adam and Eve. The words "and then he died" are repeated throughout this list in Genesis 5.

Here no character is speaking; the narrator of the book presents a genealogy, that is, a list of generations from Adam. It shows how humanity continued after Cain and Abel, and how the line advanced that would lead to Noah. The very large numbers are understood in different ways: some take them literally and others as a form of expression typical of that time. There is no complete certainty.

For today: the repetition of "and then he died" reminds us that life is brief and precious. We can ask ourselves what we will leave to those who come after us: faith, example, and love for God.
exp.40:33:
Here Joseph advises Pharaoh to appoint commissioners over the land. The phrase "take a fifth of the harvest" means to set aside one-fifth, that is, twenty percent of the crops. The words "seven years of abundance" refer to the years of plenty. The idea is to store a portion during the seven good years.

Joseph is speaking before Pharaoh, after interpreting his dreams of the cows and the heads of grain. He had already explained that seven years of plenty would come, followed by seven years of famine. Now he not only interprets the dream but proposes a practical plan to protect the people. He says that God is hastening to bring it about.

For today: when things are going well, it is wise to prepare for difficult times. We can save a little, order our spending, and be generous, trusting in God while acting with prudence.
exp.12:8:
Abram tells Lot that the whole land is open to them. He asks that they go separate ways and lets Lot choose first: if Lot goes to the left, Abram will go to the right, and if Lot goes to the right, Abram will go to the left. "Please" is the heart of his request, a gentle appeal rather than a command. "Separate yourself" means part ways.

Abram, the older uncle, is the one speaking. The herdsmen of both men were quarreling over pasture and water, and the land was already home to Canaanites and Perizzites, so the conflict looked dangerous as well as unpleasant. Abram had the right to choose first, yet he gave the better choice to Lot to keep peace within the family. Afterward Lot chose the plain of the Jordan, which looked fertile.

For today: when a conflict arises with someone close to you, seek peace before your own advantage. Yielding with humility, without resentment, can protect valuable relationships and trust that God takes care of you.
exp.2:10:
God asks Adam two questions: who told him that he was naked, and whether he has eaten from the tree he was forbidden to eat from. The questions are not asked because God lacks knowledge, but to lead Adam to admit what he has done.

The LORD God speaks after Adam and Eve have eaten the fruit and hidden themselves. Adam had said that he was afraid because he was naked. God, like a father seeking the truth, moves from "Where are you?" to asking about the cause. Right away Adam blames the woman, and she blames the serpent.

For today: when we fail, God does not ask us for excuses, but for honesty. We can stop hiding, tell the truth about what we did, and draw near to Him to ask for forgiveness and help.
exp.10:8:
This verse explains why the city was called Babel. There the LORD confused the language of the whole world, so that people could no longer understand one another. From that place the LORD scattered them over the face of all the earth.

The narrator closes the story of the tower. The people wanted to build a city and a tower to make a name for themselves and to keep from being scattered (Genesis 11:4). God stepped in and stopped that project. Some see here a judgment against human pride; others emphasize that God was directing humanity to fill the earth. Many see both. The name "Babel" is often connected with the Hebrew verb meaning "to confuse," although the name is also linked with "Babylon."

For today: do not seek to make your name great without taking God into account. Place your plans in his hands and work with humility, seeking the unity that is built under his guidance.
exp.4:11:
The verse says that Kenan was 70 years old and then became the father of Mahalalel. The phrase "became the father of" is the plain modern way of saying he had his son Mahalalel. In this list, the word "father" can mean a direct son or, according to some scholars, a more distant descendant, but the text does not make this clear.

Here no character speaks; it is the narrator of Genesis, who presents the family line from Seth to Noah. Each name shows that life continued from generation to generation, and that God's promise kept its course. Then come Kenan's remaining years and his death, as a repeated pattern.

For today: God notices lives that seem like "just a name on a list." Your daily faithfulness, even if it is simple, matters. Live today so that your family and those who follow you see your trust in God.
exp.20:29:
Abraham tells Abimelech that he is to accept the seven ewe lambs from Abraham's hand. The gift would be proof that Abraham was the one who dug the well. A "witness" here means proof or a lasting confirmation, and "ewe lambs" are young female sheep.

Abraham is speaking after he has complained to Abimelech about a well that Abimelech's servants had taken by force. Abimelech, a Philistine king, wanted a covenant of peace with him. By accepting the lambs, Abimelech publicly acknowledged that the well belonged to Abraham. That is why the place was called Beersheba, which can be understood as "well of the oath" or "well of the seven," and the text mentions both ideas.

For today: clear arrangements prevent future disputes. If there is a disagreement, try to resolve it honestly, openly and peacefully, leaving agreements that both sides recognize.
exp.10:10:
This verse says that Shem lived five hundred years after he became the father of his son Arphaxad (today this name is often spelled Arfaxad). During those years he had other sons and daughters.

It is part of Shem's family history, which continues after the tower of Babel. The passage is not a speech but a recorded account that connects the flood with Abraham. It shows that, although God scattered the peoples, the story of his promise continued through one particular family. The very long lifespans are understood in several ways, and the text does not explain them.

For today: God works in ordinary lives, even in those that appear only as a single line in the Bible. Your daily faithfulness, your family, and your influence on those who come after you also matter to God, even when no one notices them.
exp.2:18:
God tells Adam that he will have to work hard, with sweat and weariness, to get his food, and this will continue until the day he dies. "You will eat your bread" means earning your food by the sweat of your brow. "Until you return to the ground" means that you will die, and "taken out of it" means that you were taken from the ground. The body came from the dust, and to the dust it will return.

God speaks to Adam after he and Eve have eaten from the forbidden tree. This is part of the consequences of that disobedience: the ground will no longer yield its fruit easily, and death enters human experience. Even so, the passage that follows shows care: God clothes them with garments of skin. Many see here a promise of hope, though the text does not explain it.

For today: accept your work and your limits with humility. Do your labor with honesty, without believing that everything depends on you, and remember that your life is a gift from God, who continues to care for you.
exp.28:25:
Laban tells Jacob that it is not the custom in his country to marry off the younger daughter before the older one. With this he explains why he gave Leah and not Rachel. The phrase "to give ... before" refers to giving someone in marriage ahead of another.

Laban speaks here, the uncle of Jacob. Jacob had worked seven years to marry Rachel, but in the morning he found himself beside Leah, the older sister. Earlier, Jacob had deceived his father and his brother, and now he is the one deceived. Some think the custom Laban mentions was real; others believe it was a late excuse, since he did not mention it at the start. The Bible does not make this clear.

For today: honesty matters. Laban could have spoken plainly from the beginning. Let us strive to tell the truth in good time and keep what we have promised, without hiding important conditions. In this way we protect trust and avoid deep wounds in the family.
exp.33:20:
Hamor and Siquem tell the men of their city that Jacob's sons are at peace with them. They can live and trade in the land, since there is room enough for everyone. Their proposal is that the two peoples marry each other, with each side giving its daughters to the other.

Hamor and his son Siquem speak at the city gate, which was the place where public decisions were made. Siquem had dishonored Dina, and now he wants to marry her. Hamor presents the arrangement as a benefit for everyone, but the Bible shows that self-interest is also present: later in the chapter they mention gaining possession of Jacob's goods.

For today: when someone presents a proposal as good for everyone, it is wise to ask what their real motive is. Pleasant words do not always reveal a fair heart.
exp.33:28:
This verse says that Jacob's sons carried off all the possessions of the city of Shechem. They also took the women and children, and plundered everything in the houses. In the wording the reader sees, "possessions" means goods and property, and "plundered" means stripped by force.

The one who tells this is the narrator of the book. Earlier, Shechem had dishonored Dinah, their sister. Simeon and Levi killed the men by deception, and then the other brothers plundered the city. Afterward, Jacob rebukes them, because their violence put the whole family in danger. The text recounts what happened, but it does not approve of it.

For today: even though injustice hurts us deeply, revenge almost always creates more harm and reaches innocent people. We can ask God for self-control, seek justice honestly, and let Him guide us before we react in anger.
exp.46:28:
Jacob, also called Israel, senses that his death is drawing near. He calls his son Joseph and asks him to make a very serious promise: to place his hand under his thigh, an ancient gesture of solemn oath. He asks Joseph to show him kindness and faithfulness, and not to bury him in Egypt.

Jacob speaks as an old man, after living seventeen years in Egypt. God had promised his family the land of Canaan, and there Abraham and Isaac were buried. Many understand that Jacob wanted to rest in the promised land, as a sign of his trust in God. Joseph had power in Egypt, which is why Jacob makes this request of him.

For today: think about God's promises more than the comfort of the moment. Also, when someone close to us asks us for something important before they depart, let us fulfill it faithfully and with affection.
exp.46:29:
Jacob asks Joseph that, when he dies ("lie down with my fathers" is a gentle way of saying die), Joseph carry him out of Egypt and bury him with his ancestors. "Carry me out" is a direct request: Joseph is to carry him out of Egypt. Joseph promises to do it.

Jacob, now an old man after living seventeen years in Egypt, speaks. He asks Joseph for a solemn promise, and the custom of placing the hand under the thigh when swearing an oath comes from that ancient time. Jacob wants to be buried in Canaan, the land God promised to Abraham, Isaac, and their descendants. In this way he expresses his confidence that God will fulfill that promise.

For today: Jacob thought about his end with faith, not fear. We can ask ourselves whether our decisions and words show that we trust God's promises. Also, Joseph reminds us of the importance of keeping what we promise, especially to those we love.
exp.7:10:
This verse tells that the dove returned to Noah in the evening, carrying a freshly plucked olive leaf in its beak. With that, Noah understood that the water had already receded from the earth.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks. Noah had been in the ark for many months and was waiting for a sign. He had already sent the dove out once, but it came back without finding a place to land. Now it brings a small but clear sign: life was growing again. Many see here a symbol of hope, although the text does not explain it that way.
