For today: We can thank God for our blessings without living in comparison with others. Leah sought to be recognized by the other women, but our true happiness comes from knowing that God sees us and cares for us.
exp.35:14:
This verse begins a list of the leaders who descended from Esau, also called Edom. The chiefs named here led the clans that came from Esau's family. The sons of Eliphaz, the firstborn son of Esau, are named: Teman, Omar, Zepho, Kenaz, and the list goes on in the verses that follow.

The text of Genesis has no particular speaker; it is a genealogical record from the narrator. After recounting the separation between Jacob and Esau, the book details how Esau's family grew in the land of Edom. This shows that God kept his promise to make nations also from the descendants of Esau, although the line of the promise continues through Jacob.

For today: God pays attention to people and to families, even to those who seem to stand outside the center of the story. We can trust that He keeps his word and remembers each one, and we should treat everyone with respect, knowing that they matter to Him.
exp.26:36:
Isaac tells Esau that he can no longer take back what he has done. He has made Jacob your master, the one who rules over you. He has also given all of Jacob's relatives to him as servants, so they would be placed under his authority. He assured Esau that Jacob has been supplied with grain and new wine, which stand for abundance and provision. At the end, Isaac asks with sorrow what he can now do for Esau.

Isaac is speaking as an old man, nearly blind. He had meant to bless Esau, but Jacob, with the help of their mother Rebekah, deceived him and received the blessing. Esau arrives weeping and hurt. Isaac recognizes that the blessing has already been given and cannot be given again to Esau.

For today: decisions and deceptions have consequences that hurt the whole family. Let us seek honesty and trust in God, instead of taking shortcuts that wound others.
exp.16:13:
Any male who is not circumcised, that is, who has not had the foreskin (the skin covering the tip of the member) cut away, will be cut off from his people. That means he would be separated from the community of the covenant. God gives the reason: that person has broken my covenant, meaning he has rejected or disregarded it.

God is speaking to Abraham when He confirms His covenant with him. Circumcision was the visible sign of that covenant, and it was applied to sons and to the servants of the household. Interpreters debate whether "cut off" refers to death, to exile, or to exclusion from the people. The text does not specify.

For today: God desires a faith that shows in one's life, not only in words. We can ask ourselves what concrete signs show that we belong to Him.
exp.31:28:
Jacob asks the man he wrestled with to tell him his name. The man does not give it, but answers with a question: "Why do you ask my name?" Then he blessed Jacob right there. The phrase "Please tell me your name" is a polite request, and the reply is a direct question, so the man keeps his name to himself without refusing outright.

Jacob has spent the night wrestling by the river Jabbok, before meeting his brother Esau. He has just received the name Israel. The text does not explain why the visitor does not reveal his name. Jacob later understands that he had seen God, since he calls the place Peniel. Many believe it was God himself in human form, and others see him as a divine messenger.

For today: we will not always receive all the answers we seek, but God does bless us in the middle of our struggle. We can trust in him even when some mystery is left unexplained.
exp.16:17:
Abraham speaks to God and asks, "O that Ishmael might live under Your blessing!" The words "O that" express a sincere longing. To live under God's blessing means to live under his care and favor, in a relationship with him.

God had just promised Abraham, who was already a hundred years old, a son with Sarah. Abraham laughed and doubted in his heart. Then, perhaps out of love for Ishmael, the son he already had, he asks that this son be the heir. God answers that the covenant will be with Isaac, but he also promises to bless Ishmael.

We can bring to God with confidence what worries us most, even our children and loved ones. He listens, even if his answer is not exactly what we asked for.
exp.25:21:
He moved on from there and dug another well. This time no one argued over it. That is why he named it Rehoboth, a word that suggests open, roomy places. "Quarrel" means they argued or fought. "Room" means space to live and work. "Fruitful" means they would grow and prosper.

The narrator tells what Isaac experienced in the region of Gerar. The local herdsmen disputed two wells with him, which were vital in a dry land. Isaac did not insist on fighting but kept moving on. Upon finding peace, he recognized that the LORD had made room for him. Shortly afterward, at Beersheba, the LORD confirmed His promise to him.

For today: not every battle is worth fighting. Sometimes peace and gentleness open the way for God to give us room. Trust that He can give you a wide place, and give thanks to Him when He does.
exp.19:0:
Abraham left the place where he had been living and traveled to the region of the Negev, toward the south. He settled between Kadesh and Shur, desert areas, and while he was staying in Gerar, he lived as a stranger there. "Stranger" means a foreigner, someone who lives in a place without being from there or having the same rights.

The narrator of the book speaks here, traditionally identified as Moses. This verse sets up what follows: Abraham, being a stranger and feeling vulnerable, says that Sarah is his sister. The Bible does not explain all his reasons at this point, but the account shows his insecurity. Even so, God intervenes and protects Sarah.

Today: when you find yourself living in a new or uncertain place, do not let fear carry you away. God cares for you, even when you make mistakes. Trust in Him and act with sincerity.
exp.8:16:
God tells Noah again that the rainbow in the clouds is the sign of the covenant he has made. That covenant is not only with Noah and his family, but with every creature on the earth. The word "sign" means a visible mark or reminder. A "covenant" is a solemn promise.

God speaks after the flood, when Noah and his family have just come out of the ark. God promises that he will never again destroy the earth with a flood of waters. The rainbow in the clouds serves as a reminder of that promise, and the text says that God himself will see it and remember.

For today: when you see a rainbow, or when you doubt, remember that God is faithful to what he promises. You can rest in his word, even when storms come, and thank him for his care of all he has made.
exp.35:0:
This verse opens a new section of the book with the account of Esau's descendants. The word "account" refers to the family history, the sons and grandsons who came from him. The verse also makes clear that Esau is "that is, Edom," meaning his name is also linked to the people of Edom, who came from him.

Here the narrator of Genesis is speaking, not a character. This kind of heading appears several times in the book to mark the shifts between sections. After telling the story of Jacob, the account pauses to turn to Esau, Jacob's brother. This shows that he too received a line of descendants, and that God's promise to Isaac continues through the line of Jacob.

For today: God takes into account each person and each family, even those who do not carry the main thread of the story. We can treat everyone with respect and trust that God carries out his plans faithfully.
exp.33:27:
This verse says that Jacob's sons took the Shechemites' flocks and herds and donkeys. They also took everything else in the city and in the field.

Here the narrator of the story speaks. After Shechem dishonored Dinah, Simeon and Levi killed the men of the city, and their brothers plundered the place. The Bible recounts the event without approving of it, and Jacob later rebukes them for having brought danger upon his family.

For today: even when we have suffered injustice, revenge and greed only multiply the harm. We can seek justice with honesty, leave resentment in God's hands, and take care that our pain does not lead us to make others suffer.
exp.34:17:
She says that Rachel, giving birth in great pain, was dying. With her last breath, she named her son Ben-oni, which means "son of my sorrow" (some render it "son of my affliction"). But Jacob, his father, named him Benjamin, which is commonly understood as "son of the right hand," a sign of honor and favor.

This is the account of the birth of Jacob's last son, on the way near Ephrath, which is Bethlehem. Rachel, Jacob's beloved wife, names the child out of her pain. Jacob, in the midst of his own grief, chooses to give him a name that looks forward.

Today we can learn that pain is real and deserves to be acknowledged, but it does not have to define the future. We can weep and still bless, with hope, those who come after us.
exp.46:10:
So Joseph settled his father and brothers in Egypt and gave them property in the best part of the land, the district of Rameses, just as Pharaoh had ordered. "Settled" means he set them up to live there, and "property" means land that now belonged to them.

The narrator of the book recounts how Pharaoh's promise was fulfilled. Canaan was suffering a severe famine, and Jacob's family came to Egypt looking for food. Joseph, who was already a ruler, took care of them. As for "Rameses," some scholars connect it with the region of the Nile delta, but its exact location is debated.

For today: Joseph used his position to care for his family with generosity, without resentment over the past. We can ask ourselves whom God has placed near us so that we might help them with what we have.
exp.23:29:
This verse tells us that Laban, Rebekah's brother, saw the ring and bracelets that Abraham's servant had given her. He also heard what Rebekah was telling them: "The man said this to me." Then he went out and found the man standing by the camels, near the spring.

The narrator of Genesis describes how Rebekah brought the news home. Abraham's servant was looking for a wife for Isaac, and Rebekah had welcomed him generously. Laban sees the jewelry and goes out to receive him. Some readers notice that his interest in the gifts foreshadows his character, but the text does not say this directly.

Today we can learn to welcome others well. Showing hospitality is valuable, but it is worth examining our motives: serving with sincerity, not only for what we might gain.

sum.14: God tells Abram not to be afraid, and promises him a son of his own and descendants as numerous as the stars. Abram believes, and God counts him as righteous. Then God confirms his promise with a covenant: he will give the land to Abram's descendants, though first they will spend four hundred years in a foreign land.
sum.7: God remembered Noah and all the living creatures and animals that were with him in the ark, and the waters gradually went down until the ground was dry. Noah sent out a dove, which came back with an olive leaf. Later he left the ark, and he built an altar and offered a sacrifice to God. God promised never again to curse the ground or destroy every living thing, and that the seasons would never cease.
sum.44: Joseph could no longer hold back. He revealed himself to his brothers and wept with them. He told them not to be distressed, because God had sent him ahead to save lives during the famine. Pharaoh invited the whole family to come to Egypt, and when Jacob saw the wagons, his spirit revived, and he decided to go and see his son.
sum.27: Isaac blesses Jacob and sends him to Paddan-aram to find a wife among his mother's family. On the way, Jacob dreams of a ladder that connects earth and heaven, and God renews the promise of land, descendants, and companionship. Jacob recognizes this, names the place Bethel, and vows to follow God.
sum.20: God keeps his promise: Sarah, already old, gives birth to Isaac, and Abraham circumcises him when he is eight days old. Later, Hagar and Ishmael are sent away, but God takes care of them, shows them water in the desert, and promises to make Ishmael into a great nation. At the end, Abraham makes a covenant with Abimelech at Beersheba and calls on God there.
sum.32: Jacob approaches Esau humbly, bowing down seven times, and Esau receives him with an embrace and tears. Jacob insists on giving him a gift, and afterward each of them goes on his own way. Jacob settles in Succoth and then in Shechem, where he buys a plot of land and sets up an altar to God.
sum.43: Joseph has his silver cup placed in Benjamin's sack, and then has his steward catch up with the brothers and accuse them of theft. When the cup is found, Judah offers to become a servant in Benjamin's place, so that he would not bring deep grief upon their father Jacob. In this we see a changed heart, willing to sacrifice itself for another.
sum.36: Joseph, Jacob's favorite son, is hated by his brothers because of his colorful robe and because of his dreams, in which he appears to be above them. They sell him to some merchants who take him to Egypt, and they make Jacob believe that a wild animal killed him, so Jacob mourns his son with great grief.
sum.8: God blesses Noah and his sons and permits them to eat meat, but without blood. He affirms the value of human life because we are made in his image. And with the rainbow he promises never again to destroy the earth with a flood. Afterward, Noah becomes drunk, Ham disrespects his father, and Noah pronounces a curse on Canaan and blessings on Shem and Japheth.
sum.17: The LORD visits Abraham along with three men, and he welcomes them generously. They announce that Sarah will have a son, and God asks, "Is anything too hard for the LORD?" Then God reveals to Abraham that he will judge Sodom, and Abraham intercedes with humility, asking that the city be spared if there are ten righteous people in it.
sum.24: Abraham died at the age of 175, and his sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him beside Sarah. God blessed Isaac. The twelve princes descended from Ishmael are also named. Rebekah gave birth to twins, Esau and Jacob. Esau, tired and hungry, sold his birthright to Jacob in exchange for a bowl of lentil stew, showing that he looked down on it.
sum.1: God finishes his work and blesses the seventh day as a day of rest. Then he forms the man from the dust, gives him life, and places him in the garden of Eden to take care of it, with the command not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Seeing that the man was alone, God forms the woman, and the two are united as one flesh.
sum.39: In prison, Joseph serves two of Pharaoh's officials, the cupbearer and the baker, who are downcast because of their dreams. With God's help, Joseph announces that the cupbearer will be restored to his position and the baker will be hanged, and everything comes true within three days. However, the cupbearer forgets Joseph.
sum.23: Abraham, now an old man, made his servant swear that he would find a wife for Isaac from among Abraham's own relatives, not from the Canaanites. Trusting God to guide him through a prayer and through the kindness Rebekah showed him and his camels, the servant found her. Her family recognized that this was the work of God, and Rebekah agreed to go. Isaac received her as his wife and loved her.
sum.4: Genesis 5 traces the line of descendants from Adam to Noah, showing that each one lived many years, had children, and died. Only Enoch stands out: he walked with God, and God took him. The chapter ends with Noah, whose father hoped he would bring relief from the labor on the cursed ground, and with Noah's three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
sum.10: All of humanity spoke one language. In the land of Shinar, they decided to build a city and a tower so that they could make a name for themselves and avoid being scattered. God confused their languages and scattered them, and the place was called Babel. The chapter then follows the descendants of Shem down to Terah, whose son Abram, together with his barren wife Sarai, left Ur for Canaan, but stopped at Haran.
sum.19: Abraham told people in Gerar that Sarah was his sister, out of fear, and King Abimelech took her. God warned Abimelech in a dream, and Abimelech returned her with gifts. Abraham prayed, and God healed the king's household, showing that God cares for the innocent and protects his promises even when his servant fails.
sum.49: Joseph wept over his father Jacob and buried him with great honor in Canaan, in the cave of Machpelah. Afterward, his brothers feared that Joseph would take revenge on them, but Joseph forgave them and told them that God turned the evil into good in order to save many people. When Joseph was about to die, he asked his brothers to carry his bones to the promised land.
sum.38: Joseph was sold in Egypt to Potiphar, and God blessed him until he became the overseer of all of Potiphar's household. When Potiphar's wife pursued him, Joseph refused out of loyalty to God and to his master, but she falsely accused him, and he was sent to prison. There too God was with him and gave him favor.
sum.15: Sarai, who could not have children, gave her servant Hagar to Abram. But when Hagar became pregnant, she looked down on Sarai, and Sarai treated her harshly, so Hagar fled into the desert. There the angel of the LORD found her, told her to go back, promised her many descendants, and announced the son she would bear, Ishmael, meaning "God hears." Hagar realized that God sees her.
sum.34: God tells Jacob to go back to Bethel, and Jacob asks his household to put away their foreign gods and purify themselves so they can worship. There, God confirms his new name, Israel, and his promise. Afterward, Rachel dies in childbirth as she gives birth to Benjamin, and Isaac also dies. The twelve sons of Jacob are then listed.
sum.12: Abram returned from Egypt with Lot, and because the two of them had so much livestock, their herdsmen began to quarrel. Abram, showing generosity, let Lot choose first, and Lot picked the fertile plain near Sodom. Afterward God promised Abram all the land and descendants too many to count, and Abram worshiped God in Hebron.
sum.41: Jacob sends ten of his sons to Egypt to buy grain because of the famine. There, Joseph, who is now governor, recognizes them, tests them, and keeps Simeon imprisoned until they bring Benjamin. The brothers acknowledge their guilt over what they did to Joseph, and Jacob, deeply distressed, refuses to send Benjamin.
sum.28: Jacob arrives in Haran, meets his cousin Rachel at a well, and stays with his uncle Laban. He works seven years to earn Rachel as his wife, but Laban deceives him and gives him Leah first, so Jacob works another seven years for Rachel. God sees that Leah is not loved and gives her children: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah.
sum.11: God calls Abram to leave his country and promises to make him into a great nation and to bless all the families of the earth through him. Abram obeys and arrives in Canaan, where he worships God. Because of a famine, he goes down to Egypt, and there, out of fear, he says that Sarai is his sister; God intervenes, and Pharaoh lets them go.
sum.13: Four kings defeated the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah and carried off Lot, Abram's nephew, as a prisoner. Abram armed 318 of his trained servants, rescued Lot, and recovered everything that had been taken. Melchizedek, priest of God Most High, blessed him, and Abram gave him a tenth of everything. However, Abram refused to keep the riches offered by the king of Sodom.
sum.46: Joseph presents his family before Pharaoh, and Jacob blesses him. They settle in Goshen, the best land in Egypt. During the famine, Joseph buys money, livestock, and land from the people for Pharaoh, and the people come to depend on him for their survival. Before he dies, Jacob makes Joseph swear that he will bury him in the tomb of his ancestors.
sum.31: Jacob returns to his homeland and fears the meeting with his brother Esau, who is coming with four hundred men. He prays to God for protection, reminding God of his promises, and sends gifts ahead to calm Esau. That night he wrestles with a man until dawn. He is blessed, receives the name Israel, and is left limping.
sum.26: Isaac, now old and blind, wants to give his blessing to Esau, but Rebekah and Jacob deceive him, and Jacob receives the blessing. Esau weeps, is filled with hatred, and plans to kill Jacob, so Rebekah sends Jacob far away, to Haran. The chapter shows how deception and favoritism wound a family.
sum.37: Judah moved away from his brothers, and his sons Er and Onan died because of their wickedness, leaving Tamar a widow. Judah did not keep his promise to give her his son Shelah, so Tamar disguised herself and became pregnant by him. When Judah recognized his injustice, she gave birth to Perez and Zerah.
sum.48: Jacob gathers his twelve sons and, before he dies, speaks a blessing or prophetic word over each one. He rebukes Reuben, Simeon, and Levi, and gives special promises to Judah, from whom the ruler would come, and to Joseph. He then asks them to bury him in the cave of Machpelah, beside Abraham and Isaac, and he dies.
sum.40: Pharaoh dreams of seven fat cows being eaten by seven thin ones, and of seven full ears of grain being swallowed by seven scorched, withered ones. Joseph, giving God the credit, explains that seven years of plenty will come, followed by seven years of famine. Pharaoh appoints him governor over Egypt, and Joseph stores up grain to save the people.
sum.16: God appeared to Abram when he was ninety-nine years old. He changed his name to Abraham and promised him an everlasting covenant: many descendants, the land of Canaan, and that God would be his God. As a sign of this covenant, God commanded that every male be circumcised. God also announced that Sarah would have a son, Isaac, and Abraham obeyed that very same day.
sum.45: Jacob travels to Egypt with his whole family. At Beersheba, God promises him that he will go with him, that he will make his family into a great nation, and that he will bring him back. The chapter lists the seventy descendants who entered Egypt, and it tells of the tearful reunion with Joseph, who instructs them how to present themselves to Pharaoh so that they can settle in Goshen.
sum.25: Because of the famine, Isaac stays in Gerar, where God renews the promise he made to Abraham. Although Isaac lies out of fear, God blesses him, and even amid quarrels over the wells, God gives him room and peace. In the end, Abimelech acknowledges that God is with him.
sum.0: God creates the heavens, the earth, light, the seas, the plants, the stars, and the animals over six days, and he sees that everything is good. At the end, he creates man and woman in his own image, blesses them, and gives them the job of caring for creation. Everything God made was very good.
sum.21: God tests Abraham and asks him to offer Isaac, his only son, on the mountain. Abraham obeys and trusts that God will provide, but an angel stops him, and God provides a ram in place of the boy. God renews his promise to bless Abraham and, through his descendants, all the nations.
sum.47: Jacob, now old and ill, welcomes Joseph and formally adopts Joseph's sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, as his own. When he blesses them, he places his right hand on Ephraim, the younger, even though Joseph objects, and he says that God will make both of them great. He also reminds them that God will bring them back to the land of their fathers.
sum.5: When wickedness and violence filled the earth, God grieved and decided to bring a flood to destroy it. But Noah, a righteous man who walked with God, found favor, and God told him to build an ark to save his family and the animals. Noah obeyed everything God had commanded him.
sum.6: God tells Noah to enter the ark with his family and the animals, because He saw that Noah was righteous in his generation. After seven days, the flood covers the earth and every living thing dies, except those who were in the ark. In this way we see Noah's obedience and God's care in protecting him.
sum.35: Genesis 36 lists the descendants of Esau, who was also called Edom. Because both he and Jacob had become very wealthy, Esau moved to the hill country of Seir, where the Horites already lived. His sons became chiefs and kings in Edom, which shows that God also took care of Esau and his family.
sum.42: As the famine continued and the grain ran out, Jacob agreed to send Benjamin to Egypt, because Judah promised to take responsibility for him. The brothers took gifts and double the money with them. When Joseph saw Benjamin, he welcomed them into his house and held a feast for them. Moved with emotion, he wept in private, and then he served them all, giving Benjamin a much larger portion than the others.
sum.2: The serpent deceives the woman, and she and her husband eat the forbidden fruit. They feel shame and hide from God. God questions them, announces consequences of pain and hard labor, and promises a struggle between the woman's offspring and the serpent. He clothes them with animal skins and sends them out of the garden.
sum.33: Dinah went out to visit the women of the area, and Shechem took advantage of her and violated her. Afterward he wanted to marry her. Jacob's sons answered him with deceit: they demanded that every man in the town be circumcised. On the third day, while the men were still in pain, Simeon and Levi killed all the males and plundered the city. Jacob rebuked them for the danger they had put him in, but they showed no remorse.
sum.29: In Genesis 30, Rachel and Leah compete to have children, and several sons are born to Jacob through them and their servant women. Finally, God gives Rachel a son, Joseph. Afterward, Jacob makes an agreement with Laban about his wages in sheep, and by using peeled branches, his flock grows large. The text does not explain whether those branches had any real effect.
sum.22: Sarah died at the age of one hundred and twenty-seven in Hebron, and Abraham mourned for her and wept over her. Since he was a foreigner in that land, he negotiated with the Hittites and bought from Ephron the cave of Machpelah for four hundred shekels of silver. There he buried Sarah, and in this way he gained his first piece of property of his own in Canaan.
sum.18: Two angels arrive in Sodom, and Lot welcomes them into his home, but the men of the city want to harm them. The angels bring Lot and his family out before God destroys the cities with fire and sulfur; Lot's wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt. God remembers Abraham and saves Lot.
sum.3: Cain and Abel each brought an offering to God. God looked with favor on Abel's offering but not on Cain's. God warned Cain that sin was crouching at his door and that he must master it, but Cain killed his brother. As punishment, Cain was made to live as a wanderer, yet even so God protected him. Seth was born, and people began to call on the name of the LORD.
sum.9: Genesis 10 lists the descendants of Noah's three sons (Shem, Ham, and Japheth) after the flood. It shows how their families spread out and formed nations, each with its own language and territory. It highlights Nimrod, a powerful hunter with cities such as Babel, and it reminds readers that all of humanity comes from Noah.
sum.30: God tells Jacob to return to his homeland, and he leaves secretly with his family and his possessions, while Rachel takes her father's household idols. Laban catches up with him, but God had already warned Laban in a dream, and the two of them make a covenant over a heap of stones. They part in peace, and God is witness between them.
